Biological-approach/Neuroplasticity.title: Neuroplasticity
Biological-approach/Neuroplasticity.content:
PSY Biological Maguire (2000) - Taxi Driver Study, Draganski (2004), Rosenzweig, Bennet & Diamond (1972) - Rat Study

Neuroplasticity is the brain’s ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections, strengthening existing ones, and removing unused ones in response to experience, learning, injury, or environmental demands. It demonstrates that the brain is not a fixed organ but changes dynamically across the lifespan.

Key Processes

























ProcessDefinitionDendritic branchingWhen a neuron is repeatedly stimulated, its dendrites grow in number and complexity, forming stronger connections with other neurons. Practice and learning drive this process.Synaptic pruningUnder-stimulated synaptic connections are eliminated to increase efficiency. The brain removes connections that are no longer needed: “use it or lose it.”NeurogenesisThe creation of new neurons, primarily in the hippocampus. Challenges the earlier assumption that the adult brain cannot generate new cells.Cortical remappingA brain region reallocates its function following injury or sustained new demands. One area takes over the role previously performed by a damaged or disused region.

How Neuroplasticity Works
Neural networks develop through the making and breaking of synaptic connections. When we learn something, neurons that fire together repeatedly wire together (Hebb’s rule): dendrites grow and connect, creating a new memory trace. When a connection is left unstimulated, it is pruned for efficiency.
This means neuroplasticity operates in two directions:

Growth: new experience and learning produce new synaptic connections and grey matter
Pruning: disuse causes those connections to weaken and eventually be eliminated

Both directions were demonstrated in the same study by Draganski (2004): grey matter increased after three months of juggling training, then partially decreased after training stopped.

Types of Neuroplasticity
Experience-dependent plasticity: The brain changes in response to repeated experience or skill learning. This is demonstrated by Maguire (2000) in taxi drivers and Draganski (2004) in jugglers.
Compensatory plasticity: Following brain injury, surrounding regions or the opposite hemisphere take over functions previously handled by the damaged area. This is demonstrated by cortical remapping in stroke and lesion patients.
Developmental plasticity: The brain undergoes rapid synaptic growth and pruning during childhood and adolescence as it adapts to the environment it develops in.

Linked Studies
Maguire et al. (2000) - Taxi Drivers
London taxi drivers who had memorized 25,000 streets showed significantly greater posterior hippocampal grey matter volume than non-taxi drivers on MRI. The volume correlated positively with years of taxi driving experience. Supports experience-dependent structural change in the adult brain.
Draganski et al. (2004) - Juggling
Participants who learned to juggle over three months showed increased grey matter density in the mid-temporal area (V5/MT) and left posterior intraparietal sulcus. After a three-month rest period, grey matter partially decreased, demonstrating both growth (plasticity) and pruning in the same study.
Rosenzweig, Bennett & Diamond (1972) - Rat Study
Rats raised in enriched environments (toys, social interaction) developed greater cortical thickness, more synaptic connections, and higher acetylcholinesterase activity than rats in impoverished environments. Foundational evidence that environmental stimulation drives structural brain change.
Tierney et al. - Case Study
A 37-year-old male suffered a lesion to Broca’s area in the frontal lobe, impairing speech production. Over time, adjacent areas reorganized to compensate, demonstrating cortical remapping following injury.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsConvergent evidence: human MRI studies (Maguire, Draganski) and animal studies (Rosenzweig) all support structural brain change through experienceCausality: Maguire’s quasi-experimental design cannot confirm that navigation caused hippocampal growth; pre-existing differences in hippocampal size may attract people to become taxi driversObjective measures (MRI, grey matter density, cortical thickness) reduce self-report biasGeneralisability: findings from specific skills (juggling, navigation) may not apply to all types of learningDraganski (2004) demonstrates both plasticity and pruning in the same study using a controlled experimental designAnimal research (Rosenzweig): enriched lab environments may not map directly onto human cognitive environmentsNeuroplasticity has major practical applications: rehabilitation after stroke, educational practice, cognitive trainingIndividual differences in baseline neuroplasticity are not fully accounted forChallenges the once-dominant view that the adult brain is fixed and cannot changeThe mechanisms underlying structural change (exactly how experience produces grey matter increase) are not fully understood

IB Exam Relevance





























QuestionBest approach”Explain neuroplasticity with reference to one study”Maguire (2000) or Draganski (2004): define neuroplasticity, describe study in APPR format, link hippocampal/grey matter changes to the definition”Explain neural pruning with reference to one study”Draganski (2004): grey matter partially decreased after training stopped, demonstrating pruning specifically”Explain the formation of neural networks with reference to one study”Draganski (2004) or Rosenzweig: new connections form through repeated stimulation and dendritic branching”Evaluate the use of brain imaging in psychological research”Maguire (MRI/VBM) + Draganski (MRI/VBM): objective, non-invasive, but expensive and limited by quasi-experimental design”Discuss neuroplasticity” (ERQ)Maguire + Draganski as primary studies; Rosenzweig as supporting animal evidence; evaluate quasi-experimental limitations and convergent validity


Key Concept - Use It or Lose It:
Neuroplasticity is bidirectional. The brain grows new connections in response to learning and sustained stimulation, and prunes connections that fall into disuse. Draganski (2004) is the most elegant demonstration of this: both growth and pruning were observed in the same participants within the same six-month study. This has direct implications for education, rehabilitation, and understanding how both enrichment and deprivation shape the developing brain.

Biological-approach/Neurotransmission.title: Neurotransmission
Biological-approach/Neurotransmission.content:
PSY BIO Biological

Neurotransmission is the biological process by which neurons communicate with each other using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. It is the foundation of almost all behaviour, cognition, and emotion. Understanding it is essential for the Biological Approach in IB Psychology.

The Two Messaging Systems
The body uses two systems to send internal messages:


























SystemSpeedMediumPathwayRangeEndocrine systemSlowHormonesBloodstreamDistal (whole body)Nervous systemFastElectrochemical signalsNeurons and synapsesLocal and central
The nervous system divides into:

Central Nervous System (CNS): brain, brainstem, and spinal cord
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): motor and sensory neurons connecting body to brain


Structure of a Neuron

Neurons are the basic unit of the nervous system. They transmit signals both electrically (within the cell) and chemically (between cells).

































PartFunctionCell body (soma)Contains the nucleus; processes incoming signalsDendritesBranch-like extensions that receive signals from other neuronsAxonLong fibre that carries the electrical signal away from the cell bodyMyelin sheathFatty coating that insulates the axon and speeds up signal transmissionTerminal buttonsTips of the axon that release neurotransmitters into the synapseSynapseThe gap between two neurons where chemical communication occurs

How Neurotransmission Works

An electrical impulse (action potential) travels down the axon to the terminal buttons.
The terminal buttons release neurotransmitters into the synaptic gap.
Neurotransmitters bind to receptor sites on the dendrites of the next (post-synaptic) neuron.
The signal is either excitatory (making the next neuron more likely to fire) or inhibitory (making it less likely to fire).
Leftover neurotransmitters are broken down by enzymes or reabsorbed by the sending neuron through reuptake.


If neurotransmitters are blocked, depleted, or altered, the message changes, affecting behaviour, mood, cognition, or physical function.


Key Neurotransmitters
Acetylcholine (ACh)
Primary role: Memory, learning, muscle movement, and attention.

Found in high concentrations in the hippocampus, the brain region central to memory encoding.
Low ACh activity is associated with Alzheimer’s disease (significant hippocampal ACh depletion).
Agonists (increase ACh activity): Physostigmine (blocks the enzyme that breaks it down)
Antagonists (block ACh activity): Scopolamine (blocks muscarinic receptors)

Relevant studies:

Martinez & Kesner: Pharmacological manipulation of ACh in rats confirmed a causal role in spatial memory.
Rogers and Kesner: Direct hippocampal ACh blockade impaired spatial memory encoding specifically.
Antonova et al (2011): Human fMRI study showed scopolamine reduces hippocampal activation during spatial navigation.


Noradrenaline (Norepinephrine)
Primary role: Alertness, arousal, attention, and mood regulation. Also involved in the stress response (fight-or-flight).

Produced mainly in the locus coeruleus (brainstem region).
Low noradrenaline is associated with depression and reduced motivation.
High noradrenaline increases alertness and heart rate (part of sympathetic nervous system activation).
SNRIs (serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors) are a class of antidepressants that work by increasing noradrenaline and serotonin at synapses.

Relevant study:

Jarowsky et al: Pharmacologically reducing noradrenaline in healthy participants induced significant depressive symptoms, providing direct causal evidence for the catecholamine hypothesis.


Dopamine
Primary role: Reward, motivation, pleasure, and movement.

Central to the mesolimbic reward pathway (nucleus accumbens, VTA).
Excess dopamine in certain brain regions is associated with schizophrenia (dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia).
Depleted dopamine in the motor regions (substantia nigra) causes Parkinson’s disease.
Plays a key role in romantic love and addiction (see Fisher et al 2005).


Serotonin
Primary role: Mood regulation, sleep, appetite, and emotional stability.

Mostly produced in the raphe nuclei (brainstem).
Low serotonin is associated with depression, anxiety, and OCD.
SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, e.g., fluoxetine/Prozac) prevent serotonin from being reabsorbed, increasing its availability at synapses.
Marazziti et al. (1999) found serotonin levels in new romantic partners resembled those found in OCD patients, suggesting obsessive early-love thinking has a neurochemical basis.


Summary Table: Neurotransmitters & Behaviour



































NeurotransmitterAssociated WithDeficit Linked ToExcess Linked ToAcetylcholine (ACh)Memory, learning, muscle controlMemory impairment, Alzheimer’sMuscle overstimulationNoradrenalineAlertness, arousal, stress responseDepression, fatigueAnxiety, high blood pressureDopamineReward, motivation, movementParkinson’s, low motivationSchizophreniaSerotoninMood, sleep, appetiteDepression, anxiety, OCDSerotonin syndrome (rare)

Research Methods in Neurotransmission Research
Researchers use several methods to study neurotransmitters:






























MethodHow it worksExamplePharmacological manipulationAdminister drugs that act as agonists or antagonists to increase or block NT activityMartinez & Kesner (physostigmine/scopolamine in rats)Brain imaging (fMRI, PET)Measure brain activity during tasks; PET can track glucose metabolism; fMRI measures blood oxygenationAntonova et al. (fMRI + scopolamine); Raine et al. (PET scans)Animal studiesInvasive manipulation of NT levels or receptor sites; allows direct causal testingRogers & Kesner (hippocampal ACh blockade in rats)Double-blind experimentsAdminister NT-altering drugs to human participants under controlled conditionsJarowsky et al. (noradrenaline depletion)

Linked Studies



































StudyNeurotransmitterKey FindingMartinez & KesnerAChIncreasing ACh improved spatial memory in rats; decreasing it impaired itRogers and KesnerACh (hippocampus)Blocking hippocampal ACh specifically impaired memory encodingAntonova et al (2011)AChScopolamine reduced hippocampal activation and spatial memory in humansJarowsky et alNoradrenalineDepleting noradrenaline induced depressive symptoms in healthy participantsRaine et al. (1997)Brain activity (glucose metabolism)Murderers showed reduced PFC activity; links NT dysfunction to violent behaviour

IB Exam Relevance
Common SAQ prompts:

“Explain the role of neurotransmitters in human behaviour.”
“Describe one study related to neurotransmission.”
“Explain how one neurotransmitter influences behaviour.”

Common ERQ prompts:

“Discuss the relationship between neurotransmission and behaviour.”
“Evaluate research into the role of neurotransmitters in one behaviour.”
“To what extent do biological factors explain [depression / aggression / memory]?”

For SAQs: Pick one neurotransmitter (ACh or noradrenaline), define it, and describe one study fully in APPR format.
For ERQs: Use two studies (e.g., Martinez & Kesner + Antonova for ACh; or Jarowsky for noradrenaline), evaluate their methods individually, then add holistic CT on issues like animal research generalizability, ethical concerns with drug studies, or reductionism.


Key Concept - Neurotransmission & Behaviour:
Behaviour is not simply the product of conscious choice but of electrochemical communication between billions of neurons. When neurotransmitters are altered, through drugs, disease, or environmental factors, behaviour changes in predictable and measurable ways. This is why neurotransmission is foundational to the biological explanation of behaviour: it provides a mechanistic, falsifiable account of how the brain produces thought, emotion, and action.

Cognitive-approach/Dual-Processing-Model.title: Dual Processing Model (Systems 1 &2)
Cognitive-approach/Dual-Processing-Model.content:
PSY cognitive

The Dual Processing Model argues that there are two ways in which we make decisions:
- System 1 thinking: Reliant on past information and schema to make quick and effortless decisions based on limited information. 
- System 2 thinking: Much more effortful and requires conscious reasoning.
When we use System 1 thinking we tend to use Heuristics - Schema Theory.  One example of a heuristic is “anchoring bias.”

Cognitive-approach/Emotion-in-Memory.title: Emotion in Memory
Cognitive-approach/Emotion-in-Memory.content:
PSY cognitive Biological
Flashbulb Memory, Memory, Hormones In Human Behaviour

Emotions are rich and diverse, and they clearly affect how we remember things. Some memories feel permanent and photographic while others fade quickly. The key variable appears to be emotional significance: we tend to remember better those experiences that involve strong emotion. This topic examines why, and whether emotionally charged memories are truly more accurate or simply feel that way.

The Core Question
Does emotion enhance memory, distort it, or both?
The evidence suggests the answer is: both, depending on context. Emotion reliably enhances the vividness and confidence of a memory. Whether it also enhances accuracy is more contested and depends heavily on the nature of the emotional event and the method used to study it.

Flashbulb Memory Theory (Brown & Kulik, 1977)
Flashbulb Memory (FBM) is the theory that emotionally significant and surprising public events produce an unusually vivid, detailed, and lasting memory of the circumstances in which a person heard the news (not of the event itself).
Brown & Kulik proposed two key conditions for FBM formation:

Surprise (the event is unexpected)
Consequentiality (the event matters personally or nationally)

When both are present, they argued a “Now Print!” neurological mechanism is triggered, essentially photographing the moment in memory.
Criteria for a memory to qualify as a FBM:

Personal context (where you were, what you were doing)
Emotional impact
Vividness and detail
Long-lasting
Public or shared element
Strengthened by repeated rehearsal (retelling the story)


Note: FBM is a theory about the circumstances surrounding a shocking event, not about memory for the event itself.


The Biological Mechanism: Adrenaline and the Amygdala
The “Now Print!” mechanism Brown & Kulik proposed has since been given a neurobiological explanation through the work of McGaugh, Cahill, and Sharot.
How it works:

An emotionally significant event triggers the release of adrenaline (epinephrine) from the adrenal glands.
Adrenaline activates the amygdala (the brain’s emotional processing centre).
The amygdala then modulates the hippocampus, strengthening the encoding of the memory into long-term storage.
The result is a memory that is more vivid, more detailed, and more resistant to forgetting than a neutral memory encoded under normal conditions.

This process is called emotional memory consolidation.
McGaugh & Cahill (1995) provided direct causal evidence for this mechanism. In a double-blind placebo-controlled experiment, participants who received propranolol (a beta-blocker that blocks adrenaline) showed no memory enhancement for emotionally arousing story content, while the placebo group remembered the emotional section significantly better. This isolates adrenaline as the key biological variable.
Sharot et al. (2007) provided neuroimaging support. Using fMRI, they showed that 9/11 memories activated the amygdala more strongly than control memories, and that this activation correlated with the vividness and confidence of the memory. Greater proximity to Ground Zero produced greater amygdala activation, suggesting a dose-response relationship between emotional intensity and biological encoding.

Are Flashbulb Memories Accurate?
This is the central critical debate in this topic. The evidence is genuinely divided.
The case that FBMs are accurate
Yuille & Cutshall (1986) studied 13 witnesses to a real armed robbery in Vancouver. When re-interviewed 4-5 months later, their memories were remarkably accurate compared to original police transcripts. Misleading questions had almost no effect, and witnesses who reported higher stress during the event showed greater accuracy, not less.
This supports the idea that real emotional events produce robust, resistant memories, and challenges the assumption (from lab studies like Loftus & Palmer) that emotion impairs accuracy.
The case that FBMs are not reliably accurate
Neisser & Harsch (1992) tested this directly. The morning after the Challenger disaster, students completed a questionnaire about where they were and what they were doing. 2.5 years later, the same students answered the same questionnaire again. Accuracy was very low (average 4.7/7), with 25% scoring 0-2. Crucially, participants showed high confidence in their inaccurate memories, and several refused to believe their original account when shown it.
This reveals a critical dissociation: emotional significance increases confidence and vividness but does not guarantee accuracy. The memory feels like a photograph but is still reconstructive.
Reconciling the two positions

























Yuille & Cutshall (1986)Neisser & Harsch (1992)Event typeReal, personally experienced traumaNationally significant but personally distantProximityDirectly involved witnessesStudents who watched on TVResultHigh accuracyLow accuracy, high confidence
The key variable appears to be personal proximity and direct emotional involvement. Sharot et al. (2007) supports this: only participants near Ground Zero formed strong FBMs. Hearing about an event second-hand, even a shocking one, may not trigger the full adrenaline-amygdala mechanism that produces genuinely enhanced encoding.

Reliability of Flashbulb Memory as a Concept
Brown & Kulik’s original claims have been challenged on several grounds:

The study was retrospective: memories were not measured at the time, so there is no baseline for accuracy.
It relied on self-report, with no way to verify what participants actually remembered at the time.
The “Now Print!” mechanism is theoretically speculative: Brown & Kulik proposed it before neuroimaging evidence existed.
It cannot control for rehearsal: FBMs may feel vivid not because of a special encoding mechanism, but because we retell and revisit them frequently.
Social desirability: participants may report more confidence and detail to avoid appearing to have forgotten something they “should” remember.

What the evidence collectively supports:
Emotion does reliably influence memory, but the mechanism is more nuanced than a simple on/off “special” system. The amygdala and adrenaline play a genuine biological role (McGaugh & Cahill; Sharot). However, this enhanced encoding does not make memories immune to distortion (Neisser & Harsch). The confidence we feel in FBMs is not a reliable guide to their accuracy.

IB Exam Relevance
SAQ questions this topic answers:

Explain one study of the influence of emotion on one cognitive process (Brown & Kulik or McGaugh & Cahill)
Explain one ethical consideration in one study of the effect of emotion on cognition (McGaugh & Cahill: drug administration to healthy participants)
Explain the use of one research method in one study of the effect of emotion on cognition (McGaugh & Cahill: double-blind experiment; or Sharot: fMRI correlational study)

ERQ questions this topic answers:

Discuss/Evaluate the role of emotion on one cognitive process
Discuss/Evaluate research into FBM
Discuss one theory of how emotion affects one cognitive process

For SAQs: Use McGaugh & Cahill (1995) as your primary study. It is a true double-blind experiment with a clear causal mechanism, directly linking adrenaline to memory enhancement in humans.
For ERQs: Lead with McGaugh & Cahill (1995), evaluate its methodology specifically (double-blind strength, low ecological validity, drug ethics). Then bring in Sharot et al. (2007) for neuroimaging convergent validity. For holistic CT, use Neisser & Harsch (1992) to challenge whether enhanced encoding actually means enhanced accuracy, and raise the rehearsal confound as a limitation of the FBM literature as a whole.

Key Terms









































TermDefinitionFlashbulb Memory (FBM)An unusually vivid and long-lasting memory for the circumstances in which a person learned of a shocking event”Now Print!” mechanismBrown & Kulik’s proposed neurological trigger for FBM; activated by surprise and consequentialityEmotional memory consolidationThe strengthening of memory encoding through adrenaline-amygdala activation during emotional arousalAmygdalaBrain structure central to emotional processing; modulates hippocampal encoding during emotional eventsAdrenaline (epinephrine)Hormone released during emotional arousal; activates amygdala and strengthens memory encodingPropranololBeta-blocker that blocks adrenaline receptors; used by McGaugh & Cahill to pharmacologically eliminate emotional memory enhancementRehearsalRepeated retelling or recall of a memory; may explain the persistence of FBMs without requiring a special biological mechanismMetacognitive failureNeisser & Harsch’s finding that participants were confidently wrong: high confidence in an inaccurate memory

Linked Studies

































StudyRole in this topicBrown & Kulik (1977) - JFK and MLKFounding theory of FBM; “Now Print!” mechanism; personal relevance and raceMcGaugh & Cahill (1995)Causal evidence for adrenaline’s role in emotional memory consolidation; double-blindSharot et al (2007) - 911fMRI evidence for amygdala activation; proximity and FBM strength; biological supportNeisser & Harsch (1992) - Space Challenger DisasterChallenges FBM accuracy; vividness does not equal correctness; metacognitive failureYuille & Cutshall (1986) - Gun shop robberySupports accuracy of real-life emotional memories; stress enhances, not impairs, recallKulkofsky et al (2011)Cultural dimension of FBM; social sharing in collectivist cultures strengthens emotional memories

Cognitive-approach/Heuristics---Schema-T.title: Heuristics - Schema Theory
Cognitive-approach/Heuristics---Schema-T.content:
PSY cognitive Memory, Thinking and Decision Making, Reconstructive Memory

This note covers two closely related cognitive concepts: Schema Theory and Heuristics. Both explain how the brain processes information efficiently, and both have implications for memory, decision-making, and the reliability of cognitive processes.

Schema Theory
What is a Schema?
A schema is a mental representation of knowledge derived from prior experience, stored in the brain to help organise information, guide behaviour, assist recall, and make sense of new experiences.
Schemas are not passive storage systems. Humans are active information processors: the brain constantly integrates new incoming information (bottom-up, from the senses) with existing knowledge (top-down, from schemas). When information is missing, the brain fills in the gaps based on what schemas predict should be there, which frequently leads to distortions and errors.

Key functions of schemas:

Speed up perception, memory, and decision-making
Help predict what to expect based on past experience
Allow the brain to handle complexity without processing everything from scratch



Types of Schemas

























TypeDescriptionExampleSocial schemasKnowledge about the world, groups, and social situationsExpectations about how a doctor’s appointment will goSelf-schemasKnowledge and beliefs about oneself”I am good at maths”ScriptsLearned sequences of behaviour appropriate to specific situationsKnowing how to behave in a restaurant without being told
Scripts are particularly important: they are patterns of behaviour learned through interaction with the environment and are developed within a cultural context, meaning they are not universal across societies.

How Schemas are Created and Updated




















ProcessWhat happensWhen it occursAssimilationNew information is absorbed into an existing schema without changing itWhen new information fits well with what we already knowAccommodationA new schema is created or an existing one is significantly restructuredWhen new information cannot fit into any existing schema

Schemas and Memory
Schemas have a direct influence on what we remember and how accurately we remember it. Because memory is reconstructive (Bartlett, 1932), schemas act as a scaffold during recall: we remember the gist and fill in the rest based on what our schema tells us should have been there.
This produces predictable distortions:

Schema-congruent information (fitting the schema) is more likely to be remembered, but also more likely to be falsely recalled when it was not actually present.
Schema-incongruent information (not fitting the schema) is more likely to be forgotten or distorted to fit.
Schemas can lead to over-generalisations, including stereotypes, when assumptions based on prior experience are applied too broadly to new people or situations.

Linked studies:

Bartlett (1932) - War of Ghosts: Cultural schemas led British participants to distort an unfamiliar Native American folk tale through levelling, sharpening, and rationalisation.
Brewer & Treyers (1981): Participants recalled schema-congruent objects from an office as present even when they were not, while schema-incongruent objects were more likely to be forgotten or distorted.
Loftus & Palmer (1974) - Car collision: Post-event information (the verb used in a question) activated a schema of a more severe accident, leading to false memory of broken glass.


Heuristics
What is a Heuristic?
A heuristic is a mental shortcut: a simple rule or strategy that focuses on one aspect of a complex problem and ignores others, allowing faster judgements with less cognitive effort.
Heuristics are a type of schema-based processing. Rather than analysing all available information systematically (System 2 thinking), the brain defaults to fast, pattern-matching shortcuts (System 1 thinking).

Why We Use Heuristics: Cognitive Miserliness
Humans are cognitive misers: we tend to avoid deep processing when it is not strictly necessary, in order to conserve cognitive resources. This tendency arises from three factors:

Knowledge: we already have schemas that can provide a quick answer
Motivation: we often lack the desire to invest effort in a thorough analysis
Economy: deep processing is slow and cognitively expensive

The result is a trade-off: heuristics allow faster, more efficient thinking, but at the cost of accuracy and susceptibility to systematic errors (cognitive biases).

Key Heuristics
Anchoring bias (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974): the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of numerical information encountered (the anchor) when making subsequent judgements, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant.
Representativeness heuristic (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983): judging the probability of something by how closely it resembles a prototype or stereotype, ignoring statistical base rates. Produces the conjunction fallacy.
Availability heuristic: estimating the likelihood of an event based on how easily examples come to mind, which tends to overweight dramatic or recent events.
Illusory correlation (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976): perceiving a relationship between two variables (e.g., minority group membership and negative behaviour) when no such relationship exists, because both are distinctive and thus cognitively salient.

Mnemonics
Mnemonics are a positive application of heuristic processing: they use schemas and associations to encode information more efficiently.
Common techniques include:

Music, rhythm, and rhyme: exploiting the phonological loop and pattern recognition
Acronyms and chunking: grouping information into fewer, more memorable units (cf. Miller’s Magic Number 7)
Method of loci: associating information with specific locations in a mentally visualised space (e.g., the “memory palace” technique)


IB Exam Relevance

























Question typeRelevant content”Explain schema theory with reference to one study”Define schema; describe types and functions; use Bartlett or Brewer & Treyens”Explain one bias in thinking and decision-making”Define heuristics; describe anchoring bias; use Tversky & Kahneman (1974) or Englich & Mussweiler”Discuss the reliability of one cognitive process”Use schema distortions and heuristic errors to argue memory and judgement are unreliable”Explain one theory of the formation of stereotypes”Use illusory correlation (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) as a heuristic-based explanation


Key Concept - The Overlap between Schemas and Heuristics:
Both schemas and heuristics reflect the same underlying principle: the brain prioritises speed and efficiency over accuracy. Schemas provide ready-made frameworks for interpreting new information; heuristics provide ready-made rules for making decisions. Both are highly adaptive in most everyday situations, but both produce predictable, systematic errors when the shortcuts do not match the demands of the task. This is why the study of cognitive biases is, at its core, the study of what happens when efficient mental shortcuts go wrong.

Cognitive-approach/Multi-Store-Model-of-.title: Multi-Store Model of Memory (MSM)
Cognitive-approach/Multi-Store-Model-of-.content:
PSY   Memory

Transclude of Memory

In psychology a model of memory is a hypothesized representation of representation of memory. Sort of an outline of how and ‘where’ different stores and processes work according to the most actual evidence. Hence, models change over time.


This model was first proposed by Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968)
Although the model is rather simplistic, they were the first to suggest a basic structure for memory, and sparked much research based on the idea that humans are information processors.
Assumptions The model is clearly inspired by Computer Science. And is based in multiple assumptions.
- The model argues that memory consists of a number of separate locations where information is stored.
- Memory processes are sequential
- Each memory story operates in a single, uniform way. 
___
In this model Short-term Memory (STM) serves as a gateway for information to get to Long-term Memory (LTM). The various memory stores are seen as components that operate in conjunction with the permanent memory store (LTM) through processes such as attention, coding, and rehearsal.


                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

You need to pay attention in order to remember information.


The Model Suggest that information enters the brain through Sensory Memory. Which is modality specific (meaning it is related and dependent to different senses such as hearing and vision). The most important stores in the model are the visual store and the auditory store.


                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

Sensory store has limited capacity and duration,  information only stays here for a few seconds and a very small amount of information goes to STM


The capacity of the STM is believed limited. Initially Miller’s Magic Number 7 (1956) suggested that limit was around 7+/- 2 items and duration was predicted to be normally around 6 to 18 seconds. However rehearsal could facilitate the information to stay for up to 30s in the STM, before being displaced.
The LTM store is conceptualized as a vast storehouse of information, with unknown/indefinite capacity and duration. The information is not stored as a replica of the events or facts but rather as an outline, which means memory can be distorted when retrieved, as we fill in the gaps, as predicted in Heuristics - Schema Theory.

Evidence for this model

HM (Milner, 1996): Provides evidence on how STM and LTM are located in different stores in the brain.
Glanzer and Cunitz (1966): Used an interference task to prove there are two processes involved in retrieving information. Studied Primacy effect and Recency effect.


Studies that support this model:

Miller’s Magic Number 7 (1956)
HM (Milner, 1996)
Glanzer and Cunitz (1966)
Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968)


Strengths of the MSM

There is significant research to support the theory of separate memory stores - both in experimental research and biological case studies of patients with brain damage.
The model is of historical importance. It gave psychologists a way to talk about memory and much of the research which followed was based on this model.

Limitations of the MSM

The model is over-simplified. It assumes that each of the stores works as an independent unit.
The model does not explain memory distortion.
The model does not explain why some things may be learned with a minimal amount of rehearsal. For example, once bitten by a dog, that memory is quite vivid in spite of the lack of rehearsal.
There are several times that we rehearse a lot to remember information and it is not transferred to LTM.

Cognitive-approach/Reconstructive-Memory.title: Reconstructive Memory
Cognitive-approach/Reconstructive-Memory.content:
PSY cognitive Heuristics - Schema Theory, Memory, Thinking and Decision Making

Reconstructive memory is the theory that memories are not stored as complete, fixed recordings in the brain. Instead, every time we remember something, we actively reconstruct it from fragments of stored information, filling in gaps using schemas, expectations, and post-event information. This process makes memory flexible and efficient, but also fundamentally unreliable.
The concept was first systematically demonstrated by Bartlett (1932), who argued that memory is an active, meaning-making process rather than a passive playback system.

Core Principle
When we encode an experience, we do not store every detail. We store a gist shaped by our existing schemas. When we later recall it, we reconstruct the event by combining what was actually stored with what our schemas tell us should have been there. This means:

Memory is always influenced by prior knowledge (schemas)
Memory can be altered by post-event information (misinformation effect)
Memory can be influenced by the way questions are asked (leading questions)
Entirely false memories can be created through suggestion


Key Processes and Phenomena
Schema-Driven Distortion
Schemas act as a scaffold during recall. Information that fits our schemas is more likely to be remembered (and falsely recalled if absent), while schema-incongruent information is more likely to be forgotten or distorted to fit.
Bartlett (1932) identified three specific distortion processes in serial reproduction of an unfamiliar story:





















ProcessWhat happensLevellingThe memory becomes shorter; unfamiliar or incongruent details are omittedSharpeningCertain details are emphasised and become more prominent over timeRationalisationUnfamiliar or supernatural elements are reinterpreted to fit existing cultural schemas
Post-Event Misinformation
Information encountered after an event can be incorporated into the memory of that event without the person noticing. This is known as the misinformation effect.
Loftus & Palmer (1974) demonstrated that changing a single verb in a post-event question (“smashed” vs. “contacted”) altered both speed estimates and created false memories of broken glass that was never present in the original film.
False Memory Implantation
Entirely fabricated events can be implanted as genuine memories through repeated suggestion over time. Loftus & Pickrell (1995) showed that 25% of participants came to “remember” a childhood event (getting lost in a shopping mall) that had been confirmed by family members to have never occurred.
Shaw (2015) extended this further, showing that false memories of having committed a crime can be implanted in healthy adults through repeated interview techniques.
Confidence vs. Accuracy
A critical finding across reconstructive memory research is that confidence does not predict accuracy. People can hold vivid, highly confident memories that are substantially or entirely wrong.
Neisser & Harsch (1992) found that fewer than 10% of participants gave fully accurate accounts of how they heard about the Challenger disaster 2.5 years after the event, yet participants showed high confidence in their incorrect memories and sometimes refused to accept their original written accounts as genuine.
Weapons Focus / Tunnel Vision
When a threatening object such as a weapon is present during an event, attention narrows to that object, reducing encoding of peripheral details. This is sometimes called the weapons focus effect and is a specific form of the broader influence of emotional arousal and cognitive load on encoding.
Attentional Blindness
When cognitive resources are consumed by one task (high cognitive load), people fail to notice other events entirely, even prominent ones. This limits what gets encoded in the first place, creating gaps that reconstruction later fills.

Linked Studies

































StudyKey contributionBartlett (1932) - War of GhostsFirst systematic demonstration of schema-driven distortion; levelling, sharpening, rationalisationLoftus & Palmer (1974) - Car collisionPost-event verbal information alters speed estimates and creates false memoriesLoftus & Pickrell (1995) - Lost in a mallEntirely false autobiographical memories can be implanted through suggestionNeisser & Harsch (1992) - Space Challenger DisasterFlashbulb memories are not reliably accurate despite high confidenceBrewer & Treyers (1981)Schema-congruent objects falsely recalled; schema-incongruent objects forgotten or distortedYuille & Cutshall (1986) - Gun shop robberyReal-life eyewitness memories can be highly accurate; challenges lab-based findings

Strengths and Limitations of the Reconstructive Memory Framework

























StrengthsLimitationsSupported by a large and consistent body of experimental researchMuch of the evidence comes from artificial lab tasks; real-world memory may be more robust (cf. Yuille & Cutshall)Has significant real-world applications: eyewitness testimony, therapy, police interviewsDoes not fully explain why some memories (especially for highly emotional events) are highly accurateExplains why memory errors are systematic rather than randomThe role of individual differences in susceptibility to false memories is underexploredChallenges the intuitive view of memory as a recording deviceEthical concerns around research that deliberately implants false memories or distresses participants

Key Concept - Reconstructive Memory:
Memory is not a camera. It is a reconstruction: every recall is an active process of piecing together stored fragments with schema-based inferences. This is why two people who experience the same event remember it differently, why leading questions alter testimony, and why entirely false memories feel just as real as genuine ones. The reliability problem is not a flaw in the system; it is an inherent consequence of how memory is designed to work.

Cognitive-approach/WMM/Central-Executive.title: Central Executive
Cognitive-approach/WMM/Central-Executive.content:
Working Memory Model



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Think of the movie Inside out.


The central executive works as an attention direction and control system, that is supervises and monitors operations of the sub-systems of processing and storage. Can be thought of as the one to decide how and when the sub-systems are used.
The central executive is thought to have the capacity to focus attention, divide attention between two or more sources, and switch attention from one task to another.
The central executive has limited Capacity. Meaning you cannot attend to a lot of things at the same time. Additionally, it is also modality free. Therefore, it can process any sensory information, whether it be auditory or visual.

Attention Control:
Attention control was proposed by Baddeley & Hitch (1974), as the primary function of the central executive.
Attention control happens in two different levels:


The Automatic Level: Control of habitual or routinary activities that relay on Schemas (Heuristics - Schema Theory). These are controlled more or less automatically or can be considered “sub-conscious”, although not necessarily. Requiere limited amount of attention. (e.g. Cycling to school)


The Supervisory attention Level: Controls planning and decision-making. Creates new strategies, schemas and “outlines” for the Automatic level when the old ones are no longer sufficient. It is also the one used for Emergency situations and situations that require Self-regulation. Is capable of comparing alternative courses of action and choosing the most beneficial one.




                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

People are highly reliant on automatic processing for everyday things

Cognitive-approach/WMM/Phonological-Loop.title: Phonological Loop (verbal STM)
Cognitive-approach/WMM/Phonological-Loop.content:
Working Memory Model



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Think of it as your “Inner Voice” and “Inner Ear”


Phonological loop is the auditory component of the STM  and its divided into two sub-components.

The articulatory control system: Inner voice. Holds information in verbal form. Articulatory loop is also believed to hold words ready for cognitive tasks (e.g. when preparing to speak).
The Phonological Store: Inner ear. Holds auditory memory traces. Can receive direct information from sensory memory in the form of auditory material, from the LTM in the form of Verbal Information, and from the articulatory control system.



                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

Research shows that a memory trace can only last from 1.5 to 2 seconds if it is not rehearsed by the articulatory control system.

Cognitive-approach/WMM/The-Episodic-Buff.title: The Episodic Buffer
Cognitive-approach/WMM/The-Episodic-Buff.content:
Working Memory Model



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Think of it as a temporary hold for information, to maintain it accesible while another process takes place. Can be compared to the “hold” option when you are in a phone call and someone else calls.


The episodic buffer is the one that allows us to understand the world around us. While all information is being processed in separate STM stores, This Buffer, temporarily holds several sources of information active at once. While you, or your central executive decide what is needed and what requires your attention at the moment.
It can hold active auditory and Visual information as well as information / “memory traces”  or memory “outlines” from LTM, at the same time.
Baddeley & Hitch (1974) proposed the buffer as a temporary and passive display store until the information is needed, responsible for Conscious awareness. Additionally, argued that it has a limited capacity explaining why we cannot multi-task.

Cognitive-approach/WMM/Visuospatial-Sket.title: Visuospatial Sketchpad
Cognitive-approach/WMM/Visuospatial-Sket.content:
Working Memory Model



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Think of it as your “Inner Eye”



The Visuospatial Sketchpad is the Visual component of the STM. Work as a temporary store for visual and spatial information.
Can receive information either from Sensory Memory or Long-Term Memory stores

Visual processing includes the storage and manipulation of patterns and movements in two or three dimensions, and it is crucial for localization and orientation as well as for coordination.
Holds information of What, where and How. What visual information is relevant, where in space is it and how is it located, shaped, placed or how to navigate it.


                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

Is used for example, to find our way around our house and remember where we’ve left things and what those things look like.

Exam-notes/Description-of-Key-Terms.title: Description of Key Terms
Exam-notes/Description-of-Key-Terms.content:
PSY

Heuristics - Schema Theory:

Schemas are mental representations of knowledge derived from previous experience and knowledge that are stored in the brain. Schemas are used to speed up responses in daily activities.

Network or knowledge, beliefs and expectations
Influence on: Perception, Decision making (DM) and Memory


Heuristics (often used in DM or judgment formation as a ‘rule’), are mental shortcuts that involve focusing on one aspect of a complex problem and ignoring others

Cognitive Misery: We tend to use heuristics because of 3 factors;
Knowledge, motivation and economy.
we make the choice not to actively process information to save time and effort.
Avoid deep processing (usually in mundane/routine tasks) → save cognitive resources.
Cognitive Dissonance:
Real psychological discomfort experienced when holding conflicting beliefs with regards to attitudes.
Often when inconsistencies present between someones behaviour and beliefs leading to them changing either one to eliminate discomfort.
e.g., behaviour is conflicting with beliefs
1. change beliefs to justify behavior
2. change behavior to fit behaviour
Conformity: “Social animals with a basic need to belong”
When an individual adapts their behaviour to be in line with others.
Often determined by social comparison and normative social influence.
Social Identity Theory:
(Influence of a group membership on self-concept and behaviour)
A person has not just one “personal self” but, rather several social selves that correspond to group memberships.
SIT predicts that when one of our social identities becomes salient, it will have an influence on our behaviour.
Localization of function:
Theory that specific parts of the brain are responsible for specific behaviors or cognitive processes.
Neuroplasticity:
(High stimuli & learning opportunities increase density of neural connections)
Our brain’s ability to make new connections,  pathways, and change how its circuits are wired to adapt to environmental/body changes/demands.
- Dendric Branching: When we learn something, neurons connect to make a new ‘trace’ in the brain. Dendrites grow in number and connect with other neurons.
- Synaptic Pruning: When a synapse is left under-stimulated, it is believed that this is the way in which our brain removes them for efficiency purposes. This process is not fully understood as of 16/03/2026.

 Introduction
• Define Social Cognitive Learning Theory (SCLT)
• Founded by Bandura.
• Behavior is learned through observation, imitation, and vicarious reinforcement.
• Mention core processes: attention, retention, motivation, reproduction, and self-efficacy.
• State direction of the essay:
• Will evaluate the theory using research evidence (Bandura, Joy et al., Charlton et al.)
• Will explore strengths and limitations of the theory in explaining aggressive behavior.

Paragraph 1: Explanation of the Theory**
• Core Assumptions:
• Observational learning.
• Role of models (authority, attractiveness, similarity).
• Vicarious reinforcement.
• Self-efficacy.
• Importance of identification with model.

** Paragraph 2: Bandura (1961) – Bobo Doll Experiment**
• Aim, Method, Sample (boys and girls, ages 3–5).
• Key Findings:
• Children imitated aggressive behavior.
• Gender differences (boys more aggressive).
• Same-sex models more influential.
• Strengths:
• Empirical support for SCLT.
• Researcher triangulation (pre-testing).
• Limitations:
• Low ecological validity.
• Artificial setting, short-term behavior.
• Aggression on a doll ≠ real-life aggression.
• Doesn’t explain non-imitators.

** Paragraph 3: Joy et al. (1986) – Natural Experiment (TV and Aggression)**
• Introduction of TV in Canadian town → increase in aggression.
• Supports SCLT: observational learning from media models.
• Strengths:
• Real-life setting = high ecological validity.
• Limitations:
• Measurement of aggression.
• Researcher bias.

Paragraph 4: Charlton et al. (2002) – St. Helena Study
• No significant increase in aggression after TV.
• Cultural/contextual factors:
• Parental mediation.
• Lack of identification with media models (out-group).
• Supports SCLT’s emphasis on identification and self-efficacy.
• Comparison with Joy et al.
• Reinforces that context matters in observational learning.

Paragraph 5: Strengths of SCLT
• Empirical support across varied settings.
• Applies to many behaviors beyond aggression (education, therapy).
• Acknowledges cognitive and cultural aspects of behavior.
• Shows learning can occur indirectly.

** Paragraph 6: Limitations of SCLT**
• Biological factors in aggression are ignored.
• Ethical concerns in aggression research.
• Cannot fully predict behavior (e.g., non-imitators).
• Overly complex – multiple variables can be difficult to isolate.

Conclusion
• Reiterate: SCT is a valuable theory with strong support.
• Its application to aggression is credible but not complete.
• Stronger as an explanatory than predictive model.
• Should be considered alongside other perspectives (e.g., biological).
