This essay will evaluate the Social Cognitive Learning Theory through its application to aggression. The social cognitive learning theory is a theory proposed by Albert Bandura that suggests that human behavior can be learned through observation, from watching models and imitating their behavior. Effective modeling requires three conditions: attention, retention, and motivation. In order for the learning to happen, attention must be paid to the model; this can be affected by the authority, attractiveness, or desirability of the model’s behavior or the outcome of said behavior.  If the model is seen as being rewarded for a behavior, the observer will also want to receive such a reward.  This is known as vicarious reinforcement. Following the observation, the learner must be able to retain and remember the behavior. Finally, the learner must have the motivation to repeat the behavior based on the outcome expectancy. Several factors affect the learner’s motivation to replicate the behavior, such as the likeability of the model, identification with the model, and consistency of the behavior. In addition, the individual must feel that he can actually do what the model can do - in other words, there must be a feeling of self-efficacy.
Bandura’s Bashing Bobo Study (1961), explored the theory through a lab experiment investigating how aggressive behavior develops in children. His aim was to see whether or not and to what extent the children would replicate the behavior of a model assigned to them. Bandura selected 36 boys and 36 girls, ranging in age from 3 - 5 years old. The children were divided into groups to study to what extent the participants would imitate an aggressive vs. nonaggressive model as well as a same-sex vs. non-same-sex model. Bandura’s findings were that children who saw aggressive models did in fact act more aggressively themselves, boys were in general more aggressive than girls and were more influenced by male models. Girls were more physically aggressive when observing a male model but were more verbally aggressive when with a female model. The study strengthens Bandura’s theory as it was clear that the participants (both boys and girls) imitated their model.
The study is also evidence of the motivation factor of cognitive learning; boys were more influenced by male models because they identified with them and girls were more likely influenced by the female models. Boys also viewed the male model as an authority figure; one of the participants even compared the behavior of the model to that of his father. This identification provided a sense of self-efficacy - that is, the children were able to do what the model had done. Another advantage of the study is that the participants were pre-tested on their aggression levels using researcher triangulation and the outliers were removed from the experiment. A limitation of this study is that the setting is rather artificial and does have ecological validity; the encounter with the model is very brief and the children are in an unusual environment, being placed alone in a room with a stranger. The aggression is also measured on a doll and does not reflect on how the children would act with a real-life human being or animal. Finally, the study only looks at the short-term effects of observing the model and does not show that the behavior was learned and then shown again in the future; The theory also cannot explain the children that did not imitate the model.  It appears that the theory may have stronger explanatory power than predictive power for an individual’s behavior.
Joy et al. (1986) carried out a prospective natural experiment on the effects of television on the level of aggression of children. Children in a remote part of Canada were tested and observed on their levels of aggression one year prior to the introduction of television and a year after. The study found that the children were more aggressive a year after they gained access to TV.  A similar study was carried out on the island of St. Helena by Charlton et al. (2002). In contrast, the 2002 study did not find any change in aggression. Following an examination of both studies some major differences can be found in the two studies. Firstly, children in St. Helena were more likely to watch TV with their parents, so it may be presumed that they were not as easily exposed to violent television. Secondly, the majority of St. Helena is black, while the majority of Western television features white actors. Therefore, in accordance with the social cognitive theory the children in St.Helena would be viewing the behavior of an out-group, making them less likely to replicate the behavior than Canadian children observing the behavior of their white in-group. This is because they do not identify with the group and therefore may not feel a sense of self-efficacy in being able to replicate the behavior. Both studies were natural experiments and have high ecological validity since in both cases the children were observed on the playground in their regular environment. A limitation found in both studies is that aggression on the playground is difficult to quantify and it is possible that there may have been some level of researcher bias.
There are several strengths of the theory.  First, there is empirical evidence to support it.  The theory has been shown to have validity both in the lab (Bandura) and in natural environments (Joy and Charlton). The theory also can be applied to a large range of behaviors, not just aggression. It has been used in education as well as in therapy. Finally, the theory is complex and explains cultural differences in behavior. It also shows how we may learn without having to directly receive a reward or punishment. There are, however, limitations of the theory.  First, the theory is only one perspective.  It does not account for biological factors in aggression.  How biology influences SCT could be a factor.  Secondly, the studies of aggression have ethical concerns. Finally, the theory cannot explain all behavior as some children did not imitate the model in spite of meeting the criteria of the theory.
Overall, it can be concluded that despite its limitations the social cognitive theory is supported by research and can help contribute to our understanding of human behaviors.

Exam-notes/Notes-on-Paper-3.title: Notes on Paper 3
Exam-notes/Notes-on-Paper-3.content:
PSY Exam

Question 1: Always the same (methods and sampling)
1a. Method - Observation / survey / questionnaire / Focus groups / Interviews / Experiment / Case study
1b. Sampling - Opportunity / (Purposive) / Random / Volunteer / Snowball / Stratified
1c. Additional - Focus Group / Survey

Question 2: Ethics ( one of two is always asked)
2a/b Ethical considerations (CARDUD) - During study
/ On publishing
- Anonymity
- Reputation
- Knock on effect
- policy
- funding

Describe the ethical considerations that were applied and explain if further ethical considerations could be applied.
Describe the ethical considerations in reporting results and explain ethical considerations that could be taken into account when applying the findings

1)All ethical considerations in the text should be described and other considerations should be addressed
2)2 Parts, describing reporting of the results. It is important to consider anonymity and communicating results effectively

2nd hypothetical  but could focus on its potential effects on different groups, leading; leading to stress or discrimination.


Question 3: Theoretical understanding (1 of 3 is always asked)
3a. Discuss the possibility of generalizing/transferring the findings of the study
(transferability and Generalizability)
(“Refers to the extent to which the results can be applied beyond the sample and settings (sometimes in Quantitative research you want to generalize findings to a more broad population).“)
-Statistical generalization (Experiments / Survey) - representative nature of the sample
- Transferability of insight - “match” with another population
3b. Discuss how a researcher could ensure results are credible (credibility)
(“Refers to the extent to which the results of the study can be trusted.“)
- Reliability
- Details
- Triangulation
3c.  Discuss how a researcher could avoid bias (bias)
(“Refers to the extent to which results reflect reality, if results do not reflect reality, there is  Bias “traps"")
- Bias can come form researcher, Method (Res), Sample Method, Participants (E.g. modification of responses for personal benefit, Social desirability)


                  
                  Reminder
                  
                


Must make direct reference to the stimulus piece
In quantitative research, Generalizability, has a lot to do with the representative nature of the sample, size and ecological validity.
In qualitative focus is in the transferable  nature of the sample.
Ways to ensure credibility include, Method triangulation, Researcher triangulation, Data triangulation, feedback, between others.
Ways of avoiding bias in experimental research include the use of Blind controls, Sampling method, the role of reflexivity,  and triangulation, between others.
Inductive Content Analysis (ICA), used to analyze and publish results from open-ended questionnaires, interviews or focus groups.




correlational studies

Quantitative approach to studying behaviour
Correlational studies should have no manipulation from researcher.
Must yield statistical results
Most common data collection through Questionnaires and surveys or Psychometric tests (e.g. IQ tests)
Regression Analysis
Inductive content analysis (no statistical measurement but interpreting anf drawing conclusions) (Does not qualify as “correlational study” although it might show correlation between variables).


General Specifications

Duration: 1 hour
Total Marks: 24 marks
Weighting: 20% (Higher Level only)
Format: Unseen research scenario → 3 compulsory questions (no choice)
Focus: Research methods in psychology — qualitative and quantitative



                  
                  What Paper 3 Actually Tests 
                  
                

You will be given a research scenario you have never seen before and must answer all three questions about it. Success depends on knowing research methods deeply enough to apply them to any study — not memorising specific studies.



Summary Table















































QuestionTopicMarksSuggested TimeQ1aIdentify research method + 2 characteristics3 marks~3 minQ1bDescribe the sampling method used3 marks~3 minQ1cSuggest an additional/alternative research method + reason3 marks~4 minQ2Ethical considerations (one of two variants)6 marks~20 minQ3Generalisation / Credibility / Bias (one of three variants)9 marks~25 minTotal24 marks+ 5 min review

Question 1 — Research Methods & Sampling (9 marks)


                  
                  Key Rule 
                  
                

Do not use bullet points for Q1. Write in full sentences. Each question is worth 3 marks: 1 mark for correct identification + 2 marks for two correct characteristics.


1a — Identify the research method + outline two characteristics (3 marks)
Identify the method used in the stimulus, then describe two of its defining characteristics in your own words. Always link to the stimulus where possible.
Research Methods to Know

































































MethodKey CharacteristicsQualitative or Quantitative?Experiment (lab)Controlled environment; manipulation of IV; measurement of DV; random allocation possibleQuantitativeExperiment (field)Natural setting; manipulation of IV; higher ecological validity; less controlQuantitativeObservation (naturalistic)Behaviour observed in natural setting; no manipulation; high ecological validity; risk of observer biasQualitative / QuantitativeObservation (participant)Researcher joins the group being studied; rich insider data; risk of researcher biasQualitativeStructured interviewPre-set closed questions; standardised; allows comparison; less depthQuantitativeSemi-structured interviewPre-set topics but open-ended questions; conversational; allows elaboration; flexibleQualitativeUnstructured interviewNo set questions; free-flowing; very rich data; hard to replicateQualitativeFocus groupGroup discussion facilitated by researcher; explores shared views; social dynamics may affect responsesQualitativeSurvey / QuestionnaireWritten self-report; large samples possible; standardised; risk of social desirability biasQuantitativeCase studyIn-depth study of one individual or group; rich, detailed data; not generalisableQualitativeCorrelational studyMeasures relationship between two variables; no manipulation; cannot establish cause and effectQuantitative

1b — Describe the sampling method used (3 marks)
Same structure: 1 mark for identifying the correct method + 2 marks for two characteristics. Connect to the stimulus (e.g. mention the sample size or group described).
Sampling Methods to Know















































MethodHow it worksStrengthsLimitationsOpportunity / ConvenienceWhoever is available at the timeEasy and quickLikely biased; not representativeVolunteer / Self-selectedParticipants respond to an advert or requestEasy to recruit; willing participantsSelf-selection bias; not representativePurposiveResearcher deliberately selects participants with specific characteristics relevant to the studyHighly relevant sampleResearcher bias in selection; not generalisableSnowballExisting participants recruit further participants from their networkUseful for hard-to-reach groupsChain bias; not representativeRandomEvery member of the target population has an equal chance of being selectedMost representative methodDifficult and time-consuming in practiceStratifiedPopulation divided into subgroups; participants randomly selected from each in proportionRepresentative of subgroupsComplex to organise

1c — Suggest an additional (or alternative) research method + one reason (3 marks)


                  
                  Strategy 
                  
                

Suggest an additional method rather than an alternative one — it is easier to justify adding a method to complement the existing one than to argue for replacing it entirely.
Always justify your choice by connecting it to what the original study could not do (e.g. small sample, lack of depth, low ecological validity).


Example answer structure:
“An additional research method would be [method]. This is because [reason linked to the stimulus — e.g. the original study had only 12 participants, so a survey would allow a larger sample and enable statistical generalisation of the findings].”

Question 2 — Ethical Considerations (6 marks)


                  
                  Only one of the two variants below will appear — you will not get a choice. 
                  
                

You must discuss 6 ethical points in total (because the question is worth 6 marks).

Variant 2a — Ethics applied during the study
Question: Describe the ethical considerations that were applied in the study and explain if further ethical considerations could be applied.

Part 1: Identify and describe 3 ethical considerations that were actually used in the stimulus study. Quote or reference the stimulus directly.
Part 2: Identify and explain 3 additional ethical considerations that were NOT in the stimulus but could/should have been applied. Explain how they would be applied, not just what they are.


Variant 2b — Ethics in reporting and applying findings
Question: Describe the ethical considerations in reporting the results and explain ethical considerations that could be taken into account when applying the findings of the study.

Part 1: Describe how ethical considerations apply when publishing and reporting the results (e.g. anonymity, accurate representation of data).
Part 2: Explain ethical considerations for applying the findings — how might they affect different groups once published? Could they cause harm, discrimination, or be misused by media or policy?


Ethical Considerations Reference List (CARDUD +)


                  
                  Aim to know at least 8–10 of these in depth 
                  
                







































































Ethical ConsiderationWhat it meansHow to apply itInformed consentParticipants must be told the nature of the study and agree before taking partProvide a consent form; parental consent required for minorsRight to withdrawParticipants can leave at any time without penaltyMust be stated at the start; no pressure to continueConfidentialityPersonal data must not be shared or identifiableUse codes or pseudonyms; secure data storageAnonymityParticipants cannot be identified from published resultsDo not include names, locations, or identifying details in reportsProtection from harmParticipants must not experience undue physical or psychological distressDebrief after study; screen for vulnerable participantsDeceptionMisleading participants is generally avoided; if used, it must be justifiedMust be debriefed fully afterwards; mild deception may be permissibleDebriefingParticipants are informed of the true aim after the studyShould restore any distress caused; explain why deception was necessary if usedAccurate reportingData must be presented honestly; no fabrication or selective omissionNegative results must also be reported; methods must be transparentReputation of psychologyResearch must not bring the discipline into disreputeAvoid sensationalist claims; be cautious with media communicationKnock-on / societal effectsPublished findings can affect public groups beyond participantsConsider how findings might stigmatise groups or influence policyFunding / conflict of interestFunding sources may influence findingsDeclare funding sources; ensure independence of analysisCultural sensitivityResearch must be respectful of cultural norms and values of participantsAdapt consent and procedure to cultural context

Question 3 — Theoretical Understanding (9 marks)


                  
                  Only one of the three variants below will appear — you will not get a choice. 
                  
                

Must make direct and specific reference to the stimulus throughout your answer.



Variant 3a — Generalisation / Transferability
Question: Discuss the possibility of generalising / transferring the findings of the study.


                  
                  Key Distinction 
                  
                

Whether you discuss generalisation (quantitative) or transferability (qualitative) depends on the type of study in the stimulus. Know both.


If the study is quantitative → discuss Generalisation
“Refers to the extent to which findings can be applied to a broader population beyond the sample.”

Sample size — larger samples increase likelihood of being representative
Sampling method — random/stratified sampling → more representative; opportunity/snowball → less
Demographics — is the sample WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic)? This limits generalisability
Ecological validity — were conditions artificial (lab) or realistic? Low ecological validity limits generalisation to real life
Replication — have findings been reproduced across different populations?

If the study is qualitative → discuss Transferability
“Refers to the extent to which insights from the study could be relevant or meaningful in another context or population.”

Thick description — detailed, rich accounts allow readers to judge whether findings fit their own context
Purposive sample — if selected for specific characteristics, findings may transfer to others with those characteristics
Context-specificity — qualitative findings are deeply tied to the specific setting; direct generalisation is not the goal
Theoretical generalisation — findings may extend existing theory even without statistical generalisation


Variant 3b — Credibility
Question: Discuss how a researcher could ensure that the results of the study are credible.


                  
                  This question usually only appears when the stimulus study uses qualitative methods.
                  
                

“Credibility refers to the extent to which the results of the study can be trusted — i.e. do they accurately represent the participants’ reality?”

















































StrategyWhat it involvesTriangulationUsing multiple methods, researchers, or data sources to cross-check findingsMethod triangulationCombining qualitative and quantitative methods (e.g. interview + survey)Researcher triangulationMultiple researchers independently analyse the same data and compare interpretationsData triangulationCollecting data at different times, locations, or from different participant groupsMember checkingReturning findings to participants to verify they accurately reflect their experienceProlonged engagementSpending extended time in the field to build trust and deepen understandingPeer debriefingHaving colleagues scrutinise the researcher’s methods and interpretationsReflexivityResearcher acknowledges and documents their own biases and how these may have shaped findingsAudit trailKeeping a detailed record of all research decisions so the process can be independently reviewedThick / rich descriptionProviding detailed accounts that allow readers to assess credibility themselves

Variant 3c — Avoiding Bias
Question: Discuss how a researcher could avoid bias in the study.
“Bias refers to any systematic distortion that prevents results from accurately reflecting reality.”
Sources of Bias



































SourceType of BiasExampleResearcher / Experimenter biasResearcher’s expectations unconsciously influence resultsUnconsciously asking leading questions in an interviewParticipant biasParticipants modify behaviour because they are being observedSocial desirability — giving answers they think are expectedSampling biasSample does not represent the target populationUsing only university students (WEIRD sample)Confirmation biasResearcher interprets data to confirm existing beliefsIgnoring contradictory qualitative dataDemand characteristicsParticipants guess the aim and alter their behaviourGuessing the hypothesis in an experiment
Ways to Avoid Bias













































StrategyHow it reduces biasSingle-blind procedureParticipants do not know which condition they are in → reduces demand characteristicsDouble-blind procedureNeither participants nor researcher know condition allocation → eliminates experimenter biasStandardised proceduresSame instructions and conditions for all participants → reduces researcher variabilityReflexivityResearcher examines their own assumptions and documents them → reduces confirmation biasTriangulationCross-checking findings across multiple methods/researchers → reduces single-source biasRandom allocationParticipants randomly assigned to conditions → reduces selection bias in experimentsAppropriate samplingUsing random or stratified sampling → reduces sample biasPilot studyTesting procedure in advance to identify and remove sources of bias before the main studyInductive Content Analysis (ICA)Bottom-up coding of qualitative data without pre-set categories → reduces confirmation bias in analysis


                  
                  ICA Note 
                  
                

Inductive Content Analysis is a qualitative analysis technique used to analyse interviews, focus groups, and open-ended questionnaires. Categories emerge from the data rather than being imposed by the researcher. It does not produce statistical results and does not qualify as a correlational study, even if patterns emerge.



Correlational Studies — Key Points

A quantitative approach — must yield statistical results (e.g. correlation coefficient)
No manipulation of variables by the researcher
Most common data collection methods: surveys, questionnaires, psychometric tests (e.g. IQ tests)
Analysis: Pearson’s r, Spearman’s rho, regression analysis
Cannot establish cause and effect — only association between variables
Inductive Content Analysis does not qualify as a correlational study — it produces no statistical measure of correlation


Qualitative vs Quantitative — Quick Reference













































FeatureQualitativeQuantitativeData typeWords, themes, meaningsNumbers, statisticsGoalUnderstand experience / behaviour in depthMeasure, compare, generaliseCommon methodsInterviews, focus groups, case studies, naturalistic observationExperiments, surveys, correlational studiesAnalysisInductive Content Analysis, thematic analysisStatistical analysis, regressionGeneralisationTransferability of insightStatistical generalisationStrengthRich, contextual, participant-centredReplicable, objective, comparableLimitationHard to generalise; researcher bias riskLacks depth; may miss context

Exam Tips
Time Management

























TimeTask0–10 minRead stimulus carefully. Answer Q1a, Q1b, Q1c.10–30 minQ2 — ethical considerations (6 points, ~3 min each)30–55 minQ3 — generalisation / credibility / bias55–60 minReview — check all answers reference the stimulus
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Using bullet points in Q1 — write in full sentences
Only identifying the method/sampling without giving two characteristics
Suggesting an alternative rather than an additional method in Q1c (harder to justify)
Listing ethical considerations without explaining how they apply to the specific study
Writing generic answers for Q3 — every point must connect back to the stimulus
Confusing generalisation (quantitative) with transferability (qualitative)
Treating ICA as a correlational method

What Examiners Reward

Correct identification + two clearly explained characteristics (Q1)
Direct reference to the stimulus throughout all answers
Six distinct, well-explained ethical points in Q2
Correct application of generalisation vs transferability based on study type (Q3a)
Concrete strategies explained with their mechanism — not just named (Q3b/c)
Terminology used accurately and consistently

Exam-notes/Notes-on-paper-1.title: Notes on paper 1
Exam-notes/Notes-on-paper-1.content:
PSY Exam

General Specifications

Duration: 2 hours
Total Marks: 49 marks
Weighting: 50% (Standard Level) | 40% (Higher Level)
Focus: The three core approaches to psychology (Biological, Cognitive, and Sociocultural).




Section A: Short Answer Questions (SAQs) 27 marks


                  
                  Key Rule No critical thinking or evaluation is required in Section A. Focus entirely on knowledge, understanding, and application (APPR structure).
                  
                

SAQ Structure


Describe — give a detailed account of a theory, concept, or study


Explain — give a clear account of causes, reasons, or mechanisms


Outline — give a brief account; less detail than ‘describe’


3 compulsory SAQs (9 marks per SAQ)




                  
                  APPR structure 
                  
                

A — Aim: State what you are going to address and briefly define the concept.
P — Point: Describe the relevant theory or concept clearly, using psychological terminology.
P — Proof: Describe a relevant study (aim, procedure, findings, conclusion). Name researcher(s) and year.
R — Relevance: Explicitly link the study back to the question/command term.



Aim for 200–350 words per SAQ
Spend approximately 20 minutes per SAQ
No introduction or conclusion needed — be direct and focused
Always name at least one researcher and year

SAQ Markbands (0–9)

























MarksWhat examiners look for7–9Accurate, relevant knowledge; terminology used correctly; study well described; clear link to question throughout4–6Mostly relevant; some accurate knowledge but incomplete or partially linked1–3Vague or inaccurate knowledge; limited relevance; study absent or barely described
Topics by Approach
1. Biological Approach








































TopicKey Studies / ResearchersKey Terms / ConceptsNeuroplasticityMaguire (2000) - Taxi Driver Study; Draganski (2004) — juggling study;Rosenzweig, Bennet & Diamond (1972) - Rat StudyNeuroplasticity, grey matter, hippocampus, synaptic pruning, axon, dendriteNeurotransmissionRaine et al. (1997) — PET scans in murderers; studies on serotonin/dopamine in depression and schizophreniaJarowsky et alMartinez & KesnerRogers and KesnerAntonova et al (2011)Neurotransmitter, synapse, dopamine, serotonin, reuptake, agonist, antagonistHormones In Human BehaviourDabbs et al. (1995) — testosterone and violent crime; Lupien et al. (2007) — cortisol and memoryMcGaugh & Cahill (1995)Hormone, cortisol, testosterone, HPA axis, endocrine system, fight-or-flightGenetics And Human BehaviourCaspi et al. (2003) — MAOA gene and antisocial behaviour; Bouchard et al. (1990) — twin studies on IQGene, allele, genotype, phenotype, heritability, twin study, adoption study, epigeneticsEvolutionary Explanations for BehaviourBuss (1989) — mate preference across cultures; Daly & Wilson (1988) — homicide and kin selectionNatural selection, adaptation, reproductive fitness, inclusive fitness, kin selectionLocalization of functionBroca (1861) — Broca’s area; HM (Milner, 1996)Cerebral cortex, prefrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus, lateralisation, fMRI, PET, MRI

2. Cognitive Approach








































TopicKey Studies / ResearchersKey Terms / ConceptsModels of MemoryAtkinson & Shiffrin (1968) — Multi-Store Model; Baddeley & Hitch (1974) — Working Memory ModelEncoding, storage, retrieval, STM, LTM, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, episodic bufferSchema TheoryBartlett (1932) - War of Ghosts ; Brewer & Treyers (1981) - “Schema congruent” office — office studySchema, assimilation, accommodation, top-down processing, reconstructive memory, prototype, scriptCognitive BiasesLoftus & Palmer (1974) - Car collision — eyewitness testimony; Tversky and Kahneman (1974) — heuristics and biasesConfirmation bias, availability heuristic, representativeness heuristic, anchoring, post-event informationThinking & Decision-makingWason (1966) — selection task; Tversky and Kahneman (1974) — System 1 vs System 2Dual process theory, System 1 (fast/intuitive), System 2 (slow/analytical), cognitive loadEmotion & CognitionNeisser & Harsch (1992) - Space Challenger Disasterflashbulb memories; McGaugh & Cahill (1995) — adrenaline and memoryFlashbulb memory, emotional memory, stress and cognition, mood-congruent memoryCognitive processing & the brainHM (Milner, 1996) — role of hippocampus in memory; Draganski (2004) — structural changes with learningExplicit/implicit memory, procedural memory, declarative memory, anterograde/retrograde amnesia

3. Sociocultural Approach








































TopicKey Studies / ResearchersKey Terms / Concepts**Social Cognitive Learning Theory ** SCLTBandura (1961), (1963) & (1965) — Bobo Doll experimentsObservational learning, modelling, vicarious reinforcement, self-efficacy, attention, retention, reproduction, motivationSocial Identity TheoryTajfel (1971) - Klee or Kandinsky — minimal group paradigmSocial identity, in-group, out-group, categorisation, identification, comparison, in-group bias, ethnocentrismPrejudice & StereotypesSteele and Aronson (1995) — stereotype threat; Darley & Batson (1973) - Good samaritanStereotype, prejudice, discrimination, stereotype threat, implicit bias, attributionCultural DimensionsHofstede (2001) — six dimensions of national culture; Berry (1967) — conformity across culturesIndividualism vs collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity vs femininity, emic vs etic** Conformity & Compliance**Abrams et al (1990) - Asch paradigm — line experiment; Milgram (1963) — obedience study; Zimbardo’s Stanford prison experiment (1971)Conformity, normative influence, informational influence, obedience, authority, situational factorsEnculturation - Acquiring your cultural norms + AcculturationBerry (1967) — four acculturation strategies;Enculturation, acculturation, assimilation, integration, separation, marginalisation, cultural norms


Section B: Extended Response Questions (ERQs) 22 marks
3 prompts provided (one per approach). Choose and answer 1. Worth 22 marks.


                  
                  Key Rule Full essay structure is required. Critical thinking is essential and heavily rewarded. Suggested time: 60 minutes. Aim for 700–900 words
                  
                

ERQ Essay Structure


                  
                  Essay Structure 
                  
                

1. Introduction — Define key terms. State your thesis/argument clearly. Signpost what the essay will cover.
2. Study 1 — Describe aim, participants, procedure, findings, and conclusion. Link explicitly to the question.
3. Specific Critical Thinking (CT) — Evaluate Study 1 specifically: methodological strengths/limitations, ethical considerations, sample issues.
4. Study 2 — Second study, similarly described and linked to the essay question.
5. Holistic Critical Thinking (CT) — Evaluate the broader body of evidence: conflicting studies, cultural bias, ethical limitations of the field, generalisability.
6. Evaluation — Assess the overall value of the theories/studies in answering the question. Strengths and limitations of the approach.
7. Conclusion — Directly answer the question. Summarise the weight of evidence. Return to your thesis.



Critical thinking must be substantive, vague comments like ‘the study lacked ecological validity’ without explanation will not earn marks
Every paragraph should visibly link back to the question,  do not drift into irrelevant knowledge

ERQ Command Terms


                  
                  Command Terms 
                  
                

Discuss — Present evidence and arguments for and against; weigh them up and reach a balanced conclusion. Most common command term.
Evaluate — Make a judgement about the value or limitations of something using evidence. Requires a supported conclusion.
Contrast — Explicitly point out differences between two or more things. Do not describe similarities.
To what extent — Weigh up evidence and argue a clear position. Requires a definitive conclusion.


ERQ Markbands

























MarksKnowledge & UnderstandingCritical Thinking / Evaluation7–9Clear, focused answer. Accurate concepts with relevant terminology. Study well-described and linked to the question.Thorough evaluation of method, ethics, or application. Limitations clearly identified and explained.4–6Answer is mostly relevant. Some accurate knowledge but may be incomplete or partially linked.Some evaluation present but may be superficial or not fully developed.1–3Limited relevance to the question. Knowledge is vague or inaccurate.Little or no evaluation. May just describe without critical analysis.
Critical Thinking:
Specific CT — evaluating an individual study

Sample bias: Was the sample representative? (WEIRD: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic)
Methodology: Lab experiment vs field study? Controlled but low ecological validity vs ecologically valid but less controlled?
Replication: Has the study been replicated? Does it have high test-retest reliability?
Ethics: Deception, lack of informed consent, psychological harm, right to withdraw?
Demand characteristics: Did participants guess the study’s aim and change their behaviour?

Holistic CT — evaluating the body of evidence

Cultural bias: Do findings apply universally, or are they culture-specific? (e.g. collectivist vs individualist societies)
Gender bias: Were male/female samples equivalent? Are findings generalised inappropriately?
Conflicting evidence: Are there studies that contradict the claim? What does the balance of evidence suggest?
Ethical limitations: Has the field been constrained by ethical guidelines, limiting what can be studied?
Reductionism: Does the explanation oversimplify complex behaviour by reducing it to one factor?


Summary Table








































FeatureSection A (SAQs)Section B (ERQs)Number of Questions3 (Compulsory)1 (Choice of 3)Marks per Question9 marks22 marksTotal Marks27 marks22 marksCritical Thinking?NoYes (Crucial)Number of StudiesUsually 1Usually 2+Time Allocation~20 min each (60 min total)60 minutes

Exam-notes/Notes-on-paper-2.title: Notes on paper 2
Exam-notes/Notes-on-paper-2.content:
PSY Exam

General Specifications

Duration: 2 hours
Total Marks: 44 marks
Weighting: 25% (Standard Level)
Option: Psychology of Human Relationships
Format: Two sections — Section A (SAQs) and Section B (ERQ)



                  
                  How Paper 2 differs from Paper 1 
                  
                

Paper 2 is option-based: In our case all questions come from Psychology of Human Relationships only. The SAQ and ERQ format is the same as Paper 1, but questions are narrower and more applied. The same APPR and essay structures apply.



Summary Table








































FeatureSection A (SAQs)Section B (ERQ)Questions3 (all compulsory)1 (choice of 3)Marks per question9 marks22 marks (SL)Total marks22 marks22 marksCritical thinking?NoYes (crucial)Studies requiredUsually 12 or moreTime allocation~20 min each (60 min total)~60 minutes

Section A – Short Answer Questions (SAQs)
3 compulsory questions drawn from the Psychology of Human Relationships option. Each worth 9 marks. Total: 22 marks.


                  
                  Key Rule No critical thinking or evaluation is required in Section A. Focus entirely on knowledge, understanding, and application (APPR structure).
                  
                



                  
                  APPR Structure 
                  
                

A — Aim: State what you are going to address and briefly define the concept.
P — Point: Describe the relevant theory or concept clearly, using psychological terminology.
P — Proof: Describe a relevant study (aim, procedure, findings, conclusion). Name researcher(s) and year.
R — Relevance: Explicitly link the study back to the question/command term.



Aim for 200–350 words per SAQ
Spend approximately 20 minutes per SAQ
No introduction or conclusion needed

SAQ Markbands (0–9)





















MarksWhat examiners look for7–9Accurate, relevant knowledge; terminology used correctly; study well described; clear link to question throughout4–6Mostly relevant; some accurate knowledge but incomplete or partially linked1–3Vague or inaccurate knowledge; limited relevance; study absent or barely described

Section B — Extended Response Questions (ERQs)
3 prompts provided, all from Psychology of Human Relationships. Choose and answer 1. Worth 22 marks.


                  
                  Key Rule Full essay structure is required. Critical thinking is essential and heavily rewarded. Suggested time: 60 minutes. Aim for 700–900 words.
                  
                

ERQ Command Terms


                  
                  Command Terms Discuss — Present evidence and arguments for and against; weigh them up and reach a balanced conclusion. Most common command term.
                  
                

Evaluate — Make a judgement about the value or limitations of something using evidence. Requires a supported conclusion.
Contrast — Explicitly point out differences between two or more things. Do not describe similarities.
To what extent — Weigh up evidence and argue a clear position. Requires a definitive conclusion.


ERQ Essay Structure


                  
                  Essay Structure 1. Introduction — Define key terms. State your thesis/argument clearly. Signpost what the essay will cover.
                  
                

2. Study 1 — Describe aim, participants, procedure, findings, and conclusion. Link explicitly to the question.
3. Specific Critical Thinking (CT) — Evaluate Study 1 specifically: methodological strengths/limitations, ethical considerations, sample issues.
4. Study 2 — Second study, similarly described and linked to the essay question.
5. Holistic Critical Thinking (CT) — Evaluate the broader body of evidence: conflicting studies, cultural bias, ethical limitations of the field, generalisability.
6. Evaluation — Assess the overall value of the theories/studies in answering the question. Strengths and limitations of the approach.
7. Conclusion — Directly answer the question. Summarise the weight of evidence. Return to your thesis.



Critical thinking must be substantive — vague comments like ‘the study lacked ecological validity’ without explanation will not earn marks
Every paragraph should visibly link back to the question — do not drift into irrelevant knowledge

ERQ Markbands

























MarksKnowledge & UnderstandingCritical Thinking / Evaluation7–9Clear, focused answer. Accurate concepts with relevant terminology. Study well-described and linked to the question.Thorough evaluation of method, ethics, or application. Limitations clearly identified and explained.4–6Answer is mostly relevant. Some accurate knowledge but may be incomplete or partially linked.Some evaluation present but may be superficial or not fully developed.1–3Limited relevance to the question. Knowledge is vague or inaccurate.Little or no evaluation. May just describe without critical analysis.
Types of Critical Thinking
Specific CT — evaluating an individual study

Sample bias — Was the sample representative? (WEIRD: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic)
Methodology — Lab experiment vs field study? Controlled but low ecological validity vs ecologically valid but less controlled?
Replication — Has the study been replicated? Does it have high test-retest reliability?
Ethics — Deception, lack of informed consent, psychological harm, right to withdraw?
Demand characteristics — Did participants guess the study’s aim and change their behaviour?

Holistic CT — evaluating the body of evidence

Cultural bias — Do findings apply universally, or are they culture-specific? (e.g. collectivist vs individualist societies)
Gender bias — Were male/female samples equivalent? Are findings generalised inappropriately?
Conflicting evidence — Are there studies that contradict the claim? What does the balance of evidence suggest?
Ethical limitations — Has the field been constrained by ethical guidelines, limiting what can be studied?
Reductionism — Does the explanation oversimplify complex behaviour by reducing it to one factor?

Schema
Knowledge and understanding
Research into memory suggests it is malleable and is often unreliable as it may not be an accurate representation of the past. Anyhow,  it is still a useful representation to help plan for the future. Memory is not about the past but rather processes directed to future survival.

Complex process including different stages: Attention, Encoding, Storage and Retrieval (A-E-S-R).
Modeled with stores and processes: Memory has limited capacity stores, limited duration and decays
Memory is a part of information processing ⇒ It needs Attention, Rehearsal and a framework to link to

According to Loftus & Pickrell (1995) - Lost in a mall and Shaw et al. (2015); Each time we recall, our memory changes slightly, due to its reconstructive characteristics.
This can be explained from a

Biological perspective: Neural networks, recreating connections (even neuroplasticity and pruning)
Cognitive perspective: Through Schemas that “help fill in the gaps in knowledge”

Schemas: Mental representations of the world stored in the brain that guide our behaviour and information processing
Loftus & Palmer (1974) - Car collision suggested that as memory is reconstructive, there is opportunity to include post-event information and from different episodes.
Additionally Loftus & Pickrell (1995) - Lost in a mall and Shaw et al. (2015) suggested memory is Transactive. Others influence our memory and we rely on others and external sources to remember. (Memory is social)
Conclusion
Memory is:

Malleable and unreliable but useful, except for Eyewitness Testimony (EWT)
Crucial for complex information processing: Attention, Encoding, Storage/Retention and Recall
When seen as a series of stores and processes it has limited capacity and duration.
Reconstructive, so can change with each recall and post-event information can be added.

From

Biology: Can lead to Neural networks  been made and connections  strengthened faster through dendric branching.
Cognition: Schemas help organize, predict, plan and “Fill in” the gaps in knowledge.
Sociology: Memory is a social processes, Transactive; we rely &/or conform to others and external sources.

Additionally Bartlett (1932) - War of Ghosts should be mentioned as foundational theory

Transclude of Memory

ERQ trial #1
To what extent is memory reliable? 

Although memory is vital for humans and it can be very efficient (Depending on context), it is also unreliable. We rely on memory for almost every action we do, including complex information processing. Through the processes in memory we learn how to be “ourselves”. We are constantly gathering information from our surroundings through “Attention”, for it to be “Encoded” and stored to be recalled when needed in the future. However is this constant activation on the different processes what makes it malleable and unreliable. Psychologists suggest that memory is in fact reconstructive; memories are not stored as a whole but rather ‘pieced together’ every time we recall. In extension, this allows for distortion or the addition of new information. Loftus & Palmer (1974), suggested  that post-event information  can be added if it is presented in a credible manner and from a trusted source. Furthermore, Loftus & Prickrell (1995) showed that false memories can be implanted.  In this essay how these findings affect the reliability of memory is going to be discussed.
Loftus and palmer (1974), performed an experiment to study the influence of leading questions in eyewitness memories. 45  learning drivers were divided into 5 groups and shown 7  traffic accidents from driver’s education films. The study used independent sampling, meaning each participant was exposed to only one condition. Participants were asked about how fast the cars were going when they hit each other through a questionnaire. The independent variable was chaining the verb “hit” for more or less complementary verbs like “smashed” or “contacted”.
Findings showed that the groups under the condition  with the more complementary verb (e.g. smashed) on average gave higher speed estimates than those under the conditions with the least complementary verb (e.g. contacted). indicating that the “critical word” in the question consistently activated schemas, which may have influenced the memory of the accident. This distortion of memory could be attributed to its reconstructive nature, so that the actual details of the accident are not remembered but when the schema is activated by the critical verb, what aligns with the schema overwrites the memory, affecting how the participants perceived the crash. Making the memory  inaccurate and unreliable.
Eventhough this study can be considered to have high internal validity as it uses a controlled lab experiment, the fact that participants were unexperienced drivers may signify am issue with ecological validity. Moreover, as the accidents were showed through educational films, participants may not experience the same level of emotion as if it were a real accident, reducing their personal relevance, thus possibly affecting the level of attention and recall of details.
Loftus & Prickrell (1995) carried out an experiment with the aim of determining if false memories of autobiographical events can be implanted through suggestion, suggesting memory could be transactive (we rely on others or our environment to remember). Prior to the actual participant testing, families were asked about the participant’s childhood and wether if they had been lost in a mall or not. Participants were sent a questionnaire in which they were asked to recall 3 real memories and a false one (been last in a mall). Through the course of 4 weeks, participants were interviewed twice and asked to recall details of the 4 memories. In the second interview they  were debriefed, asked to rate their confidence in the memories and to guess the false memory.
25% of the participants recalled the false memory as real, although ranked it as least confident. Supporting the theory that when information comes from a trusted or credible source (family in this case) as is assimilated through repetition, false memories can be implanted, and the more practice done; the more details and confidence can be added to the memory, making it inaccurate and unreliable. Additionally, it supports the idea that memory is social (transactive) as it can be influenced by other people or external factors.
In contrast with Loftus & Palmer. As part of this study was performed via questionnaire in the participant’s natural environment, Loftus & prickrell could be argued to have high ecological validity. Nonetheless this fact could also signify contamination of the responses on the questionnaire due to lack of control (Bias). Both studies could be seen as reliable as they are reasonably easy to replicate.
Research into memory is trust worthy as accuracy, efficiency and confidence of memory can be easily tested, however some controls are needed, for instance, verifying details with the families. Additionally, method triangulation such as using both the questionnaire and interviews, can increase the credibility of the study. Experiments on memory can help the design of models, test theory and establish cause and effect relationships such as the effect of leading questions in memory perception.
Although memory is vital for planning and  decision making and it is generally efficient, it is also malleable making it highly unreliable and inaccurate at times.  Memory’s reconstructive process can lead to extraneous or inaccurate details or even complete memories to be implanted, distorting the memory, making it eyewitness testimonies hardly a fiable source. Both social or environmental factors and cognitive heuristics like schemas can cause distortions in memory.

ChatGPT Diploma evaluation
✅ 1. Knowledge and Understanding (5/6)
Strengths:
• The response demonstrates strong understanding of cognitive psychology, especially the reconstructive nature of memory.
• Appropriate psychological terms are used: encoding, schemas, reconstructive memory, transactive memory.
• The essay gives a clear explanation of memory processes and integrates cognitive terms well into the argument.
Suggestions for Improvement:
• There are minor slips in phrasing, e.g. “Depending on context” is awkwardly placed.
• The first paragraph could be slightly more concise and polished—sometimes the explanation of processes (attention, encoding, etc.) is presented without clearly linking back to the issue of reliability.

✅ 2. Use of Research (6/6)
Strengths:
• Both Loftus & Palmer (1974) and Loftus & Pickrell (1995) are highly relevant and well explained.
• Excellent explanation of methodology, IV/DV, sample, and findings.
• Evaluation of both studies includes validity, replicability, and even touches on transactive memory, which is a sophisticated extension.
Suggestions for Improvement:
• Just a minor point: Be consistent with spelling (it’s Pickrell, not Prickrell).
• Adding one more contrasting or supporting study (e.g., Yuille & Cutshall, which shows eyewitness memory can be accurate under real-world conditions) would add depth and a stronger evaluation.

✅ 3. Critical Thinking (5/6)
Strengths:
• The essay does a good job considering methodological limitations (e.g., ecological validity, lab setting).
• Shows an understanding of triangulation, schema theory, and memory being influenced socially (transactive).
• Evaluates how schema activation could lead to memory distortion and contrasts lab vs real-world settings.
• There’s clear evidence of awareness of bias, validity, and social influence on memory.
Suggestions for Improvement:
• To hit a 6, develop alternative explanations (e.g., could participants just be guessing or complying with perceived expectations?).
• A brief discussion of uncertainty or whether reconstructive memory applies equally to all memory types (e.g. flashbulb memories) would deepen the analysis.

✅ 4. Focus (2/2)
Strengths:
• Clear focus on the central question throughout.
• All research and discussion is clearly tied to memory reliability.

✅ 5. Clarity (2/2)
Strengths:
• Clear structure: intro, study 1, study 2, evaluation, conclusion.
• Generally well-written, with only a few minor grammar/spelling slips (e.g., “eventhough” → “even though”; “been last in a mall” → “been lost in a mall”).
• Transitions between paragraphs could be a little smoother in places, but meaning is always clear.

Human-relationships/Bowlby-Attachment-Th.title: Bowlby Attachment Theory
Human-relationships/Bowlby-Attachment-Th.content:
PSY HRelations Theory Human Relationships,

Bowlby’s Attachment Theory is a foundational biological and cognitive framework explaining how early emotional bonds between infants and caregivers form, why they matter for survival, and how they shape behaviour across the lifespan, including adult romantic relationships.

Core Idea
Attachment is the development of a mutual and intense emotional relationship between an infant and its caregivers. Bowlby argued that a close relationship between child and caregiver is a basic biological need, an innate pattern of behaviour shaped by evolution to promote infant survival.
Infant behaviours such as smiling, babbling, grasping, and crying are genetically-based social signals that encourage caregivers to provide food, protection, and affection.

Development of Attachment
According to Shaffer (1996), attachment develops until around age 7 months, at which point:

The infant shows separation anxiety when the primary attachment figure leaves.
The infant can discriminate between the attachment figure and strangers (linked to Piaget’s object permanence).
The infant displays stranger anxiety when unfamiliar people approach.


Harlow’s Challenge to Freud
Freud’s cupboard theory argued the mother-child bond forms because the mother provides nourishment. Harry Harlow (1958) challenged this using rhesus monkeys given both a wire mother (providing milk) and a cloth mother (providing comfort). Monkeys spent significantly more time with the cloth mother regardless of which provided food, demonstrating that contact comfort, not feeding, is the basis of attachment.

The Internal Working Model
Bowlby (1973) argued there is a continuity between early attachment and adult relationships. Children create an Internal Working Model (IWM), a cognitive schema of:

What to expect from attachment figures
Ideas about the self (am I lovable?)
How the self and others relate

The IWM guides behaviour in conflict resolution, self-disclosure, and relationship evaluation throughout life.

Children who experience love and affection come to see themselves as worthy of love.
Children who experience neglect or rejection may come to believe they deserve it, negatively affecting mental health and future relationships.


Ainsworth’s Strange Situation
Mary Ainsworth (1970) devised the Strange Situation Paradigm to measure attachment behaviour based on how a child reacts to maternal separation and reunion. She conducted the Ganda Project (Uganda: 28 children, 9 months) before replicating it in Baltimore (26 mother-infant pairs).
Attachment Types:



































TypeNameBehaviour% of childrenAInsecurely attached - AvoidantApparent indifference when mother leaves; avoids contact on return; not afraid of strangers20%BSecurely attachedUpset when mother leaves; happy on reunion; easily comforted70%CInsecurely attached - Anxious-AmbivalentVery upset when mother leaves; difficult to soothe; seeks then rejects comfort on return10%DInsecurely attached - Disorganised (Main & Solomon, 1986)No consistent reaction; associated with abuse or chronic depression in caregiver-
Evaluation of the Strange Situation:

Highly standardised; allows replication across time and cultures.
Critics argue it is highly artificial and gathers limited information.
Van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg (1988) meta-analysed 32 studies (8 countries, 2000+ infants) and found cultural differences in attachment distribution. Japanese studies showed no Type A but high Type C, associated with different child-rearing practices.
The meaning of separation differs across cultures, challenging universal interpretation.


Role of Early Attachment on Later Behaviour
Bowlby’s continuity hypothesis proposes that internal working models continue throughout the lifespan, though they can change.
Supporting research:

Hazan & Shaver (1987): childhood attachment style predicts adult romantic relationship style (secure, avoidant, ambivalent).
Simpson et al. (1996): insecurely attached individuals used more negative conflict strategies in dating couples.
Fonagy et al. (1991): prospective longitudinal study (n=96 London mothers) found a 75% match between a mother’s attachment style and her child’s security, supporting intergenerational transmission of attachment.


Evaluation of Attachment Theory





























StrengthsLimitationsCross-cultural support for basic attachment behaviours (proximity-seeking, separation anxiety)Cross-cultural differences in attachment distribution challenge universality claimsStrong empirical base (Ainsworth, Hazan & Shaver, Fonagy et al.)Deterministic risk: theory can overstate the permanence of early attachment patternsIWM provides a testable cognitive mechanism linking early experience to adult behaviourIWM is difficult to measure directly; relies on inferences from behaviourExplains both healthy and problematic adult relationship patternsIgnores other influences on adult relationships (e.g., peer relationships, culture, socioeconomic factors)Foundation for therapeutic interventions (e.g., attachment-based therapy)Overemphasis on the mother-infant dyad; underestimates the role of fathers and other caregivers

IB Connections

Approach: Biological; Cognitive; Sociocultural
Topic: Human relationships - formation; Developmental psychology
Key Concept: Internal working model, continuity hypothesis, Strange Situation, attachment types, intergenerational transmission
Useful for: “Discuss the role of attachment in human relationships” / “Evaluate Bowlby’s attachment theory” / “Discuss the influence of early experience on adult behaviour”
Paired with: Hazan & Shaver (1987), Fisher et al. (2005), Gottman (1999)



Key Concept - The Internal Working Model:
The IWM is the cognitive bridge between childhood attachment and adult relationships. It is not a rigid template but a working model, meaning it can be updated by new experiences. A child with an anxious attachment history may develop a secure style through a later positive relationship or therapy. Bowlby’s most important contribution is not determinism, but the insight that our earliest relationships teach us what to expect from intimacy, and that these lessons echo throughout our lives.

Human-relationships/Evolutionary-Explana.title: Evolutionary Explanations - Human Relationships
Human-relationships/Evolutionary-Explana.content:
PSY HRelations Biological

Evolutionary psychology applies the theory of natural selection to human behaviour, arguing that the behaviours and preferences we exhibit today exist because they maximised reproductive success in our evolutionary past. In the context of human relationships, this means attraction, mate selection, and relationship behaviour are shaped by what helped our ancestors survive and reproduce.

Core claim: Behaviours that increased reproductive success were passed on. Behaviours that reduced it were selected against. Human attraction is therefore not random but follows predictable, evolved patterns.


Key Theoretical Framework
Natural Selection and Mate Choice
Natural selection favours traits that maximise an organism’s reproductive success. In the context of attraction, this means:

We are attracted to cues that signal genetic fitness, good health, and reproductive viability
We have evolved psychological mechanisms for detecting these cues, including sensitivity to physical features, immune compatibility, and genetic diversity

Parental Investment Theory (Trivers, 1972)
The sex that invests more biologically in offspring (gestation, nursing) will be more selective in mate choice. The sex that invests less will seek to maximise the number of mating opportunities.
In humans:

Women invest more (9-month pregnancy, nursing, primary caregiving) and are therefore more selective, prioritising resources, stability, and genetic quality.
Men invest less biologically and therefore tend to be less selective and more focused on cues to fertility (youth, physical attractiveness).

This predicts universal sex differences in mate preferences across cultures.

Key Studies
Buss (1989) - Universal Mate Preferences
Aim: To investigate whether sex differences in mate preferences are universal across cultures, supporting an evolutionary explanation.
Participants: Over 10,000 participants from 37 cultures across 6 continents.
Method: Cross-cultural self-report survey. Participants rated 18 characteristics desired in a long-term mate.
Results:

Women consistently valued financial resources, ambition, and older age more than men across nearly all 37 cultures.
Men consistently valued physical attractiveness and youth more than women.
Men preferred partners approximately 2.5 years younger; women preferred partners approximately 3.5 years older.

Conclusion: The universality of sex differences supports Parental Investment Theory: women select for resource-holding capacity; men select for fertility cues. Cultural variation in specifics, but the pattern is universal.

Fisher et al. (2005) - Love as a Motivational Drive
Romantic love activates the dopaminergic reward pathway (VTA, caudate nucleus), the same system involved in motivation and goal pursuit across species. Fisher argues this system evolved to focus mating energy on one specific partner, increasing reproductive success by ensuring sustained investment. See Fisher et al 2005 for full details.

Wedekind (1995) - MHC and Immune-Based Mate Selection
Women prefer the body odour of MHC-dissimilar men, supporting an evolved mechanism for maximising offspring immune diversity. The preference reverses in women taking oral contraceptives, suggesting a direct hormonal link to evolved mate detection systems. See Wedekind (1995) for full details.

Clark & Hatfield (1989) - Sex Differences in Short-Term Mating
A field experiment on a US university campus showed 75% of men vs. 0% of women agreed to a casual sexual proposition from an attractive stranger. This directly demonstrates the sex difference in short-term mating receptivity predicted by Parental Investment Theory.

Ronay & von Hippel (2010) - Testosterone and Mate Display
96 male skateboarders took significantly more risks in the presence of an attractive female observer, with saliva testosterone levels rising in that condition. This demonstrates evolved intrasexual competition and mate display behaviour with a hormonal mechanism.

The Biochemical Basis of Attraction
The PDF source identifies a “love cocktail” of neurotransmitters and hormones involved in attraction:

































SubstanceRole in attractionDopamineMotivation and reward; drives goal-directed pursuit of a specific partnerNoradrenalineAlertness and arousal; the racing heart and sweating palms of early attractionSerotoninDrops in early love; associated with obsessive thinking about the partner (similar to OCD levels, Marazziti et al., 1999)TestosteroneIncreases sexual desire and motivates active pursuit of a partnerOxytocinReleased during touch and sex; deepens bonding and attachment in established relationships; suppresses amygdala activity, reducing anxietyVasopressinLinked to long-term pair bonding and mate guarding (Winslow et al., 1993 in prairie voles; Walum et al., 2008 in human males)

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsCross-cultural universality (Buss, 37 cultures) provides strong support for evolved preferencesMuch research is correlational: cannot establish that evolutionary pressures caused the observed preferencesBiological evidence (Fisher’s fMRI, Wedekind’s MHC, Ronay’s testosterone) grounds evolutionary claims in measurable mechanismsReductionist: reduces complex human attraction to biochemistry and genes, ignoring cognitive and sociocultural factorsParental Investment Theory generates clear, testable predictions that have been confirmed cross-culturallyAnimal generalisability: findings from prairie voles and mice are used to infer human behaviour; the leap is largeExplains sex differences in mating that are consistent across very different culturesSociocultural alternative (Eagly & Wood, 1999): sex differences in mate preference may reflect social roles and economic inequality rather than evolved psychologyConsistent with findings from multiple methods: survey (Buss), fMRI (Fisher), field experiment (Clark & Hatfield), naturalistic (Ronay)The contraceptive reversal (Wedekind) shows that modern technologies can disrupt evolved preferences, raising questions about how adaptive these mechanisms still are

IB Exam Relevance

























QuestionBest approach”Discuss evolutionary explanations for human behaviour”Buss (1989) as primary study; Clark & Hatfield as supporting; evaluate with Eagly & Wood’s social role theory as counter-explanation”Discuss biological factors in the formation of personal relationships”Fisher et al. (dopamine, motivational drive) + Wedekind (MHC, immune compatibility); evaluate reductionism”Contrast a biological and sociocultural approach to personal relationships”Fisher/Wedekind (biological) vs. Hazan & Shaver or Clark & Hatfield sociocultural framing”Evaluate the role of hormones in human behaviour”Ronay & von Hippel (testosterone) + Ditzen et al. (oxytocin)
Paired notes: Fisher et al 2005, Wedekind (1995), Buss (1989), Clark and Hatfield (1989), Ronay and von Hippel (2010)

Human-relationships/Human-Relationships.title: Human Relationships
Human-relationships/Human-Relationships.content:
PSY HRelations

The Psychology of Human Relationships is an applied option assessed in Paper 2 of IB SL Psychology, alongside Abnormal Psychology. You answer questions on your chosen option only. It examines personal relationships, social responsibility, and group dynamics through biological, cognitive, and sociocultural lenses.

The Three Topics





















TopicKey QuestionsPersonal RelationshipsHow and why do relationships form? How are they maintained? Why do they change or end?Social ResponsibilityWhy do people help or fail to help others? What promotes prosocial behaviour?Group DynamicsHow do groups form? Why does prejudice and discrimination occur? How does conflict arise and resolve?

Topic 1: Personal Relationships
Formation of Relationships
Relationships form through a combination of biological, cognitive, and sociocultural factors.
Biological approach:

Fisher et al. (2005): romantic love activates the dopaminergic reward pathway (VTA, caudate nucleus). Love is a motivational drive, not an emotion.
Wedekind (1995): women prefer the scent of MHC-dissimilar men, supporting an evolved mechanism for genetic compatibility in mate selection.
Buss (1989): universal sex differences in mate preferences across 37 cultures support evolutionary (parental investment) explanations.

Cognitive approach:

Hazan & Shaver (1987): adult romantic attachment styles (secure, avoidant, anxious-ambivalent) mirror childhood attachment patterns, mediated by the internal working model.
Markey & Markey (2007): people seek partners similar to themselves; some complementarity in dominance is associated with greater relationship satisfaction.

Sociocultural approach:

Clark & Hatfield (1989): gender differences in receptivity to casual sex reflect social norms and evolutionary pressures; 75% of men vs. 0% of women agreed to a stranger’s sexual proposition.
Ronay & von Hippel (2010): presence of an attractive female observer raised testosterone and increased risk-taking in young men, demonstrating mate display behaviour.


Communication in Relationships

Gottman (1999): the Four Horsemen (criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling) predict divorce. Contempt is the strongest predictor. Studied 124 newlywed couples over 6 years using SPAFF coding and physiological measures. Notably found the Active Listening Model was not supported.
Bradbury & Fincham (1992): attributional patterns predict satisfaction. Happy couples make relationship-enhancing attributions (situational for bad, personal for good). Unhappy couples show distress-maintaining patterns. Used 47 couples, observation + questionnaire, three coders.


Change and Dissolution

Gottman (1999): communication patterns in year 1 predict divorce years later. 17 divorces occurred in the sample after 6 years.
Felmlee (1995): fatal attractions: in 88/301 cases, the initially attractive quality became the primary reason for the breakup (fun becomes foolish, strong becomes domineering, spontaneous becomes unpredictable).


Topic 2: Social Responsibility
Bystanderism and Prosocial Behaviour

Piliavin et al. (1969): Arousal: Cost-Reward Model. On the NYC subway, a cane victim received help on 95% of trials; a drunk victim on 50%. Group size did not reduce helping in face-to-face emergencies, directly challenging diffusion of responsibility.
Darley & Batson (1973): time pressure overrode moral values; only 10% of seminary students in a hurry helped a slumped confederate, even after preparing a Good Samaritan speech.
Drury et al. (2009): shared social identity increased helping in a VR emergency simulation. Group identification, not individual disposition, determines prosocial behaviour in emergencies.


Topic 3: Group Dynamics
Prejudice and Discrimination

Tajfel (1971): minimal group paradigm showed that social categorisation alone produces in-group favouritism and out-group discrimination, even with arbitrary meaningless groups.
Sherif et al. (1954): competition produces intergroup hostility; superordinate goals reduce it. Contact alone did not reduce prejudice.
Steele & Aronson (1995): stereotype threat impaired Black students’ test performance under diagnostic framing but not non-diagnostic framing. Mechanism: threat consumes working memory resources.

Cooperation and Conflict

Sherif et al. (1954): realistic conflict theory: competition over scarce resources produces prejudice; cooperation toward superordinate goals reduces it.
Drury et al. (2009): shared identity promotes cooperation in emergencies.


The Three Approaches Applied Across All Topics

























ApproachKey LensExample StudiesBiologicalHormones, neurotransmitters, evolution, geneticsFisher et al., Wedekind, Buss, Piliavin (arousal)CognitiveSchemas, attributions, attachment models, decision-makingBradbury & Fincham, Hazan & Shaver, Steele & AronsonSocioculturalNorms, group identity, cultural context, social influenceGottman, Tajfel, Sherif, Darley & Batson, Drury

IB Exam Guidance
Paper 2 format: Same as Paper 1 — Section A (SAQ, 9 marks each) and Section B (ERQ, 22 marks). All questions are from Human Relationships only.
For SAQs: Pick one approach per question. Describe one study in APPR format and link it explicitly to the question.
For ERQs: Use 2-3 studies. Evaluate each one. Add holistic CT (e.g., cross-cultural limitations, ethical concerns, reductionism of biological accounts).
High-value contrast for ERQs: biological vs. cognitive approach to relationship formation (Fisher vs. Hazan & Shaver), or situational vs. dispositional explanations of prosocial behaviour (Piliavin vs. Darley & Batson).
