Human-relationships/Parental-investment-.title: Parental investment theory (Trivers, 1972)
Human-relationships/Parental-investment-.content:
PSY

Expanded Theory Sections for Clark & Hatfield (1989)

Evolutionary Theory of Mating Behavior
This is the main theoretical framework for interpreting the study.
It explains human attraction and mating preferences as adaptations shaped by natural selection to maximize reproductive success.
Parental Investment Theory (Trivers, 1972):


Core idea:
The sex that invests more in offspring (gestation, lactation, nurturing) will be more selective about mates.


Females: High biological investment (pregnancy, time, energy) → must be selective → seek mates with resources, protection, and commitment.


Males: Low minimum biological investment (sperm) → less selective → can maximize fitness by pursuing multiple partners.




Clark & Hatfield link:


Men’s high acceptance of casual sex supports the idea of a short-term mating strategy: maximize number of partners to increase reproductive success.


Women’s near-zero acceptance supports the idea of a long-term strategy: avoid risky short-term mating because of pregnancy risk and potential social costs.


 Sexual Strategies Theory (Buss & Schmitt, 1993):


Suggests men and women both use short-term and long-term mating strategies, but in different ways depending on context.


Men are generally more inclined to short-term mating if no constraints exist; women are more inclined to long-term unless resources and safety are guaranteed.



Cognitive Theories of Attraction**
Although evolutionary theory explains the biological side, cognitive factors also shape sexual decision-making:
 Schema Theory (Bartlett, 1932):


People develop schemas about what is “appropriate” behavior for men and women in sexual situations based on cultural norms and media.


Women may have internalized schemas linking casual sex to risk, reputation loss, or stigma, whereas men may have schemas linking casual sex to status or opportunity.


Clark & Hatfield link:

The study took place in 1980s USA, a time when social stigma for female sexuality was higher. Women’s schemas would discourage them from saying yes.

 Cost–Benefit Analysis (Cognitive Decision-Making Models):


People weigh risks and rewards before making decisions.


For women, the potential cost of casual sex (pregnancy, reputation, safety) outweighs the reward.


For men, the perceived costs are much lower, so the benefit dominates the decision.



Sociocultural Theories (Gender Role Theory)**
Social Role Theory (Eagly & Wood, 1999):


Gender differences in behavior are not just biological but also socially constructed.


Cultural norms and gender roles shape expectations:


Men are expected to be sexually assertive.


Women are expected to be sexually reserved.




Clark & Hatfield link:

In the 1980s, women saying “yes” to casual sex could face heavy social judgment. This cultural norm may explain the 0% female acceptance rate more than pure biology.


Example Exam Sentence (HL/SL)

“Clark and Hatfield (1989) provides strong evidence for evolutionary explanations of attraction, showing that men and women adopt different mating strategies due to differential parental investment. However, the results can also be explained by cognitive factors such as risk assessment and cultural schemas, as well as sociocultural factors like gender norms. This suggests that human mating behavior is best understood through an interactionist perspective.”

Human-relationships/Similarity-Attractio.title: Similarity-Attraction theory
Human-relationships/Similarity-Attractio.content:
PSY HRelations Human Relationships

Similarity-Attraction Theory proposes that people are attracted to others who are similar to themselves in attitudes, values, personality, and background. The greater the degree of similarity, the greater the interpersonal attraction. The theory was developed primarily by Donn Byrne (1971) through experimental research using the “bogus stranger” paradigm.

Core Claims

Attitude similarity is the primary driver of attraction. We are drawn to those who share our views because it validates our own worldview (reinforcement model).
Similarity reduces uncertainty and potential conflict, making interaction feel rewarding.
The relationship between similarity and attraction is roughly linear: more similarity predicts more attraction.
This applies across multiple domains: attitudes, values, personality traits, physical attractiveness level, and demographic background.


Key Supporting Studies
Byrne (1971) - Bogus Stranger Paradigm
Aim: To test whether attitude similarity causes increased attraction to a stranger.
Method: Laboratory experiment. Participants completed an attitude questionnaire. They were then given a questionnaire supposedly completed by a stranger, which was manipulated to show either high (75%) or low (25%) agreement with the participant’s own attitudes. Participants rated the stranger on attraction and likeability scales.
Results: Attraction ratings were significantly higher when the stranger’s attitudes closely matched the participant’s own. The effect was consistent across studies and replicated many times.
Conclusion: Attitude similarity directly causes increased attraction, independent of any real interaction.

Markey & Markey (2007) - see Markey & Markey (2007)
Extends the theory to real couples. Found that people describe their ideal partner in terms closely matching their own personality, and that similar couples report greater relationship harmony. However, some complementarity in dominance-related traits was associated with the best outcomes, qualifying the purely linear claim of the original theory.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsSubstantial empirical support: the bogus stranger paradigm has been replicated across many cultures and attitude domainsBogus stranger paradigm lacks ecological validity: rating a paper stranger is not the same as real relationship formationExplains a consistent real-world pattern: couples tend to share similar values, backgrounds, and attitudes (matched hypothesis)Attitude similarity may be a consequence of attraction, not a cause: couples grow more similar over time, making causation unclearSupported by real couple data (Markey & Markey, 2007): similar couples are more harmoniousComplementarity also matters: Markey & Markey (2007) found that some opposite traits (dominance) predict better outcomes, challenging a purely similarity-based modelAccounts for why homogamy (marriage within similar social groups) is universal across culturesOveremphasis on cognitive factors: ignores biological factors such as MHC-based mate selection (Wedekind, 1995), physical attractiveness, and evolutionary drivesUseful in explaining long-term relationship stability, not just initial attractionTheory does not explain why people are sometimes attracted to dissimilar others or why initial attraction based on similarity can fade (see Felmlee, 1995 - Fatal Attraction)

IB Connections

Approach: Cognitive; Sociocultural
Topic: Human relationships - formation and maintenance
Key Concept: Attitude similarity, reinforcement model, matched hypothesis, complementarity
Useful for: “Discuss the role of similarity in the formation of personal relationships” / “Evaluate one theory of the formation of human relationships” / “Discuss cognitive factors in human relationships”
Paired with: Markey & Markey (2007), Felmlee (1995), Hazan & Shaver (1987), Gottman (1999)
Contrasted with: Evolutionary explanations (Clark & Hatfield, 1989; Wedekind, 1995) which emphasise biological rather than cognitive factors in attraction



Key Concept - Similarity-Attraction Theory:
Byrne’s (1971) Similarity-Attraction Theory proposes that attitude similarity directly causes interpersonal attraction, because sharing beliefs and values with another person is reinforcing: it validates our own worldview and reduces conflict. The more similar two people are, the more attracted they will be to each other. While well-supported by experimental evidence, the theory has been criticised for its artificial methodology and for underestimating the role of complementarity and biological factors in real relationship formation.

Human-relationships/Stereotypes.title: Stereotypes
Human-relationships/Stereotypes.content:
PSY Sociocultural Social Identity Theory, Heuristics - Schema Theory, SCLT

A stereotype is an exaggerated oversimplification about an individual based on their group membership or physical features. It is a generalization, positive or negative, made about a group and then attributed to individuals within it. Stereotypes are a specific type of schema: a mental framework that organises and simplifies social information.

Sources of Stereotypes
Campbell (1967) identified two key sources:

Personal experience: direct interactions with members of a group, which may be overgeneralised
Gatekeepers: parents, media, school, and other cultural agents who transmit stereotyped beliefs through enculturation


Formation of Stereotypes
Stereotypes can be explained at multiple levels of analysis.

Cognitive Explanation: Illusory Correlation
As cognitive misers, humans use mental shortcuts called heuristics to simplify complex information and minimise cognitive effort. One such heuristic is the illusory correlation: the tendency to perceive a relationship between two variables when no such relationship actually exists.
When a minority group and a negative behaviour are both statistically rare, their occasional co-occurrence is disproportionately salient and memorable. This leads people to overestimate how often minority group members engage in negative behaviour, producing a negative stereotype with no basis in actual group differences.
Key study: Hamilton & Gifford (1976)

40 undergraduate participants read 39 behavioural statements about hypothetical Group A (26 members, majority) and Group B (13 members, minority).
The ratio of desirable to undesirable behaviours was identical for both groups (18:8 for A; 9:4 for B), so there was no real difference.
Participants significantly overestimated the number of undesirable behaviours associated with Group B and rated them more negatively.
Conclusion: stereotypes can form through purely cognitive mechanisms, without prejudice, conflict, or real group differences, purely because minority membership and negative behaviour are both distinctive.

Other heuristics involved in stereotype formation:

Availability heuristic: estimating the likelihood of something based on how easily examples come to mind; dramatic or memorable events involving out-group members are overweighted
Representativeness heuristic: judging individuals by how closely they resemble a group prototype
Confirmation bias: selectively attending to information that confirms existing beliefs while ignoring disconfirming evidence


Sociocultural Explanation: Social Identity Theory
Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) proposes that people categorise themselves and others into social groups. To maintain a positive social identity, people engage in positive distinctiveness: favouring the in-group and derogating the out-group. This process of social categorisation produces overgeneralised, often negative beliefs about out-groups.
Key study: Rogers & Frantz (1961)

Investigated prejudice and stereotyping in Rhodesian whites toward Black Rhodesians.
Found that the longer white Europeans had lived in Rhodesia, the more prejudiced they became.
Supports a conformity and SIT explanation: exposure to the dominant cultural group increased adoption of in-group stereotypes through conformity to social norms.
Challenges purely cognitive accounts: stereotypes are also actively reinforced through social belonging and cultural conformity.


Biological Underpinning
Stereotypes have neurological correlates that reflect their basis in schema and heuristic processing:

The amygdala is activated by out-group faces, producing a rapid threat-detection response before conscious evaluation occurs
Stereotypes are represented as neural networks: frequently activated associations become stronger through synaptic reinforcement (neuroplasticity)
Priming a stereotype activates its associated neural network, making related information more cognitively available (consistent with the availability heuristic)


Learning Explanation
Stereotypes can also be acquired through classical conditioning (Pavlov, 1927): repeated pairing of a neutral stimulus (e.g., a social group) with a negatively valenced unconditioned stimulus produces a conditioned negative response to the group. This explains how stereotypes can be transmitted through media, where groups are repeatedly shown in negative contexts.

Effects of Stereotypes
Stereotype Threat
Stereotype threat occurs when awareness of a negative stereotype about one’s group impairs performance on tasks relevant to that stereotype. The mechanism: threat creates anxiety which consumes cognitive resources (working memory), reducing performance.
Spotlight anxiety: the heightened self-consciousness of being a visible member of a stereotyped group in a relevant performance context.
Key study: Steele & Aronson (1995)

114 Black and white Stanford students completed a difficult verbal test.
In the stereotype threat condition (framed as a test of intellectual ability), Black students performed significantly worse than white students of equivalent SAT scores.
In the non-threat condition (framed as a laboratory problem-solving task), the performance gap virtually disappeared.
Conclusion: mere awareness of a stereotype is sufficient to impair performance, even without the individual believing the stereotype.

Spencer et al. (1999) extended this to gender: women underperformed on maths tests when told men typically do better, but not when no such framing was given.

Memory Distortion
Stereotypes shape what we remember and how we remember it, through schema-congruent processing:

Martin & Halverson (1983): children who were shown gender-inconsistent images (e.g., a girl playing with a gun) later misremembered them as gender-consistent (a boy playing with a gun), demonstrating schema-driven memory distortion
Allport & Postman (1947): in a serial reproduction task, participants misremembered a White man holding a razor as a Black man holding it, showing racial stereotypes can distort memory encoding
Payne (2001): priming participants with Black faces led them to misidentify harmless objects as weapons faster, demonstrating unconscious stereotype activation affecting perception


Prejudice and Discrimination





















TermDefinitionStereotypeA generalised belief (positive or negative) about the characteristics of a social group, attributed to individuals within itPrejudiceA negative attitude toward members of a group, based on stereotyped beliefs; an evaluative judgementDiscriminationBehaviour that treats members of a group differently based on their group membership; the behavioural expression of prejudice
Prejudice and discrimination do not always co-occur. A person may hold prejudiced beliefs without discriminating (e.g., due to social norms), or may discriminate without conscious prejudice (e.g., Fagot, 1978).

IB Exam Relevance

























QuestionBest approach”Explain one theory of the formation of stereotypes with reference to one study”Illusory correlation (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976): define stereotype, explain cognitive miser and heuristics, describe the study, link findings to formation”Discuss one or more theories of the formation of stereotypes”Hamilton & Gifford (cognitive) + Rogers & Frantz (sociocultural/SIT); contrast the two explanations”Explain one study of the effects of stereotyping on behaviour”Steele & Aronson (1995): define stereotype threat, describe study in APPR format, link to cognitive load mechanism”Discuss one or more studies of the effects of stereotyping”Steele & Aronson (1995) as primary; Spencer et al. (1999) as extension; Allport & Postman or Payne for memory effects
Linked studies:

Hamilton & Gifford (1976) - illusory correlation; cognitive formation of stereotypes
Steele and Aronson (1995) - stereotype threat; effect of stereotypes on performance
Tajfel (1971) - Klee or Kandinsky - social categorisation; SIT basis for stereotyping



Key Concept - Stereotype as Schema:
Stereotypes function as social schemas: mental frameworks that simplify the processing of information about groups. Like all schemas, they speed up social judgements but at the cost of accuracy. They are reinforced neurologically through repeated activation, which is why they persist even when individuals consciously reject them. The cognitive miser framework explains why stereotypes are so difficult to eliminate: effortful System 2 thinking is required to override them, and humans default to System 1 shortcuts under cognitive load.

IB-Psychology-IA-SL.title: IB Psychology IA SL
IB-Psychology-IA-SL.content:
IAs PSY
Psychology IA (3).pdf

Influence of the Order in Which Information is Presented on Perception and Decision Making
IB Psychology — Internal Assessment
Candidate code: lws302 Co-researchers: lws320, lws318, lws324 Word Count: 2187

Table of Contents

Introduction
Exploration
Analysis
Evaluation
Bibliography
Appendices


Introduction
Cognitive psychologists have developed multiple models to explain human cognitive processes. The dual processing model (Kahneman, 2011) explains human cognition through two systems. System 1 is fast but prone to errors and System 2 is slower but more accurate.
System 2 handles consciously monitored rational and logical reasoning for complex decisions. It is slower but more reliable than its counterpart; System 1 on the other hand, is responsible for “quick thinking” (automatic and intuitive decision-making). This system relies on the activation of pre-existing knowledge and mental shortcuts (heuristics) to optimise quick but less accurate responses (Stanovich and West, 2000).
Its reliance on heuristics is problematic as it can lead to systematic errors in judgment. Otherwise known as cognitive biases, these take place as humans are cognitive misers, and tend to rely on mental shortcuts as argued by Fiske & Taylor (1991). Heuristics have been described as “simple rules of thumb that help us navigate complex decisions but can sometimes lead to predictable errors” (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
One such bias is the Anchoring effect, where individuals base decisions on the first piece of information encountered (known as the ‘Anchor’). For instance, in Black Friday sales, displaying original prices alongside discounts can anchor consumer perception, leading to consumers perceiving discounts as more significant, hence increasing their willingness to spend. Strack & Mussweiler (1997) argued that “the anchoring effect occurs when there is only general knowledge about the value of something and little information besides the anchor value is provided.”
Strack & Mussweiler (1997) investigated how anchoring bias influences decision-making. They used an opportunity sample of 69 German undergraduates. Participants were tasked with a “general knowledge questionnaire” and first exposed to an implausible anchor, such as: “Did Mahatma Gandhi die before or after the age of 140?” In one condition, participants received a high anchor, while the other received a low anchor. Subsequently, participants were asked to provide an estimate of how old he was when he died. The study found that even absurd anchors influenced participant responses. Surprisingly, the low anchor had a greater influence than the high anchor.
Anchoring bias occurs because individuals rely on System 1 thinking, prioritizing speed over accuracy. When making university or career-related decisions, young students may rely on initial information rather than critically evaluating and investigating their options.
While Strack & Mussweiler (1997) examined anchoring influence in general knowledge tasks, this study explores whether anchoring bias extends to real-world decision-making. Specifically, our study aims to investigate whether the order of positive and negative information influences 15-year-old students’ judgment and perceptions of a university. Understanding how cognitive biases influence such judgements could inform strategies that promote more analytical and rational thinking among students.
Hypotheses
H₀: The order in which positive and negative information about a university is presented will have no significant influence on 15-year-old, northern Spain high school students’ perception of the university, as measured by their Likert scale rating (1–10) of willingness to attend. Students exposed to positive information first are predicted to show no significant difference in their median willingness-to-attend rating, compared to those exposed to negative information first (Negative Anchor).
H₁: The order in which positive and negative information about a university is presented will significantly influence 15-year-old, northern Spain high school students’ perception of the university, as measured by their Likert scale rating (1–10) of willingness to attend that university. Students who are exposed to positive information first are predicted to report a higher median willingness-to-attend rating and those who are exposed to negative information first (Negative Anchor) are predicted to report a lower median willingness-to-attend.

Exploration
This experiment used an independent sample design; participants were randomly assigned to either condition (A or B). Each participant received only one version of the review, preserving credibility and experimental integrity. This design avoided practice or fatigue effects and minimised demand characteristics, as exposure to both versions might have revealed the aim, compromising internal validity.
In Condition A (treatment group), negative aspects were presented first, serving as an anchor. In Condition B (control group), negative information was presented later to eliminate the anchoring effect.
Participants
The target population was a group of 15–16-year-old students from a private bilingual school in northern Spain, fluent in English and unfamiliar with IB psychology. An opportunity sample of 37 students, male and female (18 in condition A, 19 in condition B), was recruited via Year 11 homeroom teachers. Participants were chosen for being:

Fluent in English (avoiding language bias)
Unfamiliar with IB psychology and anchoring bias
At an age where educational decision-making becomes more relevant

This homogeneity limits generalizability, as cognitive processes may differ with age or cultural backgrounds.
Allocation
Random allocation of participants into experimental conditions was achieved using a random number generator, spreading variability across the two conditions and ensuring all participants had an equal chance of assignment.
Controls
To minimize rehearsal effects and encourage intuitive System 1 thinking, participants were given a 3-minute time constraint. Additionally, participants worked individually and in silence to prevent social desirability biases such as conformity. Standardized instructions and review materials were used for both conditions.
Ethical Considerations

Parental consent obtained for participants under 16 (see Appendix 5)
Participants were briefed (Appendix 1) on their right to withdraw from the experiment or withdraw their data at any moment
Participants were instructed to keep responses anonymous by not writing their names
All participants were debriefed (Appendix 3) after the study, eliminating any deception and undoing any stress or harm caused

Materials

Printed university reviews: Prevented demand characteristics and participants comparing versions or guessing the aim of the study.
Printed Likert scale rating paper: Ensured anonymity, avoided conformity effects and reduced peer influence. (Printing was preferred to avoid internet issues or distractions.)
Consent forms: Legal requirement for underage participants.
Random Number Generator: Ensured random allocation of participants into conditions and preserved anonymity.


Analysis
Raw data shown in Appendix 6.
Since the data was collected using Likert scales, which have ordered categories but the distance between categories is unknown or subjective, it is considered ordinal. The median was chosen as the measure of central tendency. The variability was measured using Interquartile Range (IQR), used to eliminate outliers that may distort interpretation.
Figure 1: Calculated data — Median and IQR




















Condition A (Negative anchor at beginning)Condition B (Negative anchor last)Median rating5.57.0IQR4.01.5
Students from Condition A, presented with the negative information first, reported a lower median willingness to attend the university (5.5) compared to students from Condition B, which received the negative information at the end (7.0). This suggests that the order in which information is presented does have a moderate influence (difference of 1.5 points on the Likert scale) over students’ perception, supporting the research hypothesis.
The box and whiskers plot (Appendix 7) provides further insight:

Condition A has a larger IQR (4.0), indicating greater variability when negative information was presented first.
Condition B has a smaller IQR (1.5), suggesting greater consistency in responses.
Condition A shows a wider spread of responses ranging from 2 to 9, whereas Condition B ranged from 3 to 8, suggesting greater response polarization in Condition A.
An outlier in Condition B was noted, where one participant rated significantly lower than the group.

Statistical Significance — Mann Whitney U-Test
Given the reduced sample size (N=37), independent sample design, and the ordinal nature of the data, a Mann Whitney U-Test was applied to assess statistical significance. The test was one-tailed with a significance level of 0.05 (p ≤ 0.05 indicating statistical significance).
Results (Appendix 8) support the research hypothesis:





















StatisticValueU-value87.5 (lower than critical value of 116 at p < 0.05)Z-score2.52211P-value0.00587
The P-value (0.00587) falls within the 0.05 significance level. If the null hypothesis were true, there would be a 0.587% probability of obtaining such extreme results. Thus, we confidently reject the null hypothesis.
Additionally, the mean rank difference (14.36 in Condition A vs. 23.39 in Condition B) reinforces the conclusion that information order influences decision-making. Students in Condition B, where negative information was presented last, had significantly higher willingness-to-attend ratings on average.

Evaluation
Our findings align with Strack and Mussweiler (1997), which demonstrated that individuals rely on an initial reference point when making judgements. In our study, Condition A (negative anchor first) participants reported a median willingness-to-attend rating of 5.5, whereas those in Condition B (negative anchor last) had a median rating of 7.0.
The Dual Processing Model (Kahneman, 2011) provides an explanation. Under time pressure and with limited context, participants likely relied on System 1 (fast, automatic, heuristic-based) rather than System 2 (slower, effortful, analytical). The first information presented (anchor) acted as a heuristic shortcut, explaining why those exposed to negative information first gave lower ratings.
Strengths

Independent sample design reduced demand characteristics and practice effects, since participants were only exposed to one version of the review.
Both conditions received identical content, differing only in the order of positive and negative information, effectively isolating the independent variable.
Use of standardized instructions and materials ensured consistency across conditions and minimized experimenter bias.

Limitations and Future Modifications
Limitation 1: Participant variability Differences in prior attitudes, familiarity with decision-making or susceptibility to cognitive biases may have influenced responses.

Modification: Pre-screen participants for similar levels of awareness or decision-making tendencies using a brief questionnaire.

Limitation 2: Generalizability The target population of 15-year-old bilingual private school students in northern Spain limits generalizability, as the sample lacks diversity in socioeconomic and cultural experiences. However, their age and inexperience could be a strength as it likely increased reliance on System 1 thinking, enhancing the anchoring effect.
Limitation 3: Ecological validity The controlled classroom setting may limit ecological validity.

Modification: Replicate the study in a more naturalistic setting, such as during a university fair.

Limitation 4: Attention span Some participants may have found the texts too long, leading to skim reading and shallow processing of the anchor information.

Modification: Simplify and shorten the review texts while retaining key information, and include embedded attention checks to identify disengaged participants.

Conclusion
Our findings are concurrent with those of Strack and Mussweiler (1997), showing consistency with the Dual Process Model and Tversky and Kahneman’s (1974) theory on cognitive biases and heuristics. The order in which information was presented showed a significant influence on the Likert scale score: those presented with negative information first showed a lower median score than those presented with positive information at the beginning.
Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude anchoring bias affects judgment and decision-making in 15-year-old bilingual high school students in northern Spain with no prior knowledge of IB psychology.

Appendix 3 — Debriefing

Thank you very much for participating in our experiment.
We hope this experience did not cause you any discomfort. Now that the experiment is complete, we’d like to explain the true purpose of the study. This research aimed to investigate how anchoring bias influences decision-making, even in situations as important as selecting a university.
What is anchoring bias? Anchoring bias is a psychological phenomenon where the first piece of information you receive becomes a reference point (or anchor) that influences your judgment — even when other information might be just as important or more relevant.
What did we do in this experiment? Participants were divided into two groups: In group 1, University A was presented with positive reviews first, followed by negative reviews, while University B was presented with negative reviews first, followed by positive reviews. In Group 2, the order was reversed. This setup allowed us to observe whether the order in which reviews were presented would influence your evaluation and preference between the two universities.
Why does this matter? We designed this study because anchoring bias can play a significant role in shaping real-life decisions, like choosing schools, universities, or even career paths. By understanding this cognitive bias, we can learn to be more aware of how initial information affects our thinking and improve decision-making strategies.
Bear in mind that even though your data will remain anonymous, you still have the right to withdraw your data.
If you have any questions or are interested in learning more about the final results of the experiment, feel free to contact us.
Thank you again for your participation. Do you have any feedback, questions or concerns?

Measurement of the extent pairs of related values of two variables tend to co-vary.


If one variable tends to increase with the other it is a Positive correlation. If one variable tends to decrease oppositely to the other its an inverse or Negative correlation.

Research-Methods/Observations.title: Observations
Research-Methods/Observations.content:
Qualitative Research Methods

Observations are a a Quantitative Research method, meaning it produces data in the form of detailed descriptions of behaviour.


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Behaviour is observed in a natural or controlled setting without researcher interference nor manipulation of variables


“Observations capture first hand information in a naturally occurring situation”
There are six types of observations:

Naturalistic: Subjects are observed in their natural environment
Controlled: Variables are purposefully controlled by researchers
Overt: Participants are aware of they are being observed
Covert: Participants are NOT aware of being observed
Participant: Researches integrate themselves in the group being observed
Non-participant: Researchers don’t interact nor become part of the group



                  
                  Note
                  
                

An observation can be more than one of these types at the same time
e.g. Naturalistic covert non-participant observation

When analyzing a study it is essential to look at:

Aim of the study and its purpose within its context.
The Participants, how where they selected? (Selection Method, Sampling, Credibility, Generalizability, Transferability and Bias). Why is that population of interest to the study? TheRepresentative nature of the sample
The Research Method (Eg. the above mentioned)
Design
Task and materials
Results
Interpretation


There are multiple Research Methods used in Psychology studies to study concepts.
Depending on the Aim/purpose of the study and its context one may be more conclusive than the others.
Some of the most Common Research Methods are:

Questionnaires, Surveys & Interviews
Focus Groups
Case Studies
Observations
Experiments
Correlational Studies?


Data collection techniques, is the IB’s term for the way data is collected
The technique may have the same name as the R.M., But not necessarily, in this cases the R.M. is the way you set up the study and the technique the way the data is collected.

Research Methods can be divided into two categories

























QualitativeQuantitativeQualitative data comes in the form of extensive and detailed information often in the form of text. It is the in-depth study of a particular phenomenon.Quantitative data comes in the form of numbers.Aims to go beyond what can be objectively measured and quantized. Into the realm of human experiences, interpretations and  meanings.-The Aim, is to arrive at or create numerically expressed laws that characterize behaviour of large groups of people.-Nomothetic approach. Oriented on deriving universal laws-Ideographic approach. In-depth understanding of particular case or phenomenonLooks at Variables: “Something that can take varying values”, any characteristic that is objective and quantifiable.Cannot directly study Constructs. Theoretically defined values (e.g. violence), cannot be directly observed. Data needs to be operationalized (expressed in terms of observable behaviour).-Case Studies-Observations (Naturalistic, participant…)-Interviews (Unstructured, Semi-structured, Focus groups)-Questionnaires-Experiments (Can be Field experiments, Quasi experiments, or natural experiments)-Correlational Studies (e.g. Surveys)

Within Quantitative research there are 3 main types of research.

Experimental studies: Look at Cause and effect inference. Manipulation of Independent variables (IV’s) and the effect of that manipulation over Dependent Variables (DV’s). All other potentially important variables are controlled to the maximum and are known as Controlled variables (CV’s)
Correlational Studies: Looks at Trends in Data, though descriptive studies. There is no manipulation done by the researcher over any variables. Variables are observed and their relationship quantified. It is common to correlate variables though the use of formulas. Relationships are not investigated but rather approached separately.
Descriptive studies: Looks at independent variables rather than relationships. They are used in both, Sociology and Psychology to conduct a broad investigation of a phenomenon before getting into the specifics. An common examples are Public opinion Surveys  where the distribution of answers to specific questions is measured.

Sampling


                  
                  Note
                  
                

A Sample is the group of individuals taking part in the study. Sampling, is the process of finding and recruiting the individuals


When looking at a study and it is important to differentiate between:

Population: The type of people whose behaviour we are interested in understanding
Sample: A small portion/number of people from the population chosen to represent its totality
Your sample is limited if you study only a certain or significantly small group of people. (This would be Sampling Bias).
Sampling Methods: The method used to select the sample from the population.
The sample techniques may affect the results according to the strengths and limitations of every method.


Credibility


                  
                  Note
                  
                

Degree to which results can be trusted to reflect reality. The results don’t reflect reality if there was some sort of bias on the study.


e.g./ In an interview, participants may actually guess the aim of the study and vary their responses.
e.g.2/ Researchers themselves may selectively notice supporting evidence and unintentionally ignore contracting evidence.
Is there is indication that potential sources of bias were controlled or eliminated, credibility is believed to be high.

Credibility can be increased using:

Triangulation (Method, Researcher or Different data sources)
Inductive Content Analysis (ICA)
Member checking




Bias: “Systematic deviation from the ‘truth’”
In experimental research bias comes in the form of confounding factors that may influence cause and effect relationships decreasing internal validity.
In correlational studies can occur in the level of variable measurement and level of interpretation of findings.

Biasses are systematic deviations agains something or someone that can affect the results.
Refers to the extent to which results reflect reality, if results do not reflect reality, there is Bias “traps”
Approaches in quantitative and qualitative research are different.

Social-Cultural-approach/Cognitive-Disso.title: Cognitive Dissonance
Social-Cultural-approach/Cognitive-Disso.content:
PSY Social Identity Theory



                  
                  Note
                  
                

If people behave in certain way that doesn’t fit their beliefs, they will change their beliefs to fit their behaviour.
Dissonance causes actual physical discomfort


Dissonance presents upon the presence of inconsistency between Acts Vs Beliefs


                  
                  Example
                  
                

“I smoke cigarettes” VS “I am aware that smoking is unhealthy”


Humans feel a need for consistency and tense when inconsistency is present, hence, will follow an accumulative process to solve or reduce that inconsistency as it generates tension or uncomfortable feelings.

Change a thought
Change an aspect of behaviour
Add a thought (as a form of compensation)
Trivialize the inconsistency

Social-Cultural-approach/Conformity.title: Conformity
Social-Cultural-approach/Conformity.content:
PSY Social Cultural, Abrams et al (1990) - Asch paradigm


Informational conformity
Normative
Referential conformity


Normative conformity stems from a desire for social acceptance, avoiding punishment, or gaining approval, while informational conformity is driven by the belief that others possess correct information, especially in ambiguous situations. Referential conformity is a broader concept where individuals conform to the standards and expectations of a specific reference group they identify with and aspire to join, which can encompass both normative and informational aspects of that group.



                  
                  Note
                  
                

Conformity refers to individuals changing their attitudes or behaviour as a result of real or imagined social pressures.
Conformity is a result of social comparison and indirect social influence.



Compliance


                  
                  Summary
                  
                

Refers to when individuals  change their behaviour publicly to fit in a group, while maintaining personal beliefs in private.

Identification


                  
                  Summary
                  
                

Refers to when individuals conform to a group behaviour due to the desire of being associated with them.



Internalization


                  
                  Summary
                  
                

Refers to when individuals adopt a group’s beliefs/behaviour both publicly and privately because they align with personal values.

Social-Cultural-approach/Cultural-Dimens.title: Cultural Dimensions
Social-Cultural-approach/Cultural-Dimens.content:
PSY Sociocultural Hofstede (2001), Berry (1967)

Cultural dimensions are spectrums of behaviour used to represent the norms and values of different cultures. Rather than describing individual behaviour, dimensions describe the general trends of a given culture and can be used to compare cultures with each other.
Hofstede’s framework is the most widely used model of cultural dimensions in IB Psychology. His research asked employees of the multinational company IBM to fill in surveys about workplace morale and values. He then carried out a factor analysis on the responses, focusing on key differences submitted by employees in different countries. This is an example of an etic approach: applying a standardized framework from the outside to compare cultures.
His original study covered the 40 most represented countries in the surveys. Hofstede (2001) later extended this with 30 years of data, claiming results stayed largely consistent.

The Six Cultural Dimensions

































DimensionDescriptionIndividualism vs. CollectivismThe degree to which people are integrated into groups. “I” vs. “we” orientation. In individualist cultures, everyone is expected to look after themselves and their immediate family. In collectivist cultures, people are integrated into strong, cohesive in-groups that provide support and protection.Power Distance Index (PDI)The extent to which a culture respects authority and status; the degree of acceptance of unequal distribution of power. High PDI cultures expect clear hierarchies; low PDI cultures prefer consensus.Uncertainty Avoidance Index (UAI)A society’s tolerance for ambiguity. High UAI cultures prefer strict rules and resist change. Low UAI cultures are more open to ambiguity and new ideas.Masculinity vs. FemininityMasculine societies are defined by a focus on achievement, competition, and wealth. Feminine societies focus on cooperation, relationships, and quality of life.Long-Term vs. Short-Term OrientationThe connection to the past and attitude toward the future. Short-term orientation values tradition and immediate reward. Long-term orientation focuses on perseverance and future benefit.Indulgence vs. RestraintIndulgent cultures allow people to enjoy life freely; restrained cultures suppress gratification through strict social norms. Indulgent cultures tend to believe they are in control of their lives; restrained cultures are more fatalistic.

For the exam: You only need to know one cultural dimension in depth. The IB focuses most heavily on individualism vs. collectivism, as it is the most widely researched and directly supported by multiple studies.


Individualism vs. Collectivism in Detail

































Individualist CulturesCollectivist CulturesUniqueness is valuedSocial harmony is valuedSpeaking one’s mind is importantModesty is importantSelf defined by individual achievementSelf defined by group membershipFreedom and autonomy are valuedCommon fate/history guides decision-makingRule-breaking leads to guilt and loss of self-respectRule-breaking leads to shame and loss of faceSelf-reliance is seen as a virtueShared responsibility and interdependence are a way of life
Markus and Kitayama (1991) captured this distinction with two proverbs: “In America, the squeaky wheel gets the grease; in Japan, the nail that stands out gets pounded down.” They argue that perceiving a boundary between the individual and the social environment is distinctly Western; non-Western cultures tend toward connectedness.

How Individualism vs. Collectivism Affects Behaviour
Conformity (Berry, 1967): Berry used an adapted Asch paradigm to compare conformity across three cultures. The Temne of Sierra Leone (collectivist, rice farming) showed significantly higher conformity when told what other Temne believed, even when it was incorrect. The Inuit of Baffin Island (individualist, hunting) showed lower conformity than even the Scottish reference group. Importantly, there was no significant difference within groups based on degree of Western exposure, suggesting that cultural identity itself, not degree of Westernisation, drives the effect.
Memory (Kulkofsky et al.): Social sharing of memories is stronger in collectivist cultures, where communal storytelling is a social norm. This produces stronger flashbulb memories for culturally significant events.

Evaluation of Cultural Dimensions Theory

































StrengthsLimitationsEnormous sample (116,000+ IBM employees); scores consistent across 30 years of dataIBM sample: corporate, educated employees are not representative of their national populationsFactor analysis with team-based coding; good inter-rater reliability between researchersResearcher bias in factor analysis: researchers decide which correlations are significant; risk of confirmation biasProvides a standardized, comparable framework across cultures; widely used in psychology, business, and diplomacyHofstede studied work environments only; attitudes toward work may not transfer to all areas of daily lifeEtic approach allows direct cross-cultural comparisonEtic limitation: dimensions are defined from a Western framework and may not capture concepts important to non-Western culturesConsistent with Berry (1967), Kulkofsky et al., and conformity researchCorrelational: cannot argue that culture causes these behavioursHofstede warns against the ecological fallacy himselfReduces complex cultural identities to numerical scores, risking stereotyping and stereotype threat

Ecological fallacy (Hofstede’s own warning): When comparing two cultures, it cannot be assumed that two individuals from those cultures must differ from each other, or that any one member of a culture will always demonstrate the cultural norm. Dimensions describe trends across populations, not universal rules for individuals.


IB Exam Application
Possible essay question (from your InThinking source):
“Discuss the role of one cultural dimension on human behaviour.”
Approach:

Define the dimension (individualism vs. collectivism)
Explain how it influences behaviour (conformity, memory sharing)
Use Berry (1967) and Kulkofsky as supporting studies
Evaluate the research (IBM sample, ecological fallacy, factor analysis bias, etic limitations)
Think globally: what are the difficulties of measuring culture? Can variables be operationalized? What assumptions must we accept?

Paired with: Hofstede (2001), Berry (1967), Kulkofsky, Lueck and Wilson (2010)

Social-Cultural-approach/Cultural-influe.title: Cultural influences on behaviour + cognition
Social-Cultural-approach/Cultural-influe.content:
PSY Sociocultural Cultural Dimensions, Berry (1967), Kearins (1981), Kulkofsky et al (2011), Hofstede (2001)

Culture is not just a backdrop to human behaviour — it actively shapes how people think, remember, perceive, and act. The sociocultural approach investigates how group membership, cultural norms, and shared values influence individual psychology.

What is culture?
A dynamic system of rules, explicit and implicit, established by groups in order to ensure their survival. It involves attitudes, values, norms, and behaviours shared by members of a group across generations.


Two Approaches to Studying Culture
Before studying cultural influences, it is important to understand the methodological approaches researchers use, as this affects what conclusions can be drawn.








































Etic ApproachEmic ApproachDefinitionStudies culture from the outside, using standardized tools applied across culturesStudies culture from within, immersing in that culture to understand it on its own termsGoalCross-cultural comparisonDeep cultural understandingMethodsExperiments, surveys, standardized tests, factor analysisObservation, interviews, case studies, culturally specific toolsStrengthsComparable, quantifiable, replicableRich insight, culturally valid, context-sensitiveLimitationsMay impose Western concepts on non-Western cultures; risk of ecological fallacyNot generalizable; time-intensive; researcher may go nativeExampleHofstede (2001): same survey applied across 40 countriesBolton (2001): immersive case study of cross-cultural validity of DSM diagnosis
The ecological fallacy (Hofstede’s warning): even when two cultures differ on average, you cannot assume that any two individuals from those cultures will differ, or that every member of a culture will demonstrate the cultural norm.

How Culture Influences Behaviour
Conformity
Berry (1967) demonstrated that cultural demands shape conformity. Using an adapted Asch line-matching task with three groups (approximately 120 participants each): the Temne of Sierra Leone (collectivist, farming society), the Inuit of Baffin Island (individualist, hunting society), and Scottish people as a Western reference group.

Temne participants conformed significantly more to incorrect group answers than either Inuit or Scottish participants.
Inuit participants conformed even less than the Scottish group.
No significant difference within groups based on degree of Western exposure, suggesting that cultural identity itself drives conformity, not current lifestyle.

This is based on Barry, Child & Bacon (1959), which proposed that hunting societies tend toward individualism while agricultural societies tend toward collectivism, due to the different survival demands of each.

Memory and Cognition
Spatial memory (Kearins, 1981): Aboriginal Australian children significantly outperformed white Australian children on a visual-spatial object reconstruction task across all four object conditions. Aboriginal children used direct visual encoding strategies; white children relied on verbal labelling. This shows that the cognitive strategies used in memory are not universal but are shaped by ecological and cultural demands. Crucially, Western-style cognitive tests underestimate the abilities of non-Western groups by measuring only the cognitive strategies valued in Western education.
Flashbulb memory (Kulkofsky et al., 2011): A cross-cultural study of 274 middle-class adults from five countries (USA, Germany, UK as individualist; China, Turkey as collectivist) found that:

Individualist cultures developed FBMs for a wider range of events, including international ones, placing emphasis on personal involvement and emotional response.
Collectivist cultures developed stronger FBMs for events of national or social significance, de-emphasizing individual emotional experience.
Social sharing was the strongest predictor of FBM strength across all cultures: the more an event was discussed with others, the more vivid and durable the memory. This effect was amplified in collectivist cultures where communal discussion is a social norm.


Cross-Cultural Validity of Diagnosis
Bolton (2001) used an emic approach, a case study with ICA (inductive content analysis) with 40 local participants, to investigate the cross-cultural validity of DSM diagnostic categories. His findings suggest that Western diagnostic frameworks may not translate accurately to non-Western cultural contexts, raising important questions about the ethnocentrism embedded in psychological classification systems.

Key Concepts for Exams
Enculturation: The process by which individuals learn and internalize the norms, values, and behaviours of their own culture. It is largely implicit and begins at birth through observation and participation in cultural practices.
Acculturation: The process of psychological and cultural change that occurs when individuals from one culture come into sustained contact with another. Berry (2005) identifies four strategies: integration, assimilation, separation, and marginalisation. Research (Lueck & Wilson, 2010) shows integration, maintaining both the original culture and adapting to the new one, produces the least acculturative stress.
Emic vs. etic: The emic approach yields culturally specific insight but cannot be generalized. The etic approach allows comparison but risks imposing Western assumptions onto non-Western cultures. Many researchers argue the ideal is a combined approach.

Linked Studies





































StudyKey cultural influence demonstratedBerry (1967)Culture shapes conformity; collectivist cultures conform more to group normsKearins (1981)Culture shapes cognitive strategies; ecological demands produce different memory abilitiesKulkofsky et al (2011)Culture shapes flashbulb memory formation and social sharing patternsHofstede (2001)Quantifies cultural dimensions across 40 countries; individualism vs. collectivism most relevantBolton (2001)Emic approach shows Western diagnostic categories may lack cross-cultural validityLueck and Wilson (2010)Acculturative stress is reduced by integration, not assimilation; bilingualism is protectiveBartlett (1932) - War of GhostsCultural schemas distort memory; British participants rationalized a Native American story to fit Western expectations

IB Exam Relevance





































QuestionBest studies to use”Discuss one example of a cultural influence on one behaviour”Berry (1967) for conformity; Kearins (1981) for cognition”Discuss one example of a cultural influence on one cognitive process”Kearins (1981) or Kulkofsky et al. (2011)“Explain the use of one research method in one study of cultural influences”Kearins (1981): quasi-experiment with matched samples and four conditions”Discuss one cultural dimension with reference to one study”Hofstede (2001) framework + Berry (1967) as supporting evidence”Discuss acculturation”Lueck & Wilson (2010) + Berry (2005) model”Evaluate an etic approach to studying culture”Hofstede (2001); standardized, replicable, but risks ecological fallacy”Evaluate an emic approach to studying culture”Bolton (2001); rich insight, not generalizable


Key Concept - Culture Shapes Cognition:
The most important insight from this topic is that cognitive processes once assumed to be universal, including memory strategies, conformity tendencies, and emotional responses to events, vary systematically across cultures. This is not because different cultures produce different types of people, but because culture shapes what skills are valued, practiced, and ecologically necessary. Kearins (1981) and Kulkofsky et al. (2011) together make this case across two different cognitive processes: spatial memory and flashbulb memory.

Social-Cultural-approach/Enculturation--.title: Enculturation - Acquiring your cultural norms + Acculturation
Social-Cultural-approach/Enculturation--.content:
PSY Sociocultural Cultural influences on behaviour + cognition, SCLT, Fagot (1978)

Enculturation is the lifelong process by which individuals learn and internalize the values, beliefs, norms, and behaviours of their own culture. Babies are not born with a culture; they develop one through interaction with gatekeepers such as parents, school, and the media, as well as through peers. Enculturation is not complete at any particular age — it is a continuous process that reinforces identity as a member of a culture.

Key Terms









































TermDefinitionEnculturationThe process, beginning in early childhood, by which cultural values, beliefs, and behavioural patterns are adopted by members of a societyCultural normsShared societal expectations that define what behaviour is appropriate, acceptable, or inappropriate within a cultureDirect tuitionTeaching children how to behave through reinforcing appropriate behaviour and discouraging inappropriate behaviour, either through praise or punishmentParticipatory learningChildren engage actively in a cultural activity and transfer that learning to later situations, without explicit instructionVertical transmissionThe passing of cultural norms downward from one generation to the next (e.g., parent to child)Horizontal transmissionThe transfer of cultural norms among peers of the same generationChannellingAdults indirectly guiding children toward culturally appropriate behaviour by structuring their environment and reinforcing certain activitiesValues enculturationThe enculturation of cognition: attitudes about social relationships, gender roles, time orientation, and beliefs about health, illness, and morality

How Enculturation Occurs
Enculturation does not happen through one mechanism alone. The PDF source identifies three main routes:
1. Direct tuition: Parents, teachers, or other gatekeepers explicitly tell children what to do and what not to do. Rewards reinforce culturally appropriate behaviour; punishments discourage inappropriate behaviour. This is the most visible form of enculturation.
2. Social Cognitive Theory (observational learning): Children learn by observing models in their culture and imitating behaviours that are reinforced. Vicarious reinforcement, seeing others rewarded for a behaviour, increases the likelihood of imitation. This operates without explicit instruction and often without awareness.
3. Participatory learning: Children engage in cultural activities alongside others, learning through doing rather than being told. Odden & Rochat (2004) demonstrated this in Samoa: children learned line fishing and understanding of the social hierarchy of the chief system entirely through observation and self-directed experimentation, with no adult instruction.

Enculturation and Gender Roles
One of the most studied examples of enculturation is the development of gender roles: socially constructed patterns of behaviour, attitudes, and expectations that a culture considers appropriate for boys and girls.
Gender roles are not innate; they are enculturated through:

Direct tuition: Parents explicitly encourage gender-appropriate play and discourage gender-inappropriate behaviour
Channelling: Adults structure children’s environments (e.g., toy selection) in gender-typed ways without necessarily being aware of it
Observational learning: Children observe and imitate gendered behaviour modelled by parents and peers


Key Studies
Fagot (1978) - Parental Reinforcement of Gender Roles
Method: Overt naturalistic observation of 24 families (12 with a boy, 12 with a girl). Children aged 20-24 months. Observed across five 60-minute sessions over five weeks using a checklist of 46 child behaviours and 19 parental reactions. Time sampling every 60 seconds. Two observers used to establish inter-coder reliability (0.93 for child behaviour, 0.83 for parental reaction). Parents also completed a questionnaire on sex-role socialisation after observations.
Findings: Parents reacted significantly more favourably to gender-appropriate behaviour and more negatively to gender-inappropriate behaviour. In a follow-up interview, parents’ self-perceptions did not match what was observed, indicating that gender socialisation is largely unconscious.
Link to enculturation: Demonstrates direct tuition and channelling: parents are transmitting culturally defined gender norms to children through reward and punishment, without being aware they are doing so.

Odden & Rochat (2004) - Observational Learning in Samoa
Method: Longitudinal study of 25 months on 28 children in a single Samoan village. Used both observations and interviews.
Background: Samoan culture has a very high power distance index. Social norms limit adult-child interaction time. Parents take a non-interventionist approach; children are largely left to learn on their own.
Findings: Young male children observed adult males fishing without any direct instruction. Around age 10, children would borrow adult fishing equipment and experiment independently. By age 12, most could fish alone. A multiple-choice test on the chief hierarchy system given to 46 twelve-year-olds found the majority had a broad understanding of the social rituals of their society, despite receiving no formal instruction on it until high school.
Link to enculturation: Demonstrates participatory learning and observational learning as routes to enculturation. Cultural norms, including both skills and social hierarchies, are acquired through active observation rather than direct teaching.

Kearins (1981) - Culture and Spatial Cognition
Aboriginal Australian children significantly outperformed white Australian children on visual-spatial memory tasks across all four conditions, despite object familiarity. This demonstrates values enculturation: the desert ecological environment, transmitted through parenting practices, language (cardinal directions), and songlines, shapes cognitive strategies across generations.
Link to enculturation: Cultural transmission of spatial skills through participatory learning (wayfinding from a young age), language structure (cardinal directions), and community practices (songlines) produces measurably different cognitive abilities.

Evaluation of Social Cognitive Theory as an Explanation of Enculturation

























StrengthsLimitationsTakes into account the social and cultural context in which enculturation occursCannot explain variation within cultures: why some individuals conform to gender norms more than others (e.g., non-conformists)Predicts that children acquire internal standards through reward/punishment, by personal or vicarious experience: supported by Fagot (1978)Since the majority of caregivers are women, boys and girls have very similar early experiences. SCT would predict more feminine gender identity across both sexes, which is not observedMultiple empirical studies support the notion of modelling (Bandura, Fagot, Odden & Rochat)Enculturation involves too many variables to be reduced to observational learning alone; direct tuition, participatory learning, and peers all contributeExplains unconscious transmission: Fagot showed parents were unaware of their gender-socialising behaviourDoes not account for the role of biology in gender development

SAQ Guidance: “Explain one study of enculturation”
The marking PDFs identify the following as required for full marks:

Define enculturation clearly and concisely
Choose a study that directly demonstrates the process or effects of enculturation (not just general learning)
Describe the study accurately: aim, participants, procedure, findings
Explicitly link the study back to enculturation, explaining what it demonstrates about how cultural norms are transmitted

Common mistakes (flagged in the marking PDFs):

Using Bandura’s Bobo Doll as the enculturation study. It shows how behaviour may be learned but does not directly show how a cultural norm is transmitted. It is of marginal relevance and scores only 2 marks.
Failing to define enculturation
Using an acculturation study instead of an enculturation study
Describing the study accurately but failing to link it back to the question

Best study for this SAQ: Fagot (1978). Score 7+ by: defining enculturation (including direct tuition), describing Fagot’s 24 families, naturalistic observation checklist, finding that parents reinforced gender-appropriate behaviour unconsciously, and explicitly linking this to enculturation as the process by which cultural gender norms are transmitted through reward and punishment.

IB Exam Relevance

























QuestionBest studies”Explain one study of enculturation”Fagot (1978) as primary; Odden & Rochat (2004) as alternative”Explain enculturation with reference to one human behaviour”Fagot (1978) for gender roles”Discuss one or more studies of enculturation of one behaviour”Fagot (1978) + Kearins (1981) as a cognition example”Evaluate Social Cognitive Theory as an explanation of enculturation”Odden & Rochat (2004) supporting; evaluation section above for limitations
Paired with: Fagot (1978), Bandura (1961), (1963) & (1965), Kearins (1981), Cultural Dimensions, Cultural influences on behaviour + cognition, Lueck and Wilson (2010)

Acculturation
Acculturation (Berry, 2004) is the process of cultural and psychological change that takes place as a result of contact between two or more cultural groups. At the individual level, it involves changes in a person’s behaviour, values, and identity. It differs from enculturation in a critical way: enculturation is acquiring the norms of your own culture from birth; acculturation is adapting to a different culture through sustained contact.
People may enter a new culture either voluntarily (migrant workers, expatriates, international students) or involuntarily (refugees, asylum seekers). The nature of this entry significantly shapes the acculturation experience.

Berry’s Four Acculturation Strategies (1974)
Berry proposed that individuals navigate acculturation along two dimensions: how much they value maintaining their original culture, and how much they seek a positive relationship with the new one.




















Positive relationship with new culture: YESPositive relationship with new culture: NOMaintain original culture: YESIntegration (bicultural)SeparationMaintain original culture: NOAssimilationMarginalisation

Integration: The individual maintains their original cultural identity while also engaging with and adapting to the new culture. The research evidence consistently shows this produces the best psychological outcomes.
Assimilation: The individual abandons their original culture and fully adopts the new one.
Separation: The individual maintains their original culture and minimises contact with the new culture.
Marginalisation: The individual cannot maintain the original culture (e.g., due to displacement or trauma) but is also excluded from the new one by discrimination. Associated with the worst psychological outcomes.

Berry argues the strategy chosen reflects both individual choice and the degree to which the host culture is welcoming or exclusionary.

Acculturative Stress
The tension between maintaining one’s original identity and adapting to a new culture often produces acculturative stress: the psychological, somatic, and social difficulties that accompany acculturation. It manifests as anxiety, depression, social difficulties, and physical symptoms. It is sometimes called culture shock.
A related concept is the acculturation gap: generational differences in the speed of acculturation within immigrant families. Children acculturate faster than parents through school and peer contact, creating tension when they live by different cultural expectations at home versus outside it.
Reactive identification: When discrimination is experienced, some individuals respond by strengthening their original cultural identity rather than integrating. This can be negative (hardening of oppositional attitudes) or positive (as seen in the Civil Rights movement, where a strong African-American identity became a source of empowerment).

Key Study: Lueck & Wilson (2010)
A nationally representative semi-structured interview study of 2,095 Asian Americans (including Chinese, Filipino, and Vietnamese). Interviewers were culturally and linguistically matched to participants. A randomly selected subsample was re-contacted to validate interview data.
70% of participants showed acculturative stress. Key predictors:

































FactorEffect on acculturative stressBilingual language preferenceSignificantly reduces stress: builds support networks in both communitiesEnglish-only preferencePredictor of higher stress: cuts off access to heritage community supportPerceived discriminationStrongest predictor of high stressFamily cohesion (shared values, closeness)Significantly reduces stressEconomic satisfactionLower stress among those satisfied with opportunities in the USWould migrate againLower stress among those who would make the same choice
Core finding: Integration, maintaining bilingualism and cultural ties while adapting to the new culture, is significantly more protective than assimilation. Simply learning English and abandoning the heritage culture increases, not decreases, stress.

The Immigrant Paradox
Research reveals a counterintuitive pattern: greater acculturation into the host culture is sometimes associated with worse health outcomes.

Alegria et al. (2007): Hispanics born in or long-settled in the US were more likely to be diagnosed with psychiatric disorders than recent arrivals.
Allen et al. (2008): Hispanic adolescents who speak mostly Spanish are less likely to use drugs and alcohol.

However, these studies are unidimensional: they only measure the relationship with either the host or heritage culture, not both. Wang et al. (2010), using a bidimensional approach with 119 Cuban-American students in Miami, found that biculturalism (high engagement with both cultures) was associated with higher self-esteem, lower depression, and lower anxiety. This suggests the paradox disappears when both cultural relationships are measured simultaneously.

Limitations of Berry’s Model

Focuses on the individual’s behaviour, not the behaviour or policies of the host culture.
Assumes four discrete categories; in practice, acculturation strategies may shift depending on social context (LaFromboise’s Alternation Model, 1993: people move fluidly between cultures depending on situation).
Implies a hierarchical relationship between cultures.
Too simplistic: does not account for reason for migration, cultural distance between home and host cultures, age of migration, trauma history, or socioeconomic status.


Methodological Challenges in Acculturation Research

Language: tests may be linguistically inaccessible or culturally interpreted differently
Representative samples: many variables influence the acculturation experience, making generalization difficult
Attrition: historically high dropout rates in longitudinal acculturation studies
Ethics: undocumented participants require strong anonymity protections; power dynamics between researcher and immigrant participant must be carefully managed; participants may not be familiar with their rights

The APA Presidential Task Force on Immigration (2012) summarized the challenge as: “Who is given tests in what language by whom, when, and where?”

IB Exam Relevance: Acculturation

























QuestionBest approach”Explain one study of acculturation”Lueck & Wilson (2010): define acculturation, describe method and key findings, link to Berry’s integration strategy”Discuss acculturation”Berry’s model (theory) + Lueck & Wilson (supporting integration) + limitations of Berry’s model”Explain one model of acculturation with reference to one example”Berry’s four strategies + Lueck & Wilson as evidence that integration produces least stress”Discuss ethical considerations in research on acculturation”Use the methodological section above; anonymity of undocumented participants, power dynamics, informed consent across cultures

Social-Cultural-approach/Fundamental-Att.title: Fundamental Attribution Error
Social-Cultural-approach/Fundamental-Att.content: The fundamental attribution error (FAE) is the human tendency to overestimate the influence of a person's character or personality (dispositional factors) and underestimate the influence of situational factors when explaining that person's behavior, especially negative behavior. For example, if someone cuts you off in traffic, you might think, “What a jerk!” (dispositional explanation), rather than considering they might be rushing to an emergency (situational explanation). This bias is prevalent in individualistic cultures and can lead to harsh judgments and misunderstandings.

Social-Cultural-approach/Minimal-Group-P.title: Minimal Group Paradigm
Social-Cultural-approach/Minimal-Group-P.content:
The minimal group paradigm is a psychological research method used to investigate the minimal conditions required for discrimination to occur between groups. It was developed by Henri Tajfel in the 1970s as part of his work on social identity theory.
Even arbitrary, meaningless group distinctions (like being told you’re in “Group A” or “Group B” based on a coin toss or preference for abstract art) are enough for people to show in-group favoritism and out-group discrimination.

How it Works:


Participants are randomly assigned to groups (e.g., based on trivial choices like preferring Kandinsky or Klee paintings).


They are not told who else is in their group and do not interact with other participants.


They are then asked to assign rewards or points to anonymous members of the two groups.


Results consistently show that people give more points or resources to their own group, even though group membership is arbitrary and has no real meaning.



Key Findings:
• Group identification happens quickly—even with minimal or meaningless group criteria.
• People favor their own group, even if it means the other group gets significantly less.
• This behavior forms the foundation of in-group bias, which plays a role in stereotyping, prejudice, and intergroup conflict
