Social-Cultural-approach/SCLT.title: SCLT
Social-Cultural-approach/SCLT.content:
PSY Sociocultural Bandura (1961), (1963) & (1965), Joy, Kimball & Zabrack (1986) - Notel Natural Experiment, Enculturation - Acquiring your cultural norms + Acculturation

Social Cognitive Learning Theory (SCLT) was proposed by Albert Bandura as an alternative to behaviourist accounts of learning. Where behaviourism argued that behaviour is shaped only by direct reward and punishment, Bandura argued that humans learn by observing others, retaining what they observe, and then choosing whether to imitate it. This makes SCLT both social (learning happens through watching people in a social environment) and cognitive (mental processes mediate between observation and behaviour).

Core claim: Behaviour can be learned vicariously, by observing a model being rewarded or punished for it, without the observer ever performing the behaviour themselves.


Key Concepts
The Model
A model is any person whose behaviour is observed and potentially imitated. Models do not need to be present in real life; they can be observed through media, film, or television. Factors that increase the likelihood of imitation:

Authority: models perceived as having expertise or power are more likely to be imitated
Attractiveness: physically or socially attractive models attract more attention
Similarity: observers are more likely to imitate models they perceive as similar to themselves (same sex, age, culture, in-group)
Liking: warm and friendly models are more likely to be imitated than cold, uncaring ones
Consistency: a model who behaves consistently across situations is more likely to be imitated than one whose behaviour varies


The Four Processes of Observational Learning
For imitation to occur, four internal processes must take place. The mnemonic ARMP (Attention, Retention, Motivation, Potential) covers all four.

























ProcessDescriptionAttentionThe observer must notice and attend to the model’s behaviour. Influenced by the model’s attractiveness, authority, and the desirability of the behaviour.RetentionThe observed behaviour must be encoded into memory and stored for later retrieval. Cognitive schemas help organise and retain what has been observed.MotivationThe observer must want to reproduce the behaviour. This depends on outcome expectancy: what reward or punishment the observer anticipates from performing the behaviour.Potential (Reproduction)The observer must be physically and mentally capable of performing the behaviour.
Components

























Factors Influencing social LearningFactors influencing imitation of modelAttention: attractiveness/ authority of the model, & desirability of the target behaviourConsistency: if the model behaved in a way that is consistent across situations, then the observer will be more likely to imitate the model than if the model behaves in different ways depending on the situation.Retention: Memory encoding/ integration and subsequentIdentification: there is a tendency to imitate models who ate percieved to be like usMotivation: Must want to replicate the behaviour and so understand the potential outcome of repeating the behaviour(“outcome expectancies”)Liking: Warm and friendly models are more likely to be imitated than cold, uncaring models.Potential: Observers must be physically or mentally able to carry out the behaviour - *Perceived capability = “self efficacy”, individuals with high self-efficacy recover quickly from set-backs

Vicarious Reinforcement
Vicarious reinforcement occurs when an observer sees a model being rewarded or punished for a behaviour, and adjusts their own likelihood of performing that behaviour accordingly, without ever having performed it themselves.

Seeing a model rewarded increases the likelihood of imitation.
Seeing a model punished decreases it.
This explains Bandura’s (1965) finding: children who saw the model punished showed less imitation, but when offered a reward themselves, they demonstrated they had learned the behaviour regardless — establishing the distinction between acquisition and performance.


Self-Efficacy
Self-efficacy is an individual’s belief in their own ability to successfully perform a behaviour. It is a cognitive factor that determines whether learned behaviours are translated into action.

High self-efficacy: the observer believes they can do what the model did, making imitation more likely.
Low self-efficacy: the observer doubts their ability, making imitation less likely even if attention, retention, and motivation are present.
Individuals with high self-efficacy recover more quickly from setbacks and persist longer in the face of difficulty.


Reciprocal Determinism
Bandura argued that behaviour, the person (cognitive factors), and the environment mutually influence each other in a continuous, dynamic relationship. This is called reciprocal determinism and distinguishes SCLT from simple stimulus-response behaviourism.

How SCLT Explains Enculturation
SCLT is one of the primary mechanisms through which enculturation occurs:

Children observe cultural models (parents, peers, media) performing culturally valued behaviours
Vicarious reinforcement communicates which behaviours are rewarded and which are punished within the culture
Self-efficacy develops as children successfully imitate behaviours
Over time, observed cultural norms become internalised standards for behaviour

Fagot (1978) shows this operating unconsciously: parents reinforce gender-appropriate behaviour through praise and criticism without being aware they are doing so. Odden & Rochat (2004) shows it operating without any direct instruction: Samoan children learn fishing and social hierarchy entirely through observation.

Linked Studies

























StudyWhat it demonstratesBandura (1961), (1963) & (1965)Lab evidence for observational learning, vicarious reinforcement, and same-sex model identification; 1965 follow-up distinguishes acquisition from performanceJoy, Kimball & Zabrack (1986) - Notel Natural ExperimentNaturalistic evidence: introduction of TV increased children’s aggression by 160%, supporting media modellingSt. Helena / Charlton et al. (2002)No increase in aggression after TV introduction; children watched with parents and did not identify with predominantly white Western TV models (out-group), supporting the identification and self-efficacy components of SCLTFagot (1978)Enculturation of gender roles through unconscious parental reinforcement; demonstrates SCLT in a real-world, naturalistic setting

Evaluation

































StrengthsLimitationsEmpirical support across laboratory (Bandura) and naturalistic settings (Joy et al., Charlton et al.)Cannot explain non-imitators: some children in Bandura’s study did not imitate the model despite meeting all criteria for SCLTAcknowledges cognitive processes (attention, retention, motivation) rather than treating humans as passive respondersIgnores biological factors: does not account for genetic predispositions to aggression or the role of hormones and neurotransmittersExplains learning that occurs without direct reinforcement, through vicarious experienceEcological validity concerns in lab-based studies: aggression toward a Bobo doll may not reflect real-world behaviourHas broad applied value: used in education, therapy (e.g., modelling in CBT), media regulation, and parentingReductionist in laboratory form: isolating one variable (model behaviour) ignores the full complexity of the social contextAccounts for cultural and contextual variation in behaviour: the St. Helena study shows that identification with the model is necessary for imitationStronger as an explanatory than a predictive model: cannot reliably predict which individuals will imitate and which will notReciprocal determinism makes it more dynamic and realistic than simple behaviourismEthical concerns in aggression research: deliberately inducing aggressive behaviour in young children raises significant ethical issues

IB Exam Relevance
SAQ questions:

“Explain Social Cognitive Theory with reference to one study” - Use Bandura (1961); define SCLT, describe the study in APPR format, link findings back to the components of SCLT.
“Explain one study of enculturation” - Use Fagot (1978) or Odden & Rochat (2004); Bandura is of marginal relevance for enculturation SAQs because the Bobo doll study shows general learning, not the learning of a cultural norm specifically.

ERQ questions:

“Discuss/Evaluate Social Cognitive Theory” - Use Bandura as primary study, Joy et al. and Charlton et al. as supporting/contrasting evidence. Structure: define SCLT and its components, evaluate Bandura (strengths and limitations), use Joy et al. as naturalistic support, use Charlton et al. to show the role of identification and self-efficacy in moderating the effect.
“Discuss one or more studies of enculturation of one behaviour” - Use Fagot (1978) and Joy et al. (1986); link explicitly to the SCLT mechanisms involved.

Key distinction for exams:
SCLT has stronger explanatory power than predictive power. It can explain why imitation occurs after the fact (what conditions were present) but cannot reliably predict in advance which individuals will imitate and which will not. This is a strong holistic critical thinking point for ERQs.


Key Concept - Acquisition vs. Performance (Bandura, 1965):
The most important theoretical refinement in SCLT is the distinction between learning a behaviour and performing it. Children who saw a model punished did not perform the aggressive behaviour, suggesting they had not learned it. But when offered a reward, they demonstrated the behaviour perfectly, showing they had learned it all along. This tells us that vicarious reinforcement does not determine what is learned, only whether it is performed. Exposure to media violence, for example, may teach aggressive scripts even when children do not immediately act on them.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Evolutionary-.title: Buss (1989)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Evolutionary-.content:
Study Biological Evolutionary Explanations - Human Relationships, Hormones In Human Behaviour

David Buss conducted a Cross-Cultural Survey with the aim of investigating whether sex differences in mate preferences are universal across cultures, supporting an evolutionary (biological) explanation for human relationship formation.

Aim: To investigate whether men and women differ in their mate preferences in ways predicted by evolutionary theory (parental investment and sexual selection), and whether these differences are universal across cultures.
Participants: Over 10,000 participants from 37 cultures across 6 continents and 5 islands, making it one of the largest cross-cultural studies in psychology.
Method: Cross-cultural self-report survey.

Participants rated and ranked 18 characteristics desired in a long-term mate (e.g., financial prospects, physical attractiveness, chastity, ambition, age).
They also indicated their preferred age difference between themselves and a partner.
Questionnaires were translated and back-translated to ensure accuracy.

Results:

Women consistently valued financial resources, ambition, and older age in a mate more than men, across nearly all 37 cultures.
Men consistently valued physical attractiveness and youth more than women, also across nearly all cultures.
Men preferred partners approximately 2.5 years younger; women preferred partners approximately 3.5 years older.
Differences were statistically significant and consistent across vastly different cultures.

Conclusion: The universality of sex differences in mate preferences supports an evolutionary explanation: preferences reflect evolved reproductive strategies shaped by parental investment (Trivers, 1972). Women invest more biologically (pregnancy, nursing) and select mates with resources and status; men prioritize cues to fertility (youth, physical attractiveness).

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsCross-cultural scope (37 cultures) greatly increases generalizabilitySelf-report bias: social desirability may distort responsesLarge sample size (10,000+) increases statistical reliabilitySurvey cannot establish cause-and-effect (correlation is not causation)Consistency across radically different cultures strengthens the biological argumentConcepts like “financial prospects” may not translate equally across all culturesSupports Trivers’ Parental Investment TheoryIgnores socialization; Eagly & Wood (1999) argue social roles, not biology, explain the differencesStandardized, replicable methodDemand characteristics: participants may have guessed the study’s aim

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Evolutionary explanations for behaviour; Human relationships - formation
Key Theory: Parental Investment Theory (Trivers, 1972); Sexual Selection
Useful for: “Discuss evolutionary explanations for human behaviour” / “Explain the role of biology in the formation of personal relationships”
Paired with: Clark & Hatfield (1989), Ronay & von Hippel (2010), Dabbs et al. (1995)



Key Concept - Parental Investment Theory (Trivers, 1972):
Women invest more in offspring biologically, so they are more selective in mate choice. Men invest less biologically, so they tend to maximize reproductive opportunities. This drives the differing mate preferences observed universally across cultures.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Genetics/Bouc.title: Bouchard et al. (1990)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Genetics/Bouc.content:
Study Biological Genetics And Human Behaviour

Thomas Bouchard et al. conducted a Natural Experiment using Twin Study methodology investigating the relative contributions of genetics and environment to personality, intelligence, and behaviour, by comparing identical twins raised apart from birth with those raised together.

Aim: To investigate the extent to which psychological characteristics (intelligence, personality, attitudes, and interests) are determined by genetic factors, by studying monozygotic (MZ) twins who were separated shortly after birth and raised in different environments.
Participants: 137 pairs of twins recruited over 20 years as part of the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart (MISTRA):

MZ twins reared apart (MZA): Genetically identical, raised in different families and environments
MZ twins reared together (MZT): Genetically identical, raised together (comparison group)
DZ twins reared apart (DZA): Fraternal (50% shared genes), raised apart

Participants were recruited through media coverage and self-referral from across the world.
Method: Natural experiment using twin study methodology.

Twin pairs were brought to the University of Minnesota for approximately 50 hours of medical and psychological assessment over one week.
Assessments included:

IQ tests (multiple standardized measures)
Personality inventories (e.g., Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire)
Physiological measures (heart rate, brain wave patterns, reaction time)
Interviews on life history, interests, values, and social attitudes


Concordance rates and heritability estimates were calculated for each trait.

Results:

MZ twins reared apart showed strikingly similar scores on IQ, personality, and interests, despite being raised in different environments.
IQ heritability estimate: approximately 70%, meaning roughly 70% of variance in IQ scores was attributable to genetic factors.
Personality heritability estimates: approximately 50% for most traits (e.g., extraversion, neuroticism, conscientiousness).
MZA twins were nearly as similar as MZT twins on most measures, suggesting the shared environment of growing up together contributes relatively little beyond genetic similarity.
Some pairs showed remarkable behavioural similarities (e.g., same hobbies, mannerisms, and preferences) despite having never met.

Conclusion: Genetic factors account for a substantial proportion of variance in intelligence, personality, and many behaviours. The similarity between MZA twins, who share only genes and not environment, provides strong evidence for the role of heredity in shaping human behaviour.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsMZA design is the most powerful test of genetic influence: removes shared environment as a confoundSelf-selected sample: twins volunteered after media coverage; may not be representativeLarge, diverse sample (137 pairs, recruited internationally) increases reliabilitySelective placement: adoption agencies sometimes matched twins to similar families, confounding the environment/genes separationMultiple standardized measures across a week of assessment; high methodological rigourMZ twins share a prenatal environment; prenatal influences may account for some similarityHeritability estimates are consistent with other twin and adoption studiesHeritability is population-specific: estimates apply to the sampled population and environment, not universallyFoundational for behavioural genetics; directly informs the nature-nurture debateDoes not identify which specific genes are responsible; heritability does not mean genetic determinism

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Genetics and behaviour; Nature-nurture debate
Key Concept: Heritability, concordance rates, MZ vs DZ twins, nature vs nurture
Useful for: “Explain the use of twin studies in the study of inheritance of behaviour” / “Discuss genetic explanations of behaviour” / “Evaluate research methods in the biological approach”
Paired with: Caspi et al. (2003), Kendler et al. (1992)



Key Concept - Heritability:
Heritability refers to the proportion of variance in a trait within a population that is attributable to genetic differences. Bouchard et al. (1990) found heritability estimates of around 70% for IQ and 50% for personality. Critically, heritability does not mean a trait is fixed or unchangeable; it means that, within the studied population and environment, genetic differences account for more of the variation than environmental differences do.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Genetics/Casp.title: Caspi et al. (2003)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Genetics/Casp.content:
Study Biological Genetics And Human Behaviour

Caspi et al. (2003) conducted a Correlational Study investigating the role of gene mutation (particularly the 5-HTT serotonin transporter gene) in the development of major depressive disorder (MDD).

Aim: To investigate the evidence for a gene-environment interaction for a mutation of the serotonin transporter gene (5-HTT) (involved in the re-uptake of serotonin in brain synapses)
Participants: 847 New Zealand 26-year-olds from the Dunedin Longitudinal Study, assessed for mental health on an every-other-year basis until age 21. Participants were grouped by genotype:
- Group 1: two short alleles (s/s)
- Group 2: one short, one long allele (s/l)
- Group 3: two long alleles (l/l)
Roughly 43% of people carry shorter alleles.
Method: correlational study,

Genetic analysis: DNA samples taken to determine 5-HTT genotype.
Stressful life events questionnaire: Participants self-reported frequency of 14 different stressful events between ages 21-26 (financial, employment, health and relationship stressors).
Depression: Assessed via structured psychiatric interviews.

Results:

Participants with 1+ short alleles demonstrated more symptoms of depression and suicidal ideation in response to stressful life events.
The effect was stronger for those with 3+ stressful life events. Interaction of the genes with stressful life events increased one’s likelihood of developing depression.
Those with long alleles (l/l) were more resilient to depression even under high stress.
Genotype alone (with no stressors) showed no significant difference in depression rates, confirming the interaction effect.


In a later study by Wilhelm et al (2006), the researcher looked at DNA samples from 127 people who were part of a longitudinal (25y - 5 year interval recordings of major life events and signs of depression) prospective study looking at mental health. 80% of those with s/s alleles became depressed after 3+ more negative life events in a year, while only 30% of those with l/l alleles developed illness in similar situations.

The study also found that childhood maltreatment predicted adult depression only among individuals carrying a short allele.


Conclusion: The 5-HTT gene does not cause depression directly, but moderates stress sensitivity, supporting the diathesis-stress model: genetic vulnerability + environmental stress = increased risk.

Evaluation

































StrengthsLimitationsSupporting Research and evidence (e.g., Wilhelm et al)Stressful life events were self-reported, so subjective and prone to recall bias. It may be the salience of life events which plays a role in depression.Large sample from the Dunedin study increases reliability.Sample is largely white New Zealanders, limiting cultural generalizability.also is a sample used to being studied from longitudinal study.Objective biological measures (DNA) increase internal validityAssumption that serotonin causes depressionSupports the diathesis-stress model of depressionDepression is polygenic, so we cannot isolate the 5-HTT gene as the sole factor. + some participants became depressed without carrying the s/s allelesMethodological triangulation (genetic testing, questionnaire)Ethical concerns around DNA use without full initial disclosureFailure of replication of results in later studies e.g., Risch et al (2009) ∴ low reliability

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Genetics and behaviour; Abnormal psychology (depression)
Key Concept: Gene-environment interaction; Diathesis-stress model
Useful for: Research methods in the biological approach | “Discuss the interaction between genetics and the environment” / “To what extent does genetic inheritance influence behaviour?”
Paired with: Maguire (2000), Raine et al. (1997), HM case study



Key Concept - Diathesis-Stress Model:
The diathesis-stress model proposes that a genetic predisposition (diathesis) alone is not sufficient to cause a disorder. It is the combination of genetic vulnerability and environmental stressors that triggers expression of the disorder. Caspi et al. (2003) demonstrates this directly: the 5-HTT short allele increased sensitivity to stress, but participants with no stressful life events showed no significant difference in depression rates regardless of genotype. The gene moderates the response to stress; it does not cause depression on its own.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Genetics/Kend.title: Kendler et al. (2006)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Genetics/Kend.content:
Study Biological Genetics And Human Behaviour

Kendler et al. conducted a Large-Scale Twin Study investigating the heritability of major depressive disorder (MDD), gender differences in that heritability, and whether genetic and environmental factors differ across generations.

Aim: To investigate three questions:

Whether the previously estimated 35-45% heritability of major depression holds in a large Swedish sample.
Whether there are significant gender differences in heritability of major depression.
Whether genetic and environmental factors differ across time (birth cohorts).

Participants: 15,493 complete twin pairs from the Swedish Twin Registry. Only twins whose zygosity could be verified were included. Included male-male MZ/DZ, female-female MZ/DZ, and male-female DZ pairs.
Method: Twin study using telephone interviews.

A team of trained interviewers conducted telephone interviews between March 1998 and January 2003.
Lifetime major depression was assessed using modified DSM-IV criteria.
8,056 twins met criteria for a diagnosis of major depression at some point in their lives; 322 voluntarily reported antidepressant treatment history.
Interviewers also measured shared environment (years living together) and individual-specific environment (adult personal life events).

Results:



































Sex and ZygosityTwin PairsConcordanceFemale-Female MZ2,3170.44Female-Female DZ3,1850.16Male-Male MZ1,7740.31Male-Male DZ2,5840.11Male-Female DZ5,6330.11

MZ concordance was significantly higher than DZ in both sexes, confirming a genetic contribution.
Concordance rates were significantly higher in women than men, suggesting heritability is greater for females.
Heritability estimate: 0.38 (38%), consistent with prior research.
No correlation was found between the number of years twins lived together and lifetime major depression, suggesting the shared family environment contributes little.
No significant differences in the role of genetic or environmental factors across three birth cohorts (spanning 1900-1958), including pre and post-World War II.
Some genetic risk factors for major depression appear to be sex-specific.

Conclusion: Major depression has a moderate but consistent heritability (~38%), which is higher in women than men. The individual-specific environment (unique personal life events) contributes more to depression risk than the shared environment. Genetic risk factors are partially sex-specific.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsVery large sample (15,493 twin pairs): one of the largest twin studies on depression ever conductedCorrelational: cannot establish cause-and-effect; no specific genes were identified or testedResults are consistent with prior research (35-45% heritability), strengthening reliabilitySelf-reported life events and depression history: men may under-report depression, inflating apparent gender differencesVerified zygosity: only twins with confirmed MZ/DZ status were included, increasing internal validityDiagnosis was not made directly by interviewers: they accepted clinical diagnoses reported by participants, which may be unreliable; telephone diagnosis is of questionable validityDirectly addresses gender differences in heritability, an underexplored areaTwin registry sample: volunteers may not represent the general populationConsistent with diathesis-stress model: individual-specific environment (stressful life events) matters more than shared environmentCannot determine which specific genes are involved in the 38% heritable component

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Genetics and behaviour; Depression; Twin studies as a research method
Key Concept: Heritability, MZ/DZ concordance, sex-specific genetic risk, individual vs. shared environment
Useful for: “Discuss genetic explanations of behaviour” / “Evaluate the use of twin studies in psychology” / “Discuss the role of genetics in one behaviour or disorder”
Paired with: Caspi et al. (2003), Bouchard et al. (1990)



Key Concept - MZ vs DZ Concordance Rates:
If depression were entirely genetic, MZ concordance would be 100%. If entirely environmental, MZ and DZ rates would be equal. Kendler et al. (2006) found female MZ concordance (0.44) significantly higher than female DZ (0.16), giving a heritability estimate of 0.38. The fact that concordance is far from 100% even in genetically identical twins confirms that environment, specifically individual life experiences rather than shared family environment, plays the larger role in whether the genetic predisposition is expressed.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Hormones/Dabb.title: Dabbs et al. (1995)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Hormones/Dabb.content:
Study Biological Hormones In Human Behaviour

James Dabbs et al. conducted a Quasi-Experiment / Correlational Study investigating the relationship between testosterone levels and violent criminal behaviour, providing biological evidence for the role of hormones in aggression.

Aim: To investigate whether higher testosterone levels are associated with more violent crimes and antisocial behaviour in male prison inmates.
Participants: 692 adult male prison inmates in the United States, drawn from a larger prison population.
Method: Quasi-experiment / correlational study.

Saliva samples were collected from each inmate to measure testosterone levels non-invasively.
Prison records were reviewed for type of crime committed, disciplinary infractions, and parole board decisions.
Statistical correlations were calculated between testosterone levels and each behavioural measure.

Results:

Inmates with higher testosterone levels were significantly more likely to have committed violent crimes (e.g., rape, murder, assault) compared to those with lower levels who had committed non-violent crimes (e.g., theft, drug offences).
High-testosterone inmates also had more prison disciplinary violations and were more likely to be denied parole.
The relationship was statistically significant but the effect size was modest, suggesting testosterone is one of many factors.

Conclusion: There is a positive correlation between testosterone and violent/antisocial behaviour, supporting a biological explanation for aggression. However, the correlation does not establish causation, and social/environmental factors also play a significant role.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsObjective biological measure (saliva samples), less prone to social desirability biasCorrelational: cannot establish cause-and-effect. Aggression could raise testosterone, not the reverseLarge sample (692) increases statistical reliabilityAndrocentric: all-male sample; findings cannot be generalized to womenUses official prison records, reducing self-report biasSampling bias: prison population is not representative of the general populationContributes to biological explanations of aggressionIgnores socialization, culture, and situational factors that also influence aggressionNon-invasive data collection (saliva) is ethically soundThe modest effect size suggests testosterone alone is insufficient as an explanation

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Hormones and behaviour; Aggression
Key Concept: Testosterone as a hormonal influence on behaviour
Useful for: “Discuss the role of hormones in human behaviour” / “Evaluate a biological explanation of aggression”
Paired with: Raine et al. (1997), Buss (1989), Caspi et al. (2003)



Key Concept - Testosterone & Aggression:
Testosterone is an androgen produced primarily in the testes. It has been linked to dominance-seeking and aggressive behaviour. However, the relationship is bidirectional: testosterone can increase aggression, but aggressive situations and victories can also raise testosterone levels (the ‘challenge hypothesis’).

Studies/Biological-Studies/Hormones/Newc.title: Newcomer et al. (1999)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Hormones/Newc.content:
Study Biological Hormones In Human Behaviour

John Newcomer et al. conducted a Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Experiment investigating the effect of cortisol (a stress hormone) on verbal declarative memory in healthy human participants, directly testing the causal role of cortisol in cognitive impairment.

Aim: To investigate whether elevated cortisol levels, comparable to those found during major stress or illness, impair verbal declarative memory in healthy adults.
Participants: 51 healthy adults randomly assigned to three conditions. Participants had no history of psychiatric or medical conditions that could affect cortisol levels or memory.
Method: Double-blind, placebo-controlled experiment with independent groups design.

























GroupConditionCortisol doseGroup 1High-dose cortisol160 mg/day for 4 daysGroup 2Low-dose cortisol40 mg/day for 4 daysGroup 3PlaceboSugar pill for 4 days

After 4 days of treatment, participants completed a verbal declarative memory test: they listened to a prose passage and were tested on recall of its content.
Blood samples were taken to verify cortisol levels in each condition.
Participants and experimenters were blind to condition assignment.

Results:

The high-dose cortisol group showed significantly worse verbal declarative memory than both the low-dose and placebo groups.
The low-dose cortisol group showed no significant difference from the placebo group.
The memory impairment in the high-dose group was reversible: when cortisol administration stopped, memory performance returned to baseline levels.
Blood cortisol levels in the high-dose condition were comparable to those found in patients experiencing major medical illness or severe psychological stress.

Conclusion: High levels of cortisol, equivalent to those produced during severe stress, causally impair verbal declarative memory in healthy adults. The effect is dose-dependent and reversible, suggesting cortisol interferes with hippocampal memory consolidation rather than causing permanent damage.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsDouble-blind design eliminates experimenter and participant biasArtificial administration: cortisol was taken orally, which differs from the natural stress-induced release via the HPA axisExperimental design with random allocation allows cause-and-effect conclusionsShort duration (4 days): does not reflect the effects of chronic stress-related cortisol elevationReversibility finding rules out permanent damage; isolates the mechanism to temporary hippocampal disruptionHealthy adult sample may not represent those with chronic stress conditions, where cortisol effects may differCortisol doses were clinically validated to match real-world stress levels, increasing ecological relevanceOnly verbal declarative memory was tested; other memory types and cognitive functions were not assessedSupports the broader literature on the HPA axis and stress-memory relationshipEthical concerns: administering high doses of cortisol to healthy participants carries medical risk

IB Connections

Approach: Biological; Cognitive
Topic: Hormones and behaviour; Emotion and cognition; Stress and memory
Key Concept: Cortisol, HPA axis, verbal declarative memory, hippocampus, stress and cognition
Useful for: “Discuss the effect of one or more hormones on human behaviour” / “Evaluate the role of hormones in one cognitive process” / “Discuss the relationship between stress and memory”
Paired with: McGaugh & Cahill (1995), Dabbs et al. (1995), Ronay and von Hippel (2010)



Key Concept - Cortisol & the Hippocampus:
Cortisol is the primary stress hormone released via the HPA axis (hypothalamus, pituitary gland, adrenal cortex). While short-term cortisol release can enhance memory consolidation for emotionally significant events (cf. McGaugh & Cahill), prolonged or excessive cortisol exposure impairs the hippocampus, the region critical for declarative memory. Newcomer et al. (1999) demonstrates this causal relationship directly: high cortisol impairs verbal memory in a dose-dependent, reversible manner.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Localization-.title: HM (Milner, 1996)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Localization-.content:
Localization of function, Biological  Study


Milner conducted a Longitudinal Case Study on Henry Molaison (HM), one of the most studied individuals in the history of neuroscience, whose specific pattern of memory loss following brain surgery provided landmark evidence for the localization of memory function and the role of the hippocampus.


Background:

Henry Molaison suffered a cycling accident at age 7, leading to severe epilepsy from age 10.
By age 27, seizures had become so debilitating that they prevented a normal life.
With family consent, HM underwent experimental surgery in which sections of the medial temporal lobe (including most of the hippocampus, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex) were bilaterally removed.
The surgery successfully reduced seizures, but produced unexpected and profound memory changes.

Aim: To investigate and document the nature of HM’s memory impairment following bilateral hippocampal removal, and what this reveals about the role of the hippocampus in memory.
Method: Case study using method triangulation:

Psychometric testing (IQ testing; HM’s IQ remained in the normal range)
Direct behavioural observation
Structured interviews
Cognitive memory testing (recall, recognition, learning tasks)
MRI scanning by Corkin (1997) to confirm extent of damage

Results - HM’s Memory Profile:



































Memory TypeIntact?DetailsLong-term memories (pre-surgery)IntactChildhood and pre-surgery memories were largely preservedProcedural memoryIntactCould learn new motor skills (e.g., mirror drawing task), improving with practice even without remembering doing itShort-term memory (working memory)IntactCould hold information briefly in mindNew episodic memoryImpairedCould not form new memories of events (anterograde amnesia)New semantic memoryImpairedCould not learn new factual information
Key Insight: HM could improve on motor tasks through practice, showing procedural memory is preserved, but would have no recollection of having practised, demonstrating a clear dissociation between explicit (declarative) and implicit (procedural) memory systems.
Conclusion: The hippocampus is not the site of permanent memory storage but is essential for consolidating and organizing new explicit memories (episodic and semantic). Without it, new declarative memories cannot be formed, but procedural learning remains intact.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsMethod triangulation (psychometric, observational, interview, MRI) increases validity and reliabilitySingle case study: HM’s brain damage was unique; cannot generalize directlyProvided the first clear evidence for separate memory systems (explicit vs. implicit)HM’s surgery removed multiple structures, making it impossible to isolate the hippocampus aloneLongitudinal: HM was studied for over 40 years, providing rich, detailed dataEthical concerns: HM could not consent to ongoing research due to his amnesia (family consented)Revolutionized the neuroscience of memory and inspired decades of researchHM may have had pre-existing abnormalities due to long-term epilepsyConsistent with Maguire (2000) and Draganski (2004) on hippocampal functionCannot establish exactly what each removed region contributed individually

IB Connections

Approach: Biological; Cognitive
Topic: Localization of function; Models of memory; Case study as a research method
Key Concept: Hippocampus, anterograde amnesia, explicit vs. implicit memory, procedural vs. declarative memory
Useful for: “Discuss localization of function” / “Evaluate case studies as a research method” / “Discuss models of memory”
Paired with: KF case study (Warrington & Shallice, 1970), Maguire (2000), Atkinson & Shiffrin (1968)



Key Concept - Anterograde Amnesia:
Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new long-term memories after a brain injury, while old memories remain intact. HM’s case proved that the hippocampus is essential for the consolidation of new explicit (declarative) memories. It also demonstrated that procedural memory (implicit) is stored elsewhere, likely in the basal ganglia and cerebellum, leading to the modern understanding of multiple memory systems.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.title: Draganski (2004)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.content:
Biological Study  Neuroplasticity

Draganski et al. conducted a Field Experiment using MRI scans to investigate whether learning a new motor skill (juggling) produces measurable structural changes in grey matter, directly demonstrating both neuroplasticity and neural pruning in the same participants.

Aim: To investigate whether learning to juggle causes structural changes in grey matter density in the brain, and whether these changes reverse after training stops, demonstrating both plasticity and synaptic pruning.
Participants: 24 volunteers (21 female, 3 male), aged 20-24, with no prior juggling experience, randomly assigned to:

Juggling group (n = 12): taught a three-ball cascade juggling routine and asked to practice until mastered
Non-juggling control group (n = 12): no training throughout the study

Method: Field experiment with 3 MRI scan time points. Because participants practiced at home, the IV was manipulated under natural rather than fully controlled conditions, classifying this as a field experiment.

Scan 1 (Baseline): Before training began; both groups scanned to confirm no initial grey matter differences.
Scan 2 (Post-learning): After the juggling group notified researchers they had mastered the routine; control group scanned again at the same time.
Scan 3 (After 3-month rest): Both groups scanned again after the juggling group stopped practicing.
Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was used to measure changes in grey matter density across the brain.

Results:

At baseline, there were no significant differences in grey matter between the two groups.
After learning, the juggling group showed significantly increased grey matter density in the mid-temporal area (V5/MT) in both hemispheres, a region associated with visual motion processing and the perception and spatial anticipation of moving objects.
The control group showed no changes throughout the study.
After the 3-month rest period, the grey matter in the jugglers partially decreased back toward baseline, demonstrating synaptic pruning.
Notably, changes appeared in the visual memory area rather than the cerebellum or basal ganglia, suggesting juggling relies more on visual-spatial memory than on procedural memory.

Conclusion: Learning a new skill causes measurable structural changes in grey matter in areas relevant to that skill, driven by Long Term Potentiation (LTP): repeated activation of neural pathways strengthens synaptic connections and produces dendritic branching. When training stops, reduced potentiation leads to pruning. This demonstrates that neuroplasticity operates in both directions.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsExperimental design with random assignment; can establish cause-and-effect between juggling and grey matter changesSmall sample (24 participants); limited statistical power; results may not be reliable due to averaging across few participantsThree scan time points allow tracking of both growth and pruning over time in the same participantsField experiment: participants practiced at home, introducing lack of control over confounding variables and reducing internal validityObjective VBM measures avoid self-report biasGender imbalance (21 female, 3 male); findings may not generalise equally across sexesDirectly demonstrates both neuroplasticity and pruning in the same studyVBM methodology has known limitations in precision of grey matter measurementConsistent with Maguire (2000) and Rosenzweig et al. (1972) on experience-driven structural changeJuggling is a specific visuomotor skill; findings may not generalise to other types of learning

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neuroplasticity; Neural pruning; Formation of neural networks
Key Concept: Grey matter density, LTP, dendritic branching, synaptic pruning, VBM, field experiment
Useful for: “Explain neuroplasticity with reference to one study” / “Explain neural pruning with reference to one study” / “Explain the formation of neural networks with reference to one study” / “Evaluate the use of brain imaging in psychological research”
Paired with: Maguire (2000) - Taxi Driver Study, Rosenzweig, Bennet & Diamond (1972) - Rat Study



Key Concept - Long Term Potentiation (LTP) and Pruning:
LTP is the process by which repeated activation of a neural pathway strengthens synaptic connections and leads to dendritic branching, increasing grey matter density. Draganski (2004) shows this happening in real time: learning juggling produced measurable grey matter growth in visual motion areas. When training stopped, reduced potentiation led to pruning, a partial reversal of those changes. This makes Draganski the most direct demonstration in the vault of both halves of the “use it or lose it” principle.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.filePath: Studies/Biological Studies/Neuroplasticity Studies/Maguire (2000) - Taxi Driver Study.md
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.title: Maguire (2000) - Taxi Driver Study
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.content:
Biological Study  Neuroplasticity

Eleanor Maguire et al. conducted a Quasi-Experiment using MRI scans to investigate whether extensive navigation experience causes structural changes in the hippocampus of London taxi drivers, providing some of the most compelling evidence for neuroplasticity in the adult human brain.

Aim: To investigate whether the hippocampi of London taxi drivers differ structurally from non-taxi drivers due to the exceptional navigational demands of their profession, and whether any differences correlate with years of experience.
Participants:

16 right-handed male London taxi drivers with at least 1.5 years of experience (mean: 14.3 years)
50 healthy right-handed male non-taxi-drivers as controls, matched for age and handedness

Method: Quasi-experiment (IV not manipulated; participants were already taxi drivers or not).

MRI scans were used to measure the volume and density of different hippocampal regions.
A technique called voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was used to compare grey matter density.
The correlation between years of taxi driving and hippocampal volume was calculated.
Taxi drivers in London must pass “The Knowledge”, memorizing 25,000 streets, a uniquely demanding spatial memory task.

Results:

Taxi drivers had significantly greater grey matter volume in the posterior hippocampus compared to controls.
Controls had relatively greater volume in the anterior hippocampus.
There was a positive correlation between the volume of the posterior hippocampus and the number of years spent as a taxi driver; the longer the experience, the larger the posterior hippocampus.
The total hippocampal volume was not significantly different; the change was in the distribution of volume (posterior vs. anterior).

Conclusion: The demands of spatial navigation cause structural changes in the hippocampus, demonstrating that the adult human brain retains neuroplasticity: the ability to reorganize and change in response to experience.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsObjective MRI measures avoid self-report biasQuasi-experimental: cannot confirm navigation caused hippocampal changes (could be pre-existing)Correlational data (years of experience) strengthens the environmental explanationAll-male sample: findings may not generalize to female taxi drivers or other populationsSupports neuroplasticity in the adult brain, challenging the idea that the brain stops changingSmall experimental group (16 taxi drivers), limited statistical powerConsistent with Draganski (2004) and Rosenzweig et al. (1972) on experience and brain changesCannot rule out that people with larger posterior hippocampi are simply more likely to become taxi driversReal-world occupational context increases ecological validityThe voxel-based morphometry technique has some methodological limitations

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neuroplasticity; Localization of function
Key Concept: Posterior hippocampus, spatial memory, grey matter, neuroplasticity, MRI
Useful for: “Discuss neuroplasticity” / “Evaluate the use of brain imaging in psychological research”
Paired with: Draganski (2004), Rosenzweig et al. (1972), HM case study, Antonova et al. (2011)



Key Concept - Neuroplasticity:
Neuroplasticity is the brain’s ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life. Maguire (2000) demonstrated that this occurs at a structural level: years of intensive spatial navigation literally reshapes the hippocampus. This has important implications for education, rehabilitation after brain injury, and our understanding of the limits of human learning.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.filePath: Studies/Biological Studies/Neuroplasticity Studies/Rosenzweig, Bennet & Diamond (1972) - Rat Study.md
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.title: Rosenzweig, Bennet & Diamond (1972) - Rat Study
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neuroplastici.content:
Biological Study Animal-Research Neuroplasticity, Ethical considerations

Mark Rosenzweig, Edward Bennett, and Marian Diamond conducted a Lab Experiment with rats investigating whether environmental enrichment affects brain development, one of the earliest and most influential studies on neuroplasticity.

Aim: To investigate whether the richness or poverty of an animal’s environment influences the physical development and structure of the brain (specifically cortical thickness and weight).
Participants: Laboratory rats (rattus norvegicus), randomly assigned to conditions.
Method: Lab experiment with independent groups design.

Rats were assigned to one of three conditions:

Enriched Environment (EC): 10-12 rats housed together in a large cage with toys, ladders, wheels, and objects that were changed regularly, stimulating exploration and learning.
Impoverished Environment (IC): Rats housed alone in small, bare cages with no stimulation.
Standard Colony (SC): Rats housed in small groups in standard lab cages (control condition).


Rats remained in their conditions for 80 days.
After the period, rats were sacrificed and their brains were dissected and measured.

Results:

Rats in the enriched environment showed significantly greater cortical thickness and greater overall brain weight compared to impoverished and standard conditions.
Enriched rats also showed:

Increased synaptic connections (more dendritic branching)
Greater acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity, linked to better learning and memory
Heavier occipital (visual) cortex


Results were consistent across multiple replications of the experiment.

Conclusion: Environmental experience directly influences the physical structure and weight of the brain, demonstrating neuroplasticity. A richer environment promotes greater cortical development, while impoverishment leads to underdevelopment.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsControlled lab experiment: high internal validity; random assignment reduces confoundsAnimal research: direct generalization to human neuroplasticity is limitedObjective biological measures (brain weight, cortical thickness) are not reliant on self-reportEthical concerns: rats were sacrificed; impoverished condition may constitute animal crueltyResults were replicated multiple times by the same and different research teamsEnriched environment differs from impoverished in multiple ways, making it difficult to isolate the key variableFoundational study that inspired decades of neuroplasticity researchRats are nocturnal and social; the impoverished (solitary) condition may reflect social deprivation as much as cognitive deprivationConsistent with Maguire (2000) and Draganski (2004) on brain plasticityThe specific enrichment stimuli (toys, wheels) may not map directly onto human cognitive environments

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neuroplasticity; Animal research in psychology; Ethics
Key Concept: Environmental enrichment, cortical development, synaptic connections
Useful for: “Discuss neuroplasticity” / “Evaluate the use of animal research in psychology” / “Discuss ethical considerations in research”
Paired with: Maguire (2000), Draganski (2004), Martinez & Kesner (ACh and memory)



Key Concept - Environmental Enrichment & the Brain:
Rosenzweig et al. (1972) was among the first to demonstrate that the brain is not a fixed organ but responds dynamically to experience. Enriched environments promote greater cortical thickness and synaptic density, while impoverished environments lead to underdevelopment. This has profound implications for early childhood development, education, and the effects of poverty on cognitive development.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.title: Antonova et al (2011)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.content:
Study Biological Neurotransmission

Antonova et al. conducted a Double-Blind Repeated Measures Experiment using fMRI to investigate the role of acetylcholine (ACh) in spatial memory and hippocampal activation in humans, extending animal research findings to a human sample.

Aim: To investigate whether blocking ACh receptors using scopolamine reduces hippocampal activation during a spatial memory task in healthy human participants.
Participants: 20 healthy male adults, mean age 28 years.
Method: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, repeated measures experiment.

Participants were injected with either scopolamine (a muscarinic ACh antagonist) or a saline placebo 70-90 minutes before the task.
They then performed the “Arena task”: a virtual reality spatial navigation game in which participants navigate an arena to reach a pole, remember its location over a 30-second blank screen, and then navigate to it again from a new starting point.
Participants were first trained on the task to ensure familiarity with the controls.
Brain activity was measured via fMRI across six trials.
Participants returned 3-4 weeks later and completed the task again under the opposite condition (counterbalanced repeated measures design).

Results:

Participants in the scopolamine condition showed significantly reduced hippocampal activation compared to the placebo condition.
The error rate in the scopolamine condition was higher, but this difference was not statistically significant.
The fMRI data provided the critical finding: without neuroimaging, the biological effect would have been undetectable from behaviour alone.

Conclusion: ACh plays a significant role in hippocampal activation during spatial memory encoding in humans. The study extends animal findings (Rogers & Kesner) to humans and demonstrates the value of combining pharmacological manipulation with neuroimaging.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsRepeated measures design eliminates participant variabilitySmall sample (20 males only): low statistical power and cannot generalise to womenCounterbalancing (opposite condition 3-4 weeks later) controls for practice effectsSeveral participants reported stress from the injection or fMRI enclosure, which may itself have impaired hippocampal functioningDouble-blind design eliminates experimenter and participant biasThe behavioural performance difference was not significant: only the fMRI measure showed a significant difference, suggesting the Arena task may not have been sensitive enoughfMRI provides objective biological data beyond what behaviour alone can revealScopolamine affects multiple neurotransmitter systems, not ACh alone; difficult to fully isolate ACh’s specific contributionHuman participants overcome the generalisability limitation of animal studiesEthical concerns: administering an unfamiliar drug to healthy participants carries medical risk

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neurotransmission; Localization of function
Key Concept: ACh, muscarinic antagonist, scopolamine, hippocampus, spatial memory, fMRI
Useful for: “Explain the role of one neurotransmitter in human behaviour” / “Explain the role of one antagonist” / “Evaluate the use of brain imaging in psychological research”
Paired with: Rogers & Kesner, Martinez & Kesner, HM case study, Maguire (2000)



Key Concept - Why fMRI Mattered Here:
The behavioural performance difference between scopolamine and placebo was not statistically significant. Only the fMRI revealed a significant reduction in hippocampal activation. This is an important methodological point: without brain imaging, the role of ACh would have appeared negligible from behaviour alone. It demonstrates why combining pharmacological manipulation with neuroimaging is more powerful than either method in isolation.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.title: Jarowsky et al
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.content:
Study Biological Neurotransmission, Hormones In Human Behaviour

Jarowski et al. conducted an Experiment investigating the role of noradrenaline in depression, providing pharmacological evidence for the catecholamine hypothesis: the theory that low monoamine neurotransmitter levels (particularly noradrenaline and serotonin) underlie depressive disorders.

Aim: To investigate whether artificially lowering noradrenaline levels in healthy participants induces depressive symptoms, testing the causal role of noradrenaline in depression.
Participants: Healthy adult volunteers with no prior history of depression, randomly assigned to conditions.
Method: Double-blind placebo-controlled experiment.

Group 1 (Control): Received a placebo drug with no effect on noradrenaline.
Group 2 (Experimental): Received a drug that suppresses noradrenaline synthesis or activity (noradrenaline-depleting agent).
Depressive symptoms were assessed before and after drug administration using standardized mood and depression scales.

Results:

Participants in Group 2 showed significantly more depressive symptoms after noradrenaline suppression compared to the placebo group.
Some participants in the experimental group developed persistent depressive symptoms that lasted beyond the duration of the drug’s effect.
This supports a causal link between low noradrenaline and the onset of depressive symptoms.

Conclusion: Lowering noradrenaline levels is sufficient to induce depressive symptoms in healthy individuals, providing pharmacological support for the catecholamine hypothesis of depression and the broader monoamine hypothesis.



                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

The catecholamine hypothesis (Schildkraut, 1965) proposes that depression results from a deficiency of catecholamines, particularly noradrenaline, at functionally important receptor sites in the brain. Jarowski et al. provides direct experimental support by showing that pharmacologically inducing this deficiency produces depression.



Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsExperimental design with placebo control establishes cause-and-effectSerious ethical concerns: deliberately inducing depression in healthy participants risks lasting psychological harmDouble-blind design reduces experimenter and participant biasThe drug may affect multiple neurotransmitter systems, not noradrenaline aloneProvides direct pharmacological evidence for the monoamine hypothesisDepression is multifactorial; noradrenaline is one of many contributing factorsClinically relevant; informs antidepressant drug development (e.g., SNRIs)Sample of healthy volunteers may not represent those with a biological vulnerability to depressionReplicable standardized procedureLong-term effects on some participants raise concerns about informed consent adequacy

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neurotransmission; Abnormal psychology (depression)
Key Concept: Noradrenaline, catecholamine hypothesis, monoamine hypothesis, pharmacological research
Useful for: “Discuss the role of neurotransmitters in one disorder” / “Evaluate the biological approach to understanding depression”
Paired with: Caspi et al. (2003), Martinez & Kesner, Antonova et al. (2011)



Key Concept - Monoamine Hypothesis of Depression:
The monoamine hypothesis proposes that depression is caused by a deficiency of monoamine neurotransmitters, primarily serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine, at synapses in the brain. Jarowski et al. provides direct experimental support by showing that pharmacologically reducing noradrenaline induces depressive symptoms in healthy individuals. This hypothesis underpins the mechanism of action of SSRIs (serotonin) and SNRIs (serotonin + noradrenaline) antidepressants.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.title: Martinez & Kesner
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.content:
PSY Study Biological Neurotransmission Animal-Research

Martinez and Kesner conducted a Lab Experiment on rats investigating the causal role of acetylcholine (ACh) in spatial memory, using pharmacological manipulation to either increase or decrease ACh activity and measuring the effect on maze performance.

Aim: To investigate whether acetylcholine levels in the brain have a causal effect on memory performance in rats navigating a spatial maze.
Participants: Laboratory rats, randomly assigned to three groups.
Method: Lab experiment with independent groups design.

























GroupDrugEffect on AChGroup 1 - ScopolamineMuscarinic ACh receptor antagonistReduces ACh activity by blocking receptorsGroup 2 - PhysostigmineAcetylcholinesterase inhibitor (blocks the enzyme that breaks down ACh)Increases ACh activityGroup 3 - ControlSaline injection (no drug)No change

All rats were trained on a spatial maze and then tested following drug injection.
Dependent variable: Number of errors made and time taken to complete the maze.

Results:





















GroupPerformanceScopolamine (reduced ACh)More errors, slower; significantly worse than controlPhysostigmine (increased ACh)Fewer errors, faster; significantly better than controlControlBaseline performance
Conclusion: ACh levels have a direct causal effect on spatial memory performance. Reducing ACh impairs memory; increasing ACh enhances it. This confirms acetylcholine’s critical role in the encoding and retrieval of spatial memories, likely mediated through the hippocampus.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsControlled lab experiment: high internal validity; random assignment isolates ACh as the variableAnimal research: rats’ neurochemistry is similar to humans, but direct generalization is not guaranteedThree-group design (reduce, increase, control) provides a strong comparative frameworkEthical concerns: invasive injections; animals were used as subjectsResults are consistent and clear; both directions of ACh manipulation confirmed the hypothesisDrugs may affect other neurotransmitter systems beyond ACh aloneConsistent with and complemented by Antonova et al. (2011) in human participantsArtificial maze task may not reflect the full complexity of real-world memoryHelped establish acetylcholine as key to memory; informs Alzheimer’s researchScopolamine and physostigmine affect ACh systemically, not only in the hippocampus

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neurotransmission; Animal research in psychology
Key Concept: Acetylcholine, memory, pharmacological manipulation, animal research ethics
Useful for: “Discuss the role of neurotransmitters in behaviour” / “Evaluate animal research in psychology”
Paired with: Antonova et al. (2011), Rogers & Kesner, HM case study



Key Concept - Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors:
Physostigmine works by blocking acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down ACh in the synapse. This prolongs ACh’s presence and enhances its effects. The same principle underlies drugs used to treat Alzheimer’s disease (e.g., donepezil), making Martinez & Kesner directly clinically relevant.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.title: Raine et al. (1997)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.content:
Study Biological Neurotransmission, Localization of function

Adrian Raine et al. conducted a Quasi-Experiment using PET scans to investigate whether murderers pleading not guilty by reason of insanity (NGRI) show different patterns of brain activity compared to non-murderers, providing biological evidence for the neural basis of violent behaviour.

Aim: To investigate whether murderers who pleaded NGRI show significantly different brain glucose metabolism (brain activity) compared to matched non-murderer controls, using PET scans.
Participants:

41 murderers (39 male, 2 female) who had pleaded NGRI, referred by courts or lawyers
41 matched controls (non-murderers), matched for age and sex; 6 were matched for schizophrenia diagnosis

Method: Quasi-experiment (IV was not manipulated; participants were already murderers or not).

Participants performed a continuous performance task (CPT) to activate the brain.
A PET scan (positron emission tomography) measured glucose metabolism across 14 brain regions.
Brain activity levels were compared between the two groups.

Results:

Murderers showed reduced activity in the prefrontal cortex (linked to impulse control, planning, and emotional regulation).
Reduced activity was also found in the corpus callosum, amygdala, and hippocampus.
Increased activity was found in the thalamus and caudate in the left hemisphere.
These differences suggest abnormal functioning in brain areas associated with aggression regulation and emotional processing.

Conclusion: Murderers who plead NGRI show distinct patterns of brain activity, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, supporting a biological basis for violent behaviour. However, Raine cautioned that this does not mean biology determines crime, only that it is a contributing factor.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsObjective biological measure (PET scan) avoids self-report biasQuasi-experimental: cannot establish direct cause-and-effectMatched controls reduce confounding variablesSample is NGRI murderers, not representative of all violent offendersContributes to localization of function research (prefrontal cortex)Reduced PFC activity may be a result of violence, not a causeSupports biological explanations for aggression and antisocial behaviourEthical concerns: using brain scans as legal evidence raises issues of biological determinism and criminal justice implicationsReplicable standardized procedureSmall, specific sample limits generalizability

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Localization of function; Neurotransmission; Aggression
Key Concept: Prefrontal cortex and impulse control; PET scan as a research method
Useful for: “Discuss localization of function” / “Evaluate the use of brain imaging technologies in psychology”
Paired with: HM case study, Maguire (2000), Dabbs et al. (1995)



Key Concept - Prefrontal Cortex & Impulse Control:
The prefrontal cortex (PFC) regulates decision-making, impulse control, and emotional regulation. Reduced PFC activity has been consistently linked to impulsive and aggressive behaviour. Raine et al. (1997) is a key study supporting this using neuroimaging.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.title: Rogers and Kesner
Studies/Biological-Studies/Neurotransmis.content:
Study Biological Neurotransmission Animal-Research

Rogers and Kesner conducted a Lab Experiment on rats investigating the role of acetylcholine (ACh) in spatial memory, specifically in the hippocampus, complementing Martinez & Kesner’s earlier work on ACh.

Aim: To investigate the specific role of acetylcholine (ACh) within the hippocampus in the encoding and retrieval of spatial memory in rats.
Participants: Laboratory rats, assigned to experimental conditions.
Method: Lab experiment with animal subjects.

Rats were trained to run a maze (specifically a radial arm maze or similar spatial task).
Scopolamine (an ACh antagonist that blocks muscarinic ACh receptors) was injected directly into the hippocampus to reduce ACh activity.
Rats were then tested on the maze and errors (entering already-visited arms) were recorded.
Compared to a control group that received saline injections.

Results:

Rats with reduced hippocampal ACh (via scopolamine) made significantly more errors in the spatial maze, particularly in the early stages of learning (encoding phase).
The control group navigated the maze with far fewer errors.
Blocking ACh in the hippocampus specifically impaired the ability to encode new spatial information, suggesting ACh is critical to memory formation in this brain region.

Conclusion: Acetylcholine in the hippocampus plays a critical role in spatial memory encoding, supporting the broader neurotransmitter-memory link and providing localized evidence for ACh’s function within the hippocampus specifically.

Evaluation

























StrengthsLimitationsHigh internal validity: tightly controlled lab conditions isolate ACh as the variableAnimal research: rat findings may not generalize directly to human memoryComplements and refines Martinez & Kesner’s systemic ACh findingsEthical concerns: invasive procedures (direct hippocampal injections) raise animal welfare concernsProvides localized evidence for ACh’s role specifically in the hippocampusArtificial lab setting does not reflect natural memory processesConsistent with HM case study findings on hippocampal importance in memoryCannot account for the complexity of neurotransmitter interactions

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Neurotransmission; Localization of function (hippocampus)
Key Concept: Acetylcholine and memory; hippocampus role in encoding
Useful for: “Discuss neurotransmitters and their effect on behaviour” / “Evaluate animal research in psychology”
Paired with: Martinez & Kesner, Antonova et al. (2011), HM case study



Key Concept - Acetylcholine (ACh) & Memory:
ACh is a neurotransmitter strongly associated with learning and memory. The hippocampus has dense ACh receptors and plays a central role in encoding new episodic and spatial memories. When ACh activity is blocked or reduced, memory formation is significantly impaired.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Pheromones/We.title: Wedekind (1995)
Studies/Biological-Studies/Pheromones/We.content:
Study HRelations Biological Pheromones Evolutionary Explanations - Human Relationships, Human Relationships

Wedekind conducted a Double-Blind Lab Experiment, known as the “Smelly T-Shirt Study”, to determine whether women prefer the body odour of men with dissimilar Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) genes, testing an evolutionary prediction about immune-based mate selection.

Background:

The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is a group of genes that enable the immune system to recognize pathogens.
MHC genes are co-dominant: offspring inherit and express both parental sets.
More diverse parental MHC leads to a stronger offspring immune system.
Evolutionary logic therefore predicts a mechanism for detecting MHC dissimilarity in potential mates.

Aim: To investigate whether women prefer the body odour of MHC-dissimilar men as an evolutionary mechanism to maximize offspring immune diversity.

Participants: 49 female and 44 male students from the University of Bern, Switzerland.

MHC genotyped with wide variance included.
Students drawn from different courses (women: biology/psychology; men: chemistry/physics/geography), making them unlikely to know each other.
Whether women were taking oral contraceptives was recorded.

Method: Double-blind experiment.

Men wore T-shirts for two nights and kept them in an open plastic bag during the day. Controlled conditions: perfume-free soap, no deodorant, no perfume, no alcohol, no spicy food, no tobacco, no sexual activity.
Women used a nose spray for 14 days before the experiment to support nasal mucous membrane regeneration and as a preventive measure against colds.
Women were tested in the second week after the beginning of menstruation (peak olfactory sensitivity).
Women also read Süskind’s Perfume beforehand to heighten smell awareness.
Each woman rated 7 T-shirt odours (presented in cardboard boxes with a smelling hole) for intensity (0-10) and pleasantness/sexiness (0-10, with 5 as neutral):

3 T-shirts from MHC-similar men
3 T-shirts from MHC-dissimilar men
1 unworn control T-shirt




Results:

Women rated MHC-dissimilar male odours as significantly more pleasant than MHC-similar ones.
This preference was reversed in women taking oral contraceptives, suggesting the pill disrupts natural MHC-based mate preference (mimicking pregnancy, where proximity to similar kin may be adaptive).

Conclusion: Women show a preference for MHC-dissimilar male body odour, consistent with an evolved mechanism for selecting genetically compatible mates to maximise offspring immune diversity.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsDouble-blind design minimises demand characteristics and experimenter biasSmall, homogeneous sample (young Swiss university students); limited generalisabilitySuccessfully replicated by Jacob et al. (2002)Reductionist: ignores cognitive and sociocultural influences on mate selectionFindings mirror animal research: female mice also prefer MHC-dissimilar males (Yamazaki et al., 1976)Women on oral contraceptives were included in ratings; contraceptive status may have confounded some comparisonsSupported by clinical research: couples with repeated miscarriages share more MHC than control couples (Beer et al., 1985)Odour ratings are subjective; individual differences in smell sensitivity not controlledEthical standards met: informed consent and full debriefing providedReal-world attraction involves many more cues than scent alone

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Pheromones and attraction; Evolutionary explanations for human relationships
Key Concept: MHC, genetic compatibility, olfactory cues, oral contraceptives, evolutionary mate selection
Useful for: “Discuss the role of biological factors in the formation of relationships” / “Evaluate evolutionary explanations for attraction”
Paired with: Zhou et al. (2014), Buss (1989), Clark & Hatfield (1989), Fisher et al. (2005)



Key Concept - MHC & The Contraceptive Reversal:
The contraceptive reversal finding in Wedekind (1995) is particularly significant. Oral contraceptives mimic the hormonal state of pregnancy, during which proximity to genetically similar kin (rather than dissimilar mates) may be evolutionarily advantageous. This accidental reversal of a natural preference suggests that the modern use of hormonal contraceptives may subtly interfere with evolved mate selection mechanisms, with potential implications for relationship satisfaction and fertility.

Studies/Biological-Studies/Pheromones/Zh.filePath: Studies/Biological Studies/Pheromones/Zhou et al (2014) - Boar AND & EST.md
Studies/Biological-Studies/Pheromones/Zh.title: Zhou et al (2014) - Boar AND & EST
Studies/Biological-Studies/Pheromones/Zh.content:
Study Biological Pheromones Evolutionary Explanations - Human Relationships, Human Relationships

Zhou et al. conducted a True Lab Experiment to test whether the human chemosignals androstadienone (AND) and estratetraenol (EST) influence the perception of biological sex in a manner consistent with their functioning as human pheromones.

Background:

Androstadienone (AND) is a human steroid found in male semen and sweat. It heightens sympathetic arousal, alters cortisol, and promotes positive mood in females. It activates the hypothalamus in heterosexual females and homosexual males, but not in heterosexual males or homosexual females.
Estratetraenol (EST) is the female equivalent found in urine.
A key challenge: humans lack a functional vomeronasal organ (VNO), the receptor used by most animals to detect pheromones, making human pheromone research contentious.

Aim: To investigate whether AND and EST function as sex-specific human pheromones by biasing the perception of biological sex in ways consistent with each participant’s sexual orientation.

Participants: 96 healthy non-smokers in four groups:

























GroupnHeterosexual males24Heterosexual females24Homosexual males24Bisexual/homosexual females24
Method: True experiment with manipulated IV, allowing cause-and-effect conclusions.

A point-light walker (PLW) task was used: moving dots representing human motion with deliberately ambiguous biological sex.
Participants identified the sex of the figure while exposed to one of three scents applied under the nose:

AND mixed with cloves
EST mixed with cloves
Clove oil only (control)


Completed on three consecutive days, counterbalanced to control for order effects.


Results:


























ChemosignalEffect on heterosexual femalesEffect on homosexual malesEffect on heterosexual malesEffect on bisexual/lesbian femalesANDPerceived walkers as more masculinePerceived walkers as more masculineNo significant effectNo significant effectESTNo significant effectNo significant effectPerceived walkers as more feminineEffect not statistically significant

Effects aligned with who the participant is typically attracted to, not their own biological sex.
Control odour produced no consistent directional bias.

Conclusion: AND and EST affect gender perception in a sexuality-specific manner consistent with a pheromone-like function, supporting the existence of human chemosignals that influence social perception.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsTrue experiment with manipulated IV; allows cause-and-effect conclusionsHare et al. (2017) failed to replicate the findings, questioning reliabilityCounterbalanced design controls for order effectsDoses of AND and EST used were significantly higher than natural human secretion levels, limiting ecological validityResults across different gender/sexuality groups strengthen the biological interpretationEffects were on gender perception, not actual attraction or mate choiceDirectly tests the existence of human pheromones in a controlled wayHumans lack a functional VNO; the mechanism by which AND/EST are detected remains unclearInclusion of four sexual orientation groups is a major methodological strengthSample consisted of healthy young non-smokers; generalisability is limited

IB Connections

Approach: Biological
Topic: Pheromones; Biological factors in attraction; Evolutionary explanations
Key Concept: Androstadienone (AND), estratetraenol (EST), VNO, pheromones, sexual orientation, gender perception
Useful for: “Discuss the role of pheromones in human behaviour” / “Evaluate biological explanations for attraction”
Paired with: Wedekind (1995), Buss (1989), Fisher et al. (2005)



Key Concept - Human Pheromones & the VNO Problem:
Most animals detect pheromones via the vomeronasal organ (VNO). Humans appear to lack a functional VNO, making the existence of human pheromones controversial. Zhou et al. (2014) sidesteps this by measuring behavioural effects of AND and EST, showing that these chemosignals systematically bias gender perception in a sexuality-specific way. However, failed replications (Hare et al., 2017) and the use of supra-natural doses mean the evidence remains contested.

Studies/Cog.-Studies/Emotion-and-cogniti.filePath: Studies/Cog. Studies/Emotion and cognition/Brown & Kulik (1977) - JFK and MLK.md
Studies/Cog.-Studies/Emotion-and-cogniti.title: Brown & Kulik (1977) - JFK and MLK
Studies/Cog.-Studies/Emotion-and-cogniti.content:
study  Cultural cognitive

Transclude of Flashbulb-Memory

Aim: To investigate whether people have particularly vivid and detailed memories for surprising and personally significant events (FBM formation).
Participants: 80 American adults (40 Black, 40 White), recruited via convenience sampling.
Method: Standardized Questionnaire (7 open questions)

Participants were asked whether they could recall the circumstances in which they heard about the death of public figures (e.g., Jhon F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King), as well as of someone they personally knew.
For each remembered event they described the FBM categories: place, activity, informant, others present, own affect, aftermath. (Details + personal involvement)
They also rated the personal significance of each event.
Racial differences were analyzed (e.g., whether Black participants had stronger FBM for MLK’s assassination).

Results:

90% of participants recalled significant amount of detail about these events.
75% of Black participants showed FBMs for MLK’s assassination, compared to 33% of white participants.
Events rated as more personally significant produced more vivid and complete FBMs.
