StrengthsLimitationsMatched sample (age, sex) controls for key demographic confoundsQuasi-experimental: findings are correlational; cannot establish that culture causally produced the memory differenceFour task conditions with exact significance levels (p < .001 for three conditions) strengthen the pattern of findings considerablySingle cultural comparison: replications with other indigenous groups are needed to establish reliability and generalizabilityQualitative data on behaviour provides rich insight into the different cognitive strategies each group usedThe concept of standard testing is culturally foreign to Aboriginal children; despite outdoor testing, some performance suppression may have occurredPerfect score statistics (75% of Aboriginal children vs. less than 5% of white children) demonstrate the magnitude of the difference strikinglyCannot fully isolate whether superior performance reflects cultural transmission, ecological adaptation, or other variables such as nutrition or schoolingHas important ethical and policy implications: challenges the use of Western cognitive tests with non-Western populationsThe researcher was white and Western; this power dynamic may have influenced participant behaviourKearins addresses and dismisses the genetic explanation: since these children were not raised in the desert themselves, the transmission is most likely cultural via their first-generation parentsThe specific components of desert cultural life responsible for the memory advantage remain unclear

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural; Cognitive
Topic: Cultural influences on behaviour and cognition; Enculturation; Research methods in the sociocultural approach
Key Concept: Cultural influence on cognition, visual-spatial memory, enculturation, quasi-experiment, etic vs. emic
Useful for: “Explain the use of one research method in one study of cultural influences” / “Discuss one example of a cultural influence on one cognitive process” / “Evaluate cross-cultural research methods” / “Discuss enculturation with reference to one study”
Paired with: Hofstede (2001), Kulkofsky et al (2011), Berry (1967)



Key Concept - Culture Shapes Cognition:
Kearins (1981) demonstrates that cognitive strategies are not universal but shaped by ecological and cultural demands. The magnitude of the difference is striking: 75% of Aboriginal children achieved at least one perfect score, compared to fewer than 5% of white Australian performances. The study is also a methodological lesson: tests designed within one cultural framework systematically misrepresent the abilities of people from another. And because these children were not raised as desert hunters themselves, the most plausible explanation is cultural transmission through parenting, language, and practice, not genetics.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Culture/Ku.title: Kulkofsky et al (2011)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Culture/Ku.content:
Study Sociocultural Cultural dimensions, Flashbulb Memory

Kulkofsky et al. conducted a Cross-Cultural Study investigating whether cultural dimensions, particularly individualism vs. collectivism, affect how people form and recall flashbulb memories (FBMs), examining whether the emotional and social significance of events differs across cultures.

Aim: To investigate whether culture (specifically individualism vs. collectivism) influences the formation of flashbulb memories (FBMs).
Participants: 274 middle class adults from 5 countries representing a range on the individualism-collectivism dimension:

Individualist cultures: USA, Germany, UK
Collectivist cultures: China, Turkey

Method: Cross-cultural questionnaire / interview study.

Participants were asked to recall public events that occurred during their life time (at least 1yr ago). This was used to create a “memory questionnaire”, mirroring the one used in Brown & Kulik (1977) - JFK and MLK, which included details + personal relevance.
The tools were constructed in english, translated and back-translated into the different languages.
They also reported on social sharing: how often they discussed the event with others.
The quality, vividness, and confidence of FBMs were measured and compared across cultures.

Results:

Individualist cultures (USA, Germany, UK) tended to have FBMs for a wider range of events, including international ones.
Collectivist cultures showed stronger FBMs for events with national or social relevance, compared with individualistic cultures that place greater emphasis on an individual’s personal involvement and emotional experiences.
Social sharing was a significant predictor of FBM strength across all cultures; the more participants discussed an event, the stronger and more vivid the memory. Collectivist cultures however, tend to de-emphasize individual experiences, leading to less rehearsal of the triggering event, and thus less chance of developing FMBs for personal events.

Conclusion: The formation and maintenance of flashbulb memories is culturally influenced. Social sharing, rehearsing memories through conversation, appears to be a key mechanism.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsCross-cultural design (5 countries) increases generalizabilitySelf-report measures: vividness and confidence ratings are subjectiveIdentifies social sharing as a previously underemphasized mechanism in FBMCannot establish whether social sharing causes stronger FBMs or results from themLinks cognitive psychology (FBM) to sociocultural factorsEvents tested may not be equally significant across all culturesChallenges purely biological (Brown & Kulik “Now Print!”) accounts of FBMSampling issues: participants may not be representative of their national cultureAdvances understanding of cultural cognitionDifficult to fully operationalize “collectivism” at the individual level

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural; Cognitive
Topic: Cultural dimensions; Flashbulb memory; Cultural influences on cognition
Key Concept: Individualism vs. collectivism; social sharing; cultural cognition
Useful for: “Discuss cultural influences on cognitive processes” / “Evaluate the role of cultural dimensions in behaviour” / “one theory of hoe emotion may affect one cognitive process”

Key Concept - Social Sharing & Memory:
Kulkofsky et al. highlights that memory is not purely an individual, biological process. Social sharing, talking about events with others, actively reinforces and shapes memories. This is especially relevant in collectivist cultures where communal storytelling and group remembering are integral social practices.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Culture/Lu.title: Lueck and Wilson (2010)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Culture/Lu.content:
Acculturation Study Sociocultural Enculturation - Acquiring your cultural norms + Acculturation, Cultural dimensions

Lueck and Wilson conducted a Survey Study using Semi-Structured Interviews investigating which linguistic and social factors predict acculturative stress in Asian immigrants and Asian Americans, testing whether integration (maintaining both cultures) is more protective than assimilation.

Aim: To investigate which linguistic and social variables predict acculturative stress in a nationally representative sample of Asian immigrants and Asian Americans.
Participants: 2,095 Asian Americans from the National Latino and Asian American Study (NLAAS).

1,271 were first-generation immigrants who arrived in the US aged 18 or older.
The remainder were born in the US to first-generation immigrant parents.
Multiple Asian cultures represented: approximately 600 Chinese, 508 Filipino, 520 Vietnamese, and 467 other Asians.

Method: Semi-structured interviews.

Interviews conducted either face-to-face or over the internet.
Interviewers were matched to participants by cultural and linguistic background.
A randomly selected subsample was re-contacted to validate interview data (member checking).
Variables measured included: acculturative stress, language proficiency, language preference, perceived discrimination, family cohesion, and socioeconomic status.

Results:

70% of participants (1,433 of 2,095) showed acculturative stress.
Bilingual language preference was associated with significantly lower acculturative stress.
English-only preference was a predictor of higher acculturative stress.
Perceived discrimination (prejudice, harassment, threats) was the strongest predictor of high stress.
Family cohesion (shared values and beliefs) significantly reduced stress.
Economic satisfaction and willingness to migrate again were associated with lower stress.

Conclusion: Acculturative stress is not reduced by assimilation. Maintaining bilingualism, cultural ties, and family cohesion are the strongest protective factors. This supports integration over assimilation as the healthier acculturation strategy, consistent with Berry’s model.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsLarge, diverse sample (2,095 across four Asian cultural groups) increases reliabilityOnly studied Asian Americans: findings may not generalise to Latino, African, or European immigrant groupsCulturally matched interviewers increase comfort and reduce social desirability biasSemi-structured interviews are time-consuming, costly, and open to interviewer effectsMember checking (validation subsample) strengthens credibility of dataConstructs are subjective: acculturative stress and economic satisfaction are difficult to measure objectively or compare across individualsRandom sampling from a national database reduces selection biasEcological fallacy risk: assuming all Asian cultures share collectivist values without measuring individual-level collectivismConsistent with Berry’s integration model; challenges the assumption that assimilation reduces stressCorrelational: cannot establish whether language preference causes stress levels or stress levels cause language preference

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Acculturation; Cultural influences on individual behaviour
Key Concept: Acculturative stress, protective factors, risk factors, integration, bilingualism
Useful for: “Explain one study of acculturation” / “Discuss one model of acculturation with reference to one example”
Paired with: Berry’s Acculturation Model, Hofstede (2001)



Key Concept - Integration over Assimilation:
Lueck & Wilson (2010) directly challenges the assumption that dropping one’s original culture reduces stress. Bilingualism and cultural maintenance are protective; English-only assimilation is a risk factor. Discrimination is the single most harmful variable. Together these findings support Berry’s integration strategy as the most psychologically healthy approach to acculturation.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Culture/Mi.title: Miranda and Matheny (2000)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Culture/Mi.content:
PSY Study Sociocultural Acculturation Enculturation - Acquiring your cultural norms + Acculturation, Cultural dimensions

Alexis Miranda and Kenneth Matheny conducted a Correlational Study using Questionnaires investigating which socio-psychological factors predict acculturative stress in Latino immigrants to the United States, identifying both risk factors and protective factors that influence how well an individual adjusts to a new culture.

Background:

Acculturative stress is the psychological and social difficulty experienced when an individual adapts to a new culture. It is linked to anxiety, depression, identity conflict, and reduced well-being.
Berry’s (1990) model argues that acculturative stress is shaped by multiple interacting factors, not a single cause. Miranda & Matheny directly tested this claim.
Protective factors reduce acculturative stress; risk factors increase it. Identifying these factors has practical implications for mental health support services for immigrant populations.

Aim: To investigate which socio-psychological factors in the lives of Latino immigrants to the United States would predict and decrease the level of acculturative stress.

Participants: A random sample of 197 Spanish-speaking Latino immigrants, recruited from two social service agencies in the United States.





































DemographicDetailGender63% female, 37% maleMean age28.7 yearsMean age at migration22.5 yearsMean length of US residence3.9 yearsMexican ancestry47%Central American34%South American19%
Method: Correlational study using self-report questionnaires and standardized psychometric tests.
Participants completed a battery of instruments measuring:





























InstrumentWhat it measuredAIRS (American International Relations Scale)Level of acculturation (language use, cultural practices, social interactions)Family cohesion and adaptability scaleStrength of family structure and closenessAcculturative stress scaleLevel of psychological stress related to cultural adaptationCoping resources effectiveness scaleQuality and efficacy of strategies used to manage stressDemographic questionnaireAge, gender, nationality, length of US residence, language proficiency

Results:

Five predictor variables together explained acculturative stress in Latino immigrants:

Coping resources: Immigrants with effective coping strategies showed significantly less acculturative stress. Insufficient coping was the single largest predictor of acculturative stress.
Degree of acculturation: Higher acculturation (greater adoption of US cultural norms and language) was associated with lower stress.
Language use: Greater English proficiency and use was associated with lower acculturative stress. Spanish-only speakers showed significantly higher stress.
Family cohesion: Immigrants with stronger, more cohesive family structures experienced less stress.
Length of residence: Longer time in the US was associated with lower acculturative stress and higher acculturation levels.



Conclusion: Acculturative stress is not caused by a single factor but is shaped by multiple interacting socio-psychological variables. The findings support Berry’s (1990) assertion that acculturative stress is multifactorial. Protective factors (coping strategies, English proficiency, family cohesion, longer residence) buffer individuals against stress, while their absence constitutes risk. The study suggests that the closer an immigrant moves toward integration (engaging with the new culture while retaining family and identity), the less stress they experience.

Evaluation

































StrengthsLimitationsRandom sampling from social service agencies increases the representativeness of the sample within this populationCorrelational design: cannot establish cause-and-effect; acculturative stress may influence family cohesion rather than the reverseLarge sample (n=197) for a study of this type; includes multiple Latin American nationalities, widening scopeSelf-report questionnaires: vulnerable to social desirability bias; participants may underreport stress or overreport family closenessMultiple standardized instruments used; triangulation of measures increases construct validityWEIRD-adjacent limitation: recruited from social service agencies, so participants may already be more distressed or more engaged with support systems than the general immigrant populationGender-balanced sample (63% female, 37% male); findings are not androcentricResults may not generalize beyond Latino immigrants in the US; different cultural groups face different stressorsSupports and extends Berry’s (1990) multifactorial model of acculturative stressNo quantitative data reported for the length-of-residence finding, reducing precisionFindings have direct clinical and policy applications: identifying protective factors allows targeted interventionsRecruited from only two social service agencies, limiting geographic and demographic diversity within the Latino immigrant population

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Acculturation; Cultural influences on individual behaviour; Enculturation
Key Concept: Acculturative stress, protective factors, risk factors, coping strategies, family cohesion, Berry’s model
Useful for: “Discuss one study of acculturation” / “Evaluate research into acculturative stress” / “Discuss the effect of acculturation on behaviour” / “Explain one study of assimilation”
Paired with: Lueck and Wilson (2010) (same topic, different population: Asian Americans)
Linked theory: Berry’s (1990/2005) model of acculturation strategies


Comparison with Lueck & Wilson (2010)
Miranda & Matheny and Lueck & Wilson are the two core acculturation studies for IB. They are frequently used together and can be directly compared:













































FeatureMiranda & Matheny (2000)Lueck & Wilson (2010)PopulationLatino immigrantsAsian Americans (first and second generation)n1972,095MethodQuestionnaire / correlationalSemi-structured interview / correlationalKey protective factorsCoping strategies, English proficiency, family cohesion, length of residenceBilingual language preference, family cohesion, no discrimination, economic satisfactionKey risk factorInsufficient coping resourcesPerceived discriminationSupports Berry?YesYesSamplingRandom (2 agencies)Random (national database)
Both studies confirm that acculturative stress is multifactorial and that integration (engaging with the new culture while maintaining original identity and family ties) is more protective than assimilation. The key difference is that Lueck & Wilson explicitly finds that dropping the native language increases stress, while Miranda & Matheny finds that gaining English reduces stress — these are not contradictory but complementary: bilingualism is the optimal state.


Key Concept - Protective Factors in Acculturation:
Miranda & Matheny (2000) operationalizes Berry’s theoretical claim that acculturative stress is multifactorial. Rather than asking whether acculturation causes stress, it asks what makes stress more or less likely. The answer is that coping resources, language competence, family support, and time all interact to either buffer or amplify the difficulty of cultural adaptation. This shifts the clinical focus from the immigrant as a problem to the absence of support structures as the problem.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SCLT/Bandu.title: Bandura (1961), (1963) & (1965)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SCLT/Bandu.content:
study Sociocultural SCLT, Ethical considerations

Bandura conducted a series of Lab Experiments on children demonstrating that aggression can be learned through observation, forming the empirical foundation for Social Cognitive Learning Theory (SCLT).

Useful for: “Discuss social cognitive theory” / “Evaluate ethical considerations in psychological research” / “Discuss research methods in the study of the individual and the group”




                  
                  Note
                  
                

Core Principle of SCLT: Learning occurs not only through direct reward and punishment (behaviourism), but through observation and vicarious reinforcement, watching others being rewarded or punished for their behaviour.



Aim: To demonstrate that children who observe an adult model behaving aggressively towards a Bobo doll will imitate that aggression when given the opportunity, even without direct reward.
Bandura predicted:
- Children will imitate the behaviour of the models
- Children will imitate the behaviour of same-sex models to a greater degree
Participants: 72 children (36 boys, 36 girls) from Stanford University Nursery School, mean age 52 months (~4.3 years). One male and one female adult model were used.
Method: Lab experiment with independent groups design and matched pairs pre-testing. Groups were pre-matched on aggression levels based on nursery school teacher evaluations, to control for pre-existing aggression as a confounding variable. 3 main IVs:

Condition: aggressive model / non-aggressive model / no model (control)
Sex of the child
Sex of the model (same-sex vs. opposite-sex)

Group structure (8 experimental groups + control):



































Aggressive ModelNon-Aggressive ModelBoys - same-sex model66Boys - opposite-sex model66Girls - same-sex model66Girls - opposite-sex model66Control (no model)n/a24
Children were pre-tested to asses their aggressiveness. They were observed in a nursery and judge their behaviour on a 1-5 scale. Children were then match in each group so that they had similar levels of aggression
Procedure - Three Stages:
Stage 1 - Model exposure (10 minutes):

Child was taken to the room and settled in their play area with “high-interest” items (potato prints, stickers).
Adult model was escorted to the opposite corner with toys and a Bobo doll.
Non-aggressive condition: Model played quietly with the blocks, ignoring the Bobo doll.
Aggressive condition: After 1 minute, model turned to the Bobo doll and attacked it in a scripted, specific way: sitting on it, punching its nose, hitting it with a mallet, tossing it in the air, and using specific verbal phrases (“Sock him in the nose!”, “Hit him down!”, “Pow!”).

Stage 2 - Mild aggression arousal:

Child was taken to another room with very attractive toys, but after beginning to play, was told: “These are my best toys. I’m saving them for other children.”
This was designed to create mild frustration, to increase the likelihood of aggression being expressed.

Stage 3 - Test room (20 minutes):

Child was taken to a room containing both aggressive toys (Bobo doll, mallet, dart guns) and non-aggressive toys (tea set, crayons, toy cars).
Behaviour was observed through a one-way mirror and coded by raters.

Results:

Children in the aggressive condition showed significantly more imitative aggression than those in the non-aggressive or control conditions, both physical and verbal.
Boys imitated physical aggression more than girls overall.
Same-sex model effect: Boys imitated the male aggressive model more; girls showed more verbal aggression after observing the female model.
Children also showed non-imitative aggression: novel aggressive acts not modelled, suggesting generalised disinhibition, not just copying.

Conclusion: Aggression can be learned through observation without direct reinforcement. Children are more likely to imitate same-sex models and male models (who show more physical aggression). The study supports SCLT’s core claim that behaviour can be acquired through observational learning and vicarious reinforcement.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsControlled lab experiment: high internal validity; clear manipulation of IVsLow ecological validity: a Bobo doll is designed to be hit; children may not treat it as a real targetOperationalized aggression precisely: specific scripted acts, observed through one-way mirrorDemand characteristics: children may have perceived hitting Bobo as the expected behaviourResults were replicated in the 1963 and 1965 follow-up studiesEthical concerns: deliberately inducing aggression and frustration in young childrenFoundational for SCLT and media violence research (Joy et al., 1986)Does not measure long-term effects; laboratory aggression does not equal real-world violenceInfluenced media regulation, parenting theory, and educational practiceOnly measured imitation immediately after exposure; not long-term behaviour change

Follow-up Studies

















StudyKey AdditionBandura (1963)Compared live model vs. film vs. cartoon model; all produced similar aggression levelsBandura (1965)Added vicarious reinforcement conditions: children who saw the model punished showed less imitation, but equally when offered a reward for reproducing the acts, showing they had learned the behaviour but did not always perform it
The 1965 study introduced the important distinction between learning (acquisition) and performance, a key refinement of SCLT.

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural; Cognitive (observational learning)
Topic: Social Cognitive Learning Theory; Aggression; Ethics; Research methods
Key Concept: Observational learning, vicarious reinforcement, modelling, acquisition vs. performance
Useful for: “Evaluate SCLT” / “Discuss ethical considerations in developmental psychology research”
Paired with: Joy, Kimball & Zabrack (1986), Darley & Batson (1973)



Key Concept - Acquisition vs. Performance (Bandura, 1965):
Bandura’s 1965 follow-up showed that all children had learned the aggressive behaviour through observation, but only performed it when they expected a reward. This distinction between learning (cognitive acquisition of a behaviour) and performance (actually doing it) is crucial: it means exposure to media violence may teach aggressive scripts even if children do not immediately act aggressively.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SCLT/Joy,-.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SCLT/Joy, Kimball & Zabrack (1986) - Notel Natural Experiment.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SCLT/Joy,-.title: Joy, Kimball & Zabrack (1986) - Notel Natural Experiment
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SCLT/Joy,-.content:
study Sociocultural SCLT, Ethical considerations

Joy, Kimball and Zabrack conducted a Natural Experiment investigating the effect of television introduction on children’s aggressive behaviour in a real Canadian community, providing naturalistic evidence for Social Cognitive Learning Theory (SCLT) in a non-laboratory setting.

Aim: To investigate whether the introduction of television to a community that previously had no TV access would lead to increases in children’s aggressive behaviour, compared to communities that already had TV.
Participants: Children from three Canadian towns, studied longitudinally:

Notel (“no television”): A town that had never received TV reception due to geography, about to receive TV for the first time.
Unitel: A town with access to one TV channel.
Multitel: A town with access to multiple TV channels.

Method: Natural experiment with longitudinal observational and rating measures.

Phase 1 (baseline): Children’s aggressive behaviour was measured before Notel received TV, and at the same time in Unitel and Multitel as comparison points.
Phase 2 (follow-up, 2 years later): The same measures were taken after Notel had received TV for 2 years.
Measures of aggression:

Direct observation of children in the playground (physical and verbal aggression coded)
Peer ratings of aggression
Teacher ratings of aggression



Results:

Notel: Children’s observed physical aggression increased by approximately 160% after 2 years of TV access, a dramatic and statistically significant rise.
Unitel and Multitel: No significant increase in aggression over the same period.
Increases in aggression were found for both boys and girls, and for both physical and verbal aggression.
There was no significant difference in favourite shows between more and less aggressive children, suggesting it was general TV exposure, not specific violent content, that mattered.
Males were more physically aggressive than females overall.

Interpretation:

The most likely explanation was observational learning (SCLT): children in Notel learned new aggressive scripts and behaviours from TV models.
An alternative interpretation was arousal: novelty of TV may have heightened general arousal, leading to increased aggression. However, this alone does not explain the sustained 2-year increase.

Conclusion: The introduction of television caused a significant increase in children’s aggressive behaviour, providing strong naturalistic support for SCLT, that aggression is learned through observation of media models.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsNatural experiment: high ecological validity; behaviour observed in real-world settingsCannot fully control all variables that changed in Notel over the 2 years alongside TV introductionLongitudinal design tracks real change over time in the same communityAttrition: some children may have been lost to follow-up, affecting comparabilityMultiple measures (observation, peer ratings, teacher ratings) provide method triangulationThe towns were not identical; pre-existing cultural or demographic differences may have influenced resultsControl communities (Unitel, Multitel) provide a strong comparative baselineCannot determine which types of TV content drove the increase; general TV vs. specifically violent programmingConsistent with Bandura (1961/63/65) laboratory findings; supports SCLT in a naturalistic contextResearchers’ coding of aggressive behaviour may have been subjective

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Cognitive Learning Theory; Media and behaviour; Aggression
Key Concept: Observational learning, media violence, naturalistic research, SCLT
Useful for: “Evaluate SCLT” / “Discuss the influence of media on behaviour” / “Evaluate natural experiments in psychology”
Paired with: Bandura (1961/63/65), Darley & Batson (1973)



Key Concept - Natural Experiment:
A natural experiment is a study where the independent variable occurs naturally, without manipulation by the researcher. Joy et al. (1986) is a textbook example: the “treatment” (TV introduction) happened independently of the researchers, who simply took advantage of the situation to measure its effects. This gives the study high ecological validity but limits experimental control.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Abrams et al (1990) - Asch paradigm.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Abrams et al (1990) - Asch paradigm
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study SIT Conformity, Social Identity Theory

This note covers both Asch’s original conformity paradigm (1951) and Abrams et al.’s (1990) extension, which introduced Social Identity Theory as an explanation for when and why conformity occurs.

Part 1: Asch (1951) - The Line Judgment Paradigm
Aim: To investigate the extent to which social pressure from a majority group influences an individual to conform, even when the correct answer is obvious.
Participants: 50 male college students who believed they were participating in a “vision test.”
Method: Lab experiment.

Participants were placed in groups of 7-9 people, of whom all but one were confederates.
They were shown a standard line and asked to match it to one of three comparison lines; the correct answer was always obvious.
After several correct trials, confederates began giving unanimous incorrect answers.
The real participant always answered second to last, hearing the majority’s wrong answer before giving their own.

Results:

On critical trials, 32% of responses were conforming (incorrect).
75% of participants conformed at least once across 18 critical trials.
25% never conformed at all.
In a control condition (no confederates), error rate was less than 1%.

Conclusion: Social pressure from a unanimous majority causes a significant proportion of people to give answers they know to be wrong, demonstrating normative social influence (conforming to be accepted) and possibly informational social influence (doubting one’s own judgement).

Part 2: Abrams et al. (1990) - SIT Extension of Asch
Aim: To investigate whether social identity (in-group vs. out-group status of the confederates) moderates conformity, as predicted by Social Identity Theory.
Participants: Psychology students at the University of Dundee.
Method: Lab experiment with 2x2 independent groups design.
Two IVs:

Group membership of confederates: In-group (fellow psychology students) vs. out-group (ancient history students)
Visibility of response: Public vs. private

Results:

77% conformed at least once overall.
Conformity was highest in the in-group public condition: participants conformed most when the majority were fellow in-group members and their response was visible.
Conformity was lowest in the out-group condition: participants resisted influence from out-group members.
There was no significant difference between out-group public and private conditions, suggesting conformity to out-groups is avoided regardless of visibility.

Conclusion: Conformity is not simply about majority pressure; it is moderated by social identity. People conform to in-group norms to maintain group membership and social identity, but resist influence from out-groups. This supports SIT’s claim that group membership shapes social behaviour.

Evaluation (Abrams et al.)





























StrengthsLimitationsExtends Asch by adding a theoretically motivated IV (in-group vs. out-group)Lab setting: artificial task; conformity in real social contexts may differProvides empirical support for SIT in a controlled experimental designSample: psychology students from one university; low generalizabilityStandardized procedure with high replicabilityThe in-group/out-group manipulation may not have been equally salient for all participantsClearly demonstrates that conformity is socially motivated, not just perceptualOnly tests conformity to majority; does not address minority influenceConsistent with Tajfel & Turner’s (1979) theoretical frameworkResults may reflect demand characteristics in the public conditions

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Identity Theory; Conformity; Group dynamics
Key Concept: Normative social influence, informational social influence, in-group conformity, SIT
Useful for: “Discuss the role of social identity in group behaviour” / “Evaluate research on conformity”
Paired with: Tajfel (1971), Sherif et al. (1954), Zimbardo (1971)



Key Concept - Normative vs. Informational Social Influence:
Normative influence: conforming to be liked and accepted, even while privately disagreeing. Informational influence: conforming because you genuinely doubt your own judgement and believe the group may be right. Asch’s paradigm produces primarily normative influence; participants knew the group was wrong but went along anyway. Abrams et al. shows that this effect is strongest with in-group members, because acceptance by the in-group matters more to social identity.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Darley & Batson (1973) - Good samaritan.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Darley & Batson (1973) - Good samaritan
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study SIT Ethical considerations, Experiments

John Darley and Daniel Batson conducted a Field Experiment investigating whether situational factors (specifically time pressure) rather than dispositional factors (such as religiosity or moral concern) determine whether people help someone in need.

Aim: To investigate whether the degree of hurry a person is in (situational variable) affects helping behaviour, and whether the topic of a speech they had just prepared (moral priming) has any effect, testing situational vs. dispositional explanations of prosocial behaviour.
Participants: 40 seminary students (students training to be ministers) at Princeton Theological Seminary, all confirmed to be religious, controlling for dispositional religiosity.
Method: Field experiment with independent groups design.
Two independent variables:

Speech topic (dispositional prime):

Half prepared a speech on the Good Samaritan (Biblical parable about helping)
Half prepared a speech on job opportunities for seminary graduates


Degree of hurry (situational variable):

Low hurry: “You have plenty of time, head over now.”
Medium hurry: “You’re right on time, head over now.”
High hurry: “You’re late, they’re expecting you.”



Procedure:

Participants were sent across campus to deliver their speech in another building.
Along the route, they encountered a confederate slumped in a doorway, coughing and groaning, appearing to be in distress.
Whether the participant stopped to help (and the quality of help) was recorded as the DV.

Results:





















Condition% Who HelpedLow hurry63%Medium hurry45%High hurry10%

Speech topic had no significant effect: even those who had just prepared the Good Samaritan speech often walked past without helping when in a hurry.
Some participants in the high-hurry condition literally stepped over the confederate.

Conclusion: Situational factors, specifically time pressure, were the dominant predictor of helping behaviour, overriding dispositional factors like religiosity and even moral priming. This challenges the assumption that prosocial behaviour is driven primarily by personality or values.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsHigh ecological validity: real campus setting, real confederate in distressEthical concerns: confederate feigned distress; participants were deceived and not fully debriefed until laterControlled variables (all seminarians, same confederate, same location) increase internal validitySample: seminary students are not representative of the general populationClearly demonstrates the power of situation over moral dispositionParticipants may have noticed the same person on different occasions, creating potential awareness issuesResults are counterintuitive and compelling; even Good Samaritan speech-givers often did not helpOnly measures a binary helping decision; does not capture quality or nature of help offeredConsistent with Zimbardo’s findings on situational power over behaviourCannot fully rule out demand characteristics in some conditions

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Identity Theory; Prosocial behaviour; Situational vs. dispositional explanations
Key Concept: Situational attribution, prosocial behaviour, time pressure, bystander effect
Useful for: “Discuss situational explanations of human behaviour” / “Evaluate research on prosocial behaviour”
Paired with: Drury et al. (2009), Zimbardo (1971), Sherif et al. (1954)



Key Concept - Situational vs. Dispositional Explanations:
Dispositional explanations attribute behaviour to internal characteristics (personality, values, beliefs). Situational explanations attribute behaviour to external context (time pressure, social norms, environment). Darley & Batson (1973) powerfully demonstrates that even people with strong prosocial values will fail to help when situational demands are pressing, a profound challenge to moral consistency assumptions.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Drury et al (2009) - SIT and helping in Emergencies.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Drury et al (2009) - SIT and helping in Emergencies
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study VR SIT Ethical considerations, Social Identity Theory

John Drury et al. conducted a Lab Experiment using Virtual Reality investigating whether shared social identity increases prosocial (helping) behaviour during a simulated emergency, overcoming the ethical barriers of studying real disasters.

Background - Levine et al. (2005):
A related study tested in-group bias on helping with 45 male Manchester United fans. A confederate fell and cried out in pain wearing either a Manchester United shirt, a Liverpool FC shirt, or a plain shirt. Participants were most likely to help the Manchester United fan and least likely to help the Liverpool or plain-shirt wearer, showing that in-group membership, not general goodwill, drives helping.
Aim: To investigate the role of social identity and group categorization in prosocial (helping) behaviour during a simulated emergency.
Participants: 40 University of Sussex students, aged 20-25.
Method: Lab experiment using VR with independent groups design.

Priming: Participants read a report about a deadly fire and imagined sensory details to increase psychological realism.
Scenario: Participants were presented with a VR simulation of a fire emergency in the London Underground and had to escape while deciding whether to help or push others.
Group identification condition: Participants were told they were part of a group of England football supporters returning from a match.
Individual identification condition: Participants were told they were just individuals returning home.
The size of the crowd in the VR simulation was either 8 or 32 people (this had no significant effect on results).

Results:

Participants in the group identification condition provided significantly more help to others and pushed fewer people than those in the individual identification condition.
A shared social identity increased the likelihood of prosocial behaviour in an emergency: when people perceive themselves as part of a collective, they are more likely to act for the benefit of the group rather than just themselves.

Conclusion: Group identity plays a significant role in promoting prosocial behaviour during emergencies. Social categorization shapes whether people help or prioritize self-preservation.

Evaluation

























StrengthsLimitationsEthically sound: VR allowed researchers to study a high-stakes emergency without putting participants in real dangerHighly artificial: participants are aware they are in a simulation; genuine fight-or-flight panic cannot be replicatedHigh internal validity: controlled VR environment allows researchers to isolate social identity as the cause of helping behaviourDemand characteristics: participants may have guessed the aim after reading the fire report, or treated the simulation as a gameMundane realism: VR provides a more immersive experience than text-based scenarios, leading to more authentic behavioural dataGeneralizability: sample limited to University of Sussex students; their behaviour may not represent how different demographics would reactSupports Social Identity Theory in a prosocial contextCrowd size manipulation had no effect, which was unexpected and limits interpretation

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Identity Theory; Prosocial behaviour; Ethics in research; VR methodology
Key Concept: Social identity, group categorization, prosocial behaviour, in-group bias, VR as a research method
Useful for: “Discuss the role of social identity in group behaviour” / “Evaluate the use of VR in psychological research” / “Discuss prosocial behaviour”
Paired with: Darley & Batson (1973), Tajfel (1971), Sherif et al. (1954)



Key Concept - Social Identity and Helping:
Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) predicts that we are more likely to help members of our in-group because their welfare is tied to our own social identity. Drury et al. (2009) confirms this in an emergency context: shared group identity transforms a crowd of individuals into a collective that looks out for each other, with significant implications for emergency management and evacuation planning.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Festinger (1956) - UFO Cult
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study SIT  Observations, Ethical considerations

Festinger carried out a Participant Naturalistic Observation with the aim of studying cognitive dissonance within a small UFO doomsday cult called “the seekers”.

Cult Members believed a great flood was approaching and only “true believers” would be rescued.
Festinger wanted to study the reaction of people in the cult after finding their belief (Doomsday event) was in fact not true; and the foot-in-door paradigm (studies the level of commitment exhibited by members).

Aim: Festinger wanted to find out how the members of the cult would cope when they realized that this apocalyptic event did not happen.
The goal of the observations was to determine the degree to which each member was convinced of the truth of the belief system. Foot-in-the-door paradigm; level of commitment exhibited by members.
The theory was that the more of a commitment they had made, the less likely they were to change their behavior, even despite a major disappointment.
Participants: UFO cult “the seekers”
Procedure: Covert participant naturalistic observation.
- Festinger learned about the prophecy via a news paper and train a team of 8 observers for a month
- The cult was located in two homes
- Observers pretended to be true believers
- Observers were students or staff members in the department of psychology and had experience in interviewing and observation techniques
- Observes documented what actions had and would be taken as the flood approached
-
Results: According to Festinger, they rationalized the situation in a way that maintained their sense of self-esteem.
Cognitive dissonance; they invested so much into this belief,  that the predictions turning out to be wrong, led to extreme anxiety. One way to alleviate this anxiety was to justify their behavior (accepting the message given by their leader).
Evaluation:
- There are concerns with regard to the observation as there was no regular pattern of activities, and the participants didn’t live in the cult houses. They only attended meetings there.
- The observers were not informed until only a few days before the meetings would take place.
- Taking notes was vary difficult and they would have to rely on memory 3-4h after the meetings.
- The study was the first of its type
- Supported theory on Cognitive dissonance
- Ethical concern; Trust
- Stories told by observers to gain access to the cult, validated their beliefs + participant observations may allow the observer to influence participants behaviour.
- Observers reported having other duties, mental and physical fatigue, which may have affected the way data was recorded
- No standardized tool of assessment / No measurement of strength of beliefs a few days before/after the event



Cognitive dissonance
“People aft according to their beliefs and then change their beliefs to fit their actions”

Transclude of Cognitive-Dissonance

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Piliavin et al. (1969) - Subway Samaritan.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Piliavin et al. (1969) - Subway Samaritan
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study HRelations Sociocultural Ethical considerations, Social Identity Theory

Irving Piliavin, Judith Rodin and Jane Piliavin conducted a Field Experiment investigating helping behaviour on the New York City subway, examining how situational factors such as type of victim, race, and the presence of a model influence whether bystanders intervene. The study directly challenged the diffusion of responsibility hypothesis.

Background: Following Darley & Latané’s laboratory demonstrations of the bystander effect, Piliavin et al. moved research into a naturalistic setting to test whether diffusion of responsibility would hold in a face-to-face, unavoidable emergency. They proposed the Arousal: Cost-Reward Model as an alternative explanation for helping behaviour.
Aim: To investigate the effect of type of victim (ill vs. drunk), race of victim, and presence of a model on the speed and frequency of helping behaviour in a real-world setting.
Participants: Approximately 4,450 passengers on New York City subway trains travelling between Harlem and the Bronx on weekdays between 11:00am and 3:00pm. Opportunity sample; approximately 45% Black, 55% white. Around 43 passengers per carriage, with approximately 8.5 in the critical area near the victim.
Method: Field experiment with independent groups design.

Four research teams of 4 confederates each (2 male, 2 female) conducted 103 trials on trains that did not stop between two stations, giving a 7.5-minute journey window.
After approximately 70 seconds into the journey, the male confederate victim collapsed and lay on the floor.
Independent variables:

Type of victim: either carrying a cane (ill, appearing physically disabled) or smelling of alcohol and carrying a bottle in a paper bag (drunk)
Race of victim: Black or white confederate
Model behaviour: whether a second confederate helped early (70 seconds) or late (150 seconds), and whether they stood in the critical or adjacent area


Dependent variables: time taken for a passenger to help, total number of helpers, race and sex of helpers, verbal comments made.
Two female confederates recorded observations from seats in the carriage.

Results:

Cane condition: spontaneous help given on 95% of trials (62/65); median time to help: 5 seconds.
Drunk condition: spontaneous help given on 50% of trials (19/38); slower response.
No diffusion of responsibility effect: group size did not significantly reduce helping in the cane condition; more bystanders sometimes meant more help, not less.
Race effects: in the cane condition, race of victim had little effect. In the drunk condition, there was more same-race helping.
Modelling: when a model helped early, others were more likely to follow.
As time passed without help in the drunk condition, some bystanders moved away from the area.

Conclusion: Helping behaviour in face-to-face emergencies is primarily determined by the costs and rewards of helping, not by diffusion of responsibility. An ill victim (low cost of helping, high social approval) receives near-universal help. A drunk victim (higher cost: possible violence, vomiting, embarrassment) receives less. Piliavin et al. proposed the Arousal: Cost-Reward Model: witnessing an emergency creates arousal which motivates action, and the chosen response depends on a rapid cost-benefit calculation.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsHigh ecological validity: real subway, real bystanders, genuine unscripted behaviourSerious ethical concerns: no informed consent, no right to withdraw, no debriefing; participants may have experienced distress from witnessing or failing to helpLarge sample (~4,450 passengers) increases representativeness within the NYC subway populationCannot control extraneous variables: passenger density, temperature, prior experiences on the journeyInter-rater reliability: two independent observers cross-checked dataLimited generalizability: NYC subway passengers are not representative of all populations; results may differ in rural, less urban settingsDirectly challenges diffusion of responsibility theory in a real-world settingSome participants may have encountered the same trial more than once if they used that route regularlyProvides the Arousal: Cost-Reward Model as a theoretically grounded alternative explanationDeceit was inherent to the design; ethical standards today would prevent this study from being run

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural; Biological (arousal)
Topic: Prosocial behaviour; Bystanderism; Social responsibility; Ethical considerations
Key Concept: Arousal: Cost-Reward Model, bystanderism, diffusion of responsibility, situational factors in helping, field experiment
Useful for: “Discuss bystanderism” / “Discuss prosocial behaviour” / “Evaluate research on factors affecting helping” / “Discuss ethical considerations in the study of social responsibility”
Paired with: Darley & Batson (1973) - Good samaritan, Drury et al (2009) - SIT and helping in Emergencies



Key Concept - Arousal: Cost-Reward Model:
Piliavin et al. proposed that witnessing an emergency generates psychological arousal (discomfort, distress). This arousal motivates the bystander to act, but the specific action chosen depends on a rapid mental calculation: what are the costs and rewards of helping vs. not helping? A cane victim presents low costs (physically manageable, socially approved) and high rewards (reduced arousal, social approval), producing near-universal help. A drunk victim presents higher costs (possible violence, embarrassment), tipping the calculation toward inaction or avoidance. Crucially, this model predicts that diffusion of responsibility will be weaker in face-to-face settings where the costs of inaction (sustained arousal, moral discomfort) are also high.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Sherif et al (1954) - Robbers cave.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Sherif et al (1954) - Robbers cave
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study SIT Ethical considerations, Social Identity Theory

Muzafer Sherif et al. conducted a Field Experiment investigating how intergroup conflict develops between groups and whether it can be reduced through superordinate goals, cooperative tasks requiring intergroup collaboration to achieve a shared outcome.

Aim: To investigate (1) whether intergroup conflict would naturally emerge between two groups of boys given competitive conditions, and (2) whether superordinate goals could reduce that conflict.
Participants: 22 white, middle-class, Protestant boys aged 11-12 from Oklahoma City, USA. All were strangers to each other, psychologically well-adjusted, and matched across groups for ability and background. Parents were not told the full nature of the study.
Method: Field experiment at Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma, a summer camp setting.
Three phases:
Phase 1 - In-group formation (1 week):

The boys were divided into two groups (later named the Eagles and the Rattlers), kept completely separate.
Each group bonded through cooperative activities: hiking, camping, swimming.
Both groups developed group norms, hierarchies, and names spontaneously.

Phase 2 - Intergroup conflict (1 week):

The two groups were brought into direct competition through a tournament (baseball, tug-of-war, etc.), with prizes only for the winning group.
Researchers observed the development of:

In-group favouritism: strong loyalty and positive stereotypes of their own group
Out-group hostility: name-calling, raiding each other’s cabins, burning the rival’s flag
Clear derogatory stereotyping of the out-group (“sneaky,” “cheats”)



Phase 3 - Conflict reduction (1 week):

Contact alone (eating together, watching films) did NOT reduce hostility; it actually increased tension.
Only superordinate goals, tasks requiring the two groups to work together (e.g., fixing the camp’s water supply, pulling a stalled truck), successfully reduced conflict and led to cross-group friendships.

Results:

Intergroup competition reliably produced hostility, stereotyping, and discrimination between the groups.
Superordinate goals progressively reduced hostility and led to spontaneous intergroup friendship by the end of Phase 3.
Supports the view that conflict arises from competition over resources (Realistic Conflict Theory), not pre-existing prejudice.

Conclusion: Intergroup conflict can develop rapidly between groups placed in competition, even without prior hostility. It can be reduced not through simple contact but through cooperation toward shared goals, with real-world implications for reducing prejudice and ethnic conflict.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsHigh ecological validity: real camp setting; behaviour was natural and spontaneousSerious ethical concerns: boys were deceived; aggression was deliberately induced without full parental consentRich qualitative data: detailed observations of real social dynamicsSampling bias: all-white, middle-class, Protestant boys from one city; very low generalizabilityClear demonstration of both conflict formation and reduction in the same studyResearchers intervened at multiple points; difficult to isolate a single IVSupports Realistic Conflict Theory and Social Identity TheoryThe study has been criticized for being staged; Sherif may have interfered more than reportedLongitudinal field design tracks real behavioural change over timeCannot replicate exactly; unique setting, specific sample

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Identity Theory; Group dynamics; Prejudice and discrimination
Key Concept: In-group favouritism, out-group hostility, superordinate goals, Realistic Conflict Theory
Useful for: “Discuss the formation of in-group and out-group behaviour” / “Evaluate methods used to reduce prejudice”
Paired with: Tajfel (1971), Zimbardo (1971), Darley & Batson (1973)



Key Concept - Superordinate Goals:
A superordinate goal is an objective that is compelling for both groups but cannot be achieved by either group alone, requiring cooperation. Sherif et al. showed that contact alone does not reduce prejudice (and may increase it), but working together toward a shared goal does. This has been applied to school desegregation programmes (e.g., the Jigsaw Classroom technique).

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Tajfel (1971) - Klee or Kandinsky.md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Tajfel (1971) - Klee or Kandinsky
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study SIT Minimal Group Paradigm, Social Identity Theory

Tajfel conducted a Lab Experiment demonstrating that social categorization alone, with no history of conflict, competition, or personal interaction, is sufficient to produce in-group favouritism and out-group discrimination. This became the foundation for Social Identity Theory (SIT).

Aim: To investigate whether a minimally significant group is sufficient to produce discrimination against an out-group and favouritism toward an in-group.
Participants: 48 schoolboys aged 14-15 from a school in Bristol, UK, all of whom knew each other before the study.
Method: Lab experiment using the Minimal Group Paradigm.
Procedure:


Categorization: Boys were shown paintings by Kandinsky and Klee and asked which they preferred. They were then told they had been assigned to a group based on their preference (Klee group or Kandinsky group). They did not know which artist painted which work, making the grouping essentially meaningless. (Minimal group paradigm)


Point allocation task: Each boy was given a booklet of matrices and asked to allocate points to pairs of other boys, one from his group and one from the other. They were never allocating points to themselves.


Three allocation strategies were available:

Maximum Joint Profit (MJP): Give both boys as many points as possible
Maximum In-Group Profit (MIP): Give the in-group member as many points as possible regardless of the out-group’s score
Maximum Differentiation (MD): Give the in-group member more points than the out-group member, even if this means sacrificing overall points for both



Results:

Boys rarely chose Maximum Joint Profit; they did not try to maximize overall points.
The dominant strategy was Maximum Differentiation: boys sacrificed total points in order to ensure their in-group member received relatively more than the out-group member.
This occurred even though the groups were meaningless, temporary, and anonymous.

Conclusion: The Minimal Group Paradigm demonstrates that social categorization alone is sufficient to produce discrimination. People do not need real conflict, history, or personal stakes to favor their in-group over an out-group; mere awareness of group membership triggers in-group favoritism. This is the empirical basis for Social Identity Theory.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsHigh internal validity: controlled lab setting isolates social categorization as the sole IVLow ecological validity: artificial task (point matrices) does not reflect real-world discriminationReplicable: the MGP has been replicated with many different populations and group criteriaDemand characteristics: boys may have treated the task as a competition or game (“screw-you effect”)Foundational for Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979)Sample of teenage boys from one school; low generalizability to other ages, cultures, gendersShows discrimination emerges from categorization, not competition or prejudiceCannot explain why categorization leads to favouritism; SIT offers the theoretical explanationElegant minimal design; clearly demonstrates the phenomenon with few confoundsThe point allocation system was complex; some boys may not have fully understood the trade-offs

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Identity Theory; Group dynamics; Prejudice and discrimination
Key Concept: Minimal Group Paradigm, social categorization, in-group favouritism, out-group discrimination
Useful for: “Discuss Social Identity Theory” / “Evaluate research on prejudice and discrimination”
Paired with: Sherif et al. (1954), Abrams et al. (1990), Zimbardo (1971)



Key Concept - Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979):
SIT proposes that part of our self-concept (social identity) is derived from our membership in social groups. To maintain positive social identity, we favour our in-group and derogate out-groups, not because of real conflicts, but simply because group membership matters to our sense of self. Tajfel (1971) provides the empirical foundation: even trivial, arbitrary group membership triggers this tendency.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.filePath: Studies/Sociocultural Studies/SIT Studies/Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment (1971).md
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.title: Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment (1971)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/SIT-Studie.content:
Study SIT Role-Based Behaviour, Ethical considerations

Philip Zimbardo conducted a Simulation Study investigating how social roles and situational factors influence behaviour, demonstrating that ordinary people can rapidly adopt extreme behaviours when placed in a role-defined social structure.

Aim: To investigate whether participants would conform to the social roles of prisoner and guard in a simulated prison environment, and whether situational rather than dispositional factors would drive their behaviour.
Participants: 24 male college students (emotionally stable, psychologically healthy, screened via personality tests), randomly assigned to roles:

Guards (11 participants): Given uniforms, mirrored sunglasses, batons, and told to maintain order.
Prisoners (10 participants): “Arrested” at home by real police, processed, given smocks and numbers, deindividuated.
A small number were alternates who were not used.

Method: Simulation/role-playing study, not a true experiment (no independent variable was systematically manipulated).

A mock prison was set up in the basement of Stanford University’s psychology department.
The study was planned to last 2 weeks.
Zimbardo himself took the role of Prison Superintendent, which has been criticized for compromising his objectivity.

Results:

Within days, guards became increasingly authoritarian, dehumanizing, and abusive: forcing prisoners to do push-ups, denying toilet privileges, staging humiliating roll-calls at night.
Prisoners became passive, distressed, and depressed; 3 were released early due to severe emotional breakdown.
Participants appeared to fully internalize their roles, losing sight of their real identities.
The study was stopped after 6 days (not 2 weeks) when Zimbardo’s colleague Christina Maslach observed the conditions and objected strongly.

Conclusion: Situational factors and assigned roles can powerfully shape behaviour, sometimes overriding personal values. The situation rather than individual personality largely determined how both guards and prisoners behaved.


Later Reinterpretation - SIT Perspective (Reicher & Haslam, 2006):
The BBC Prison Study (2001) replicated a similar scenario and found that groups did not inevitably become abusive; behaviour depended on group identity and leadership. Reicher & Haslam argued that Zimbardo’s results reflected social identity dynamics (guards actively identifying with their role and enforcing it) rather than automatic role conformity. This suggests the situation does not determine behaviour mechanically: group identity and active identification are key mediators.


Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsHigh mundane realism: participants appeared to genuinely internalize their rolesSerious ethical violations: no right to withdraw was honoured; psychological harm was caused; deception was usedDemonstrates the power of situation over dispositionZimbardo played the role of Superintendent, creating a lack of objectivity; he may have encouraged guard aggressionHighly influential: shaped thinking on obedience, prisons, and dehumanizationCannot generalize: volunteer sample, artificial setting, American college men onlyRelevant to understanding prison reform, torture, and war atrocitiesNot a true experiment; no control group; many confounding variablesSupported by real-world parallels (Abu Ghraib)Recent reanalysis (Le Texier, 2018) revealed Zimbardo coached guards to act tough, undermining the “spontaneous” claim

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural
Topic: Social Identity Theory; Role-based behaviour; Situational vs. dispositional explanations
Key Concept: Social roles, deindividuation, situational attribution, simulation methodology
Useful for: “Discuss situational vs. dispositional explanations of behaviour” / “Evaluate ethical considerations in social psychology research”
Paired with: Sherif et al. (1954), Tajfel (1971), Darley & Batson (1973)



Key Concept - Situational vs. Dispositional Attribution:
Zimbardo’s study challenges the fundamental attribution error, the tendency to explain others’ behaviour through personality rather than situation. His finding that ordinary, psychologically healthy students became abusive guards suggests that the situation (role, uniform, power structure) was the primary driver of behaviour. However, more recent critiques show the picture is more complex: guards were coached, and social identity (active identification with a role) matters more than passive role assignment.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Stereotype.title: Hamilton & Gifford (1976)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Stereotype.content:
Study Sociocultural Stereotypes, Heuristics - Schema Theory

Hamilton and Gifford conducted a Lab Experiment demonstrating that illusory correlation can cause stereotypes to form purely through cognitive mechanisms, without any prior prejudice or real group differences.
Background: An illusory correlation is the tendency to perceive a relationship between two variables when none exists. It is rooted in the availability heuristic (System 1 thinking): when minority group membership and negative behaviour are both statistically rare, their co-occurrence is distinctive and disproportionately memorable, leading people to overestimate the association.
Aim: To investigate whether a distinctiveness-based illusory correlation can produce stereotypic beliefs about a minority group in the absence of any real difference between groups.
Participants: 40 American undergraduates (20 male, 20 female).
Method: Lab experiment with repeated measures design.

Participants were shown slides describing behaviours performed by members of two fictional groups:

Group A: 26 members (majority)
Group B: 13 members (minority)


Behaviours were either desirable or undesirable, in the same ratio for both groups:
























DesirableUndesirableTotalGroup A18826Group B9413

Afterwards, participants rated each group on positive and negative traits and estimated how many undesirable behaviours each group had performed.

Results:

Participants recalled more positive traits for Group A (74%) than Group B (54%).
Participants recalled more negative traits for Group B (65%) than Group A (55%).
Group B was rated more negatively overall, despite the two groups being objectively identical in their ratio of positive to negative behaviours.

Conclusion: Stereotypes can form through purely cognitive mechanisms. The co-occurrence of minority group membership and negative behaviour was disproportionately salient, leading participants to develop a negative stereotype of Group B with no real basis.
Link to question: This demonstrates the cognitive formation of stereotypes through the illusory correlation heuristic, without prejudice, conflict, or social learning.


Key Concept - Illusory Correlation:
When two things are both rare, their co-occurrence is cognitively salient and easier to recall, making it feel as though they are related even when they are not. This is sufficient to produce negative stereotypes about minority groups from statistical rarity alone.

Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Stereotype.title: Steele and Aronson (1995)
Studies/Sociocultural-Studies/Stereotype.content:
Study Sociocultural Stereotypes, Social Identity Theory

Steele and Aronson conducted a Lab Experiment investigating stereotype threat, the phenomenon where awareness of a negative stereotype about one’s social group impairs performance on tasks relevant to that stereotype.

Aim: To investigate whether making Black students aware of a racial stereotype about intellectual ability would negatively affect their performance on a standardized verbal test, compared to when the test was not framed in a stereotype-threatening way.
Participants: 114 male and female Black and White undergraduates from Stanford University. SAT verbal scores were collected prior to the study to ensure all participants were within the norm of verbal performance, minimizing participant variability.
Method: Lab experiment with independent groups design.

All participants completed a standardized test of verbal ability, similar to the SAT.
There were two independent variables:

Race of the participant (Black or White)
Test framing (diagnostic vs. non-diagnostic)


Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions with equal numbers in each:

Stereotype threat condition (diagnostic): Told the test was a measure of intellectual ability, activating the stereotype that Black students perform worse academically.
Non-threat condition (non-diagnostic): Told the test was a problem-solving task, with no implications for intellectual ability.


Performance scores were compared across conditions and racial groups.
There was no significant difference between male and female participants, so gender was not included in the analysis.

Results:

In the stereotype threat condition, Black students performed significantly worse than White students of equivalent SAT scores.
In the non-threat condition, the performance gap between Black and White students virtually disappeared; Black students performed equally well to White students.
White students’ performance was not significantly affected by the framing.

Conclusion: Mere awareness of a negative stereotype about one’s group is sufficient to impair cognitive performance, a phenomenon Steele & Aronson termed stereotype threat. The threat is proposed to consume cognitive resources (attention, working memory) needed for the task, reducing performance. However, this mechanism was not directly measured in this first variation of the experiment.

Evaluation





























StrengthsLimitationsControlled lab experiment: random assignment to conditions establishes cause-and-effect between framing and performanceStanford student sample: not representative of all Black Americans; limits generalizabilitySAT score screening minimizes participant variability in prior verbal abilityIndependent samples design: a matched-pairs design may have been a better approach to control for individual differencesHas been widely replicated across many groups (women in maths, elderly in memory tasks)Stereotype threat was not directly measured in this first variation: racial identity salience and stress levels during the exam were not assessed; the performance difference alone does not confirm stereotype threat was the mechanismHighly impactful in education, policy, and social psychologyDemand characteristics: participants may have inferred the study’s purpose from the framingHighlights how social identity and stereotypes affect cognitive performanceEffect size varies across replications; some meta-analyses find smaller effects than the original study

IB Connections

Approach: Sociocultural; Cognitive (cognitive load, working memory)
Topic: Stereotypes; Social identity; Cultural influences on behaviour and cognition
Key Concept: Stereotype threat, social identity, cognitive load, in-group/out-group
Useful for: “Discuss the effects of stereotypes on behaviour” / “Evaluate sociocultural explanations of cognitive performance”
Paired with: Hamilton & Gifford (1976), Tajfel (1971) - Klee or Kandinsky



Key Concept - Stereotype Threat:
Stereotype threat occurs when an individual is in a situation where they risk confirming a negative stereotype about their social group. This awareness creates psychological pressure that is proposed to divert cognitive resources away from the task, reducing performance. Critically, the threat does not require the individual to personally believe the stereotype; awareness of its existence is sufficient. However, Steele & Aronson (1995) did not directly measure stereotype threat in this first variation; later variations of the experiment confirmed the mechanism.
